stem: A14-year-old African American girl has her right breast removed because of a large mass. The tumor weighs 1400 g and has a bulging, very firm, lobulated surface with a whorl-like pattern, as illustrated here. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fibroadenomas are well-demarcated and firm and can be large in young African American girls.
_raw_ans: 38. d. Fibroadenoma Fibroadenomas are well-demarcated and firm and can be large in young African American girls.

stem: A33-year-old pregnant woman notices a persistent, painless lump in the left breast. On examination the left breast has a single mobile mass without evidence of skin changes or lymphadenopathy in the neck or axilla. An ultrasound demonstrates a solid, 1-cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. A core-needle biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma. The patient is in her first trimester of pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
options: Termination of the pregnancy followed by total mastectomy
Immediate administration of chemotherapy followed by modified radical mastectomy after delivery of the baby
Segmental mastectomy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and adjuvant radiation therapy shortly after surgery
Total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
explanation: Immediate surgery, such as total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy, is recommended during the first trimester.
_raw_ans: 39. d. Total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy Immediate surgery, such as total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy, is recommended during the first trimester.

stem: A40-year-old woman presents with a rash involving the nipple-areola complex for the last month with associated itching. On physical examination there is crusting and ulceration of the nipple with surrounding erythema involving the areola and surrounding skin, no palpable breast masses, and no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Corticosteroid cream to the affected area
Mammogram and biopsy of the affected area
explanation: This patient has Paget disease of the breast and needs a mammogram and biopsy to confirm and manage accordingly.
_raw_ans: 40. d. Mammogram and biopsy of the affected area This patient has Paget disease of the breast and needs a mammogram and biopsy to confirm and manage accordingly.

stem: A35-year-old female has a 6-month history of a 2-cm breast mass which was biopsied and consistent with a fibroadenoma. She now comes into the office reporting that the mass has rapidly enlarged and is now 10 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this lesion?
options: Wide local excision with a rim of normal tissue
Excision, postoperative radiotherapy, and systemic chemotherapy
explanation: Large or rapidly enlarging fibroadenomas may represent phyllodes tumors, which require wide excision with a rim of normal tissue to reduce recurrence risk.
_raw_ans: 41. a. Wide local excision with a rim of normal tissue Large or rapidly enlarging fibroadenomas may represent phyllodes tumors, which require wide excision with a rim of normal tissue to reduce recurrence risk.

stem: A41-year-old woman has noted unilateral nipple discharge from her right breast. No associated mass is identified on ultrasound or mammogram. Which of the following is the next appropriate step in her management?
options: Nipple areolar excision with central lumpectomy
explanation: Pathologic nipple discharge should be further investigated with duct excision if no mass is identified.
_raw_ans: 42. d. Major duct excision Pathologic nipple discharge should be further investigated with duct excision if no mass is identified.

stem: A36-year-old woman whose mother has just undergone treatment for breast cancer is asking about how this affects her and what can be done to lessen her chances of having the disease. Which of the following is the least significant risk factor for breast cancer?
options: Paternal relative with breast cancer BRCA1 mutation
Excessive estrogen exposure—early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity
explanation: Dietary fat intake has not been strongly linked to breast cancer risk compared to other factors.
_raw_ans: 43. a. Dietary fat intake Dietary fat intake has not been strongly linked to breast cancer risk compared to other factors.

stem: Tumor not palpable, clinically positive ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes fixed to one another; no evidence of metastases.
explanation: Fixed or matted nodes are associated with poor prognosis, corresponding to Stage III.
_raw_ans: 44. d. Stage III Fixed or matted nodes are associated with poor prognosis, corresponding to Stage III.

stem: Tumor 4.0 cm; clinically positive, movable axillary ipsilateral lymph nodes; no evidence of metastases.
explanation: Tumor >2cm but ≤5cm with positive lymph nodes corresponds to Stage II.
_raw_ans: 45. c. Stage II Tumor >2cm but ≤5cm with positive lymph nodes corresponds to Stage II.

stem: Tumor 2.1 cm, clinically negative lymph nodes; no evidence of metastases. Final pathology shows only ductal carcinoma in situ.
explanation: Ductal carcinoma in situ is stage 0, as it is in situ.
_raw_ans: 46. a. Stage 0 Ductal carcinoma in situ is stage 0, as it is in situ.

stem: Tumor not palpable, but breast diffusely enlarged and erythematous, clinically positive supraclavicular nodes; no evidence of metastases.
explanation: Inflammatory breast cancer with fixed supraclavicular nodes is Stage III.
_raw_ans: 47. d. Stage III Inflammatory breast cancer with fixed supraclavicular nodes is Stage III.

stem: Tumor 0.5 cm, clinically negative lymph nodes, pathological lumbar fracture.
explanation: Pathological lumbar fracture indicates distant metastasis, corresponding to Stage IV.
_raw_ans: 48. e. Stage IV Pathological lumbar fracture indicates distant metastasis, corresponding to Stage IV.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has a mammogram that demonstrates diffuse suspicious mammographic calcifications suggestive of multicentric disease. Biopsy of one of the lesions reveals ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). What is the most appropriate surgical management?
options: Lumpectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy
Simple mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
explanation: Multicentric DCIS is best treated with simple mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy.
_raw_ans: 49. E. Simple mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy Multicentric DCIS is best treated with simple mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has a 6-cm palpable mass that is biopsy-proven ductal adenocarcinoma. She undergoes neoadjuvant chemotherapy which reduces the tumor to 3 cm in size. However, she has palpable axillary lymph nodes; FNA demonstrates adenocarcinoma. She desires breast-conservation therapy if possible. What is the most appropriate surgical option?
options: Lumpectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy
Simple mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
explanation: Lumpectomy with axillary dissection and radiation is appropriate in patients desiring breast conservation with confirmed nodal metastasis.
_raw_ans: 50. D. Lumpectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy Lumpectomy with axillary dissection and radiation is appropriate in patients desiring breast conservation with confirmed nodal metastasis.

stem: A neglected 82-year-old woman presents with a locally advanced breast cancer that is invading the pectoralis major muscle over a broad base. She is otherwise in good health. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Lumpectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy
Simple mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
explanation: Radical mastectomy may be indicated in cases of extensive invasion of the pectoralis major muscle.
_raw_ans: 51. E. Radical mastectomy Radical mastectomy may be indicated in cases of extensive invasion of the pectoralis major muscle.

stem: What is the recommended chemotherapy regimen for breast cancer?
explanation: The recommended chemotherapy for breast cancer includes AC followed by T or the TCHP regimen, which are standard combinations used especially for HER2-positive disease.
_raw_ans: 52. C. Adriamycin/cyclophosphamide/Taxol (AC followed by T) or Taxol/cyclophosphamide/Herceptin/Pertuzumab (TCHP) The recommended chemotherapy for breast cancer includes AC followed by T or the TCHP regimen, which are standard combinations used especially for HER2-positive disease.

stem: What are indications for post-mastectomy radiation therapy?
options: ≥4 positive lymph nodes or tumor >5 cm in size
Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with no lymphovascular invasion
Triple negative breast cancer without lymph node involvement
explanation: Post-mastectomy radiation therapy is indicated when the risk of locoregional recurrence is high, such as in patients with 4 or more positive lymph nodes or large primary tumors >5 cm.
_raw_ans: 53. C. ≥4 positive lymph nodes or tumor >5 cm in size Post-mastectomy radiation therapy is indicated when the risk of locoregional recurrence is high, such as in patients with 4 or more positive lymph nodes or large primary tumors >5 cm.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with strong family history of breast cancer is told certain chromosomes are linked. Which chromosome is most associated?
explanation: BRCA1 on 17q, BRCA2 on 13q linked with breast cancer.
_raw_ans: 54. D. Chromosome 17 BRCA1 on 17q, BRCA2 on 13q linked with breast cancer.

stem: A 45-year-old woman asks about screening mammograms in the UK. At what ages do women undergo screening as part of the National Programme?
explanation: Currently every 3 years from 50 to 70 (extension pilot 47–73).
_raw_ans: 55. A. 50-70 Currently every 3 years from 50 to 70 (extension pilot 47–73).

stem: A 54-year-old woman with a 5 cm right breast lump and fixed axillary nodes, no supraclavicular nodes, moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, no distant mets. What is the TNM stage?
explanation: Large tumour + fixed ipsilateral axillary nodes, no metastasis => Stage 3.
_raw_ans: 56. C. Stage 3 Large tumour + fixed ipsilateral axillary nodes, no metastasis => Stage 3.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with a 4 cm breast lump, no palpable nodes. Wide excision and clearance show well-differentiated tumour, no lymph involvement. Approx 5-year survival?
explanation: % Likely stage 2 (T2N0), 5-year survival ~70%.
_raw_ans: 57. B. 71% Likely stage 2 (T2N0), 5-year survival ~70%.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with a painless breast lump, skin dimpling, nipple retraction. Biopsy: adenocarcinoma with fibrosis. Most common type?
explanation: Most common histological type is invasive ductal carcinoma.
_raw_ans: 58. A. Ductal Most common histological type is invasive ductal carcinoma.

stem: A 39-year-old woman has left-sided breast cancer, ER–, well-differentiated, ~6.5 cm, ipsilateral nodes, no distant mets. Next step?
options: Neoadjuvant chemo then surgery + axillary clearance
explanation: Stage III ER– tumour => neoadjuvant chemo + definitive surgery.
_raw_ans: 59. A. Neoadjuvant chemo then surgery + axillary clearance Stage III ER– tumour => neoadjuvant chemo + definitive surgery.

stem: A middle-aged woman has a scaly red rash on her nipple/areola, sore, bleeds occasionally. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Scaly erythematous nipple lesion is classic Paget’s of breast (DCIS).
_raw_ans: 60. E. Paget disease Scaly erythematous nipple lesion is classic Paget’s of breast (DCIS).

items.stem: A lactating woman presents with a tender, erythematous, and warm area in the breast. There is no fluctuation. Bilateral axillary lymph nodes are tender.
items.explanation: Common during lactation. Pain, redness, and tenderness with systemic signs are key features.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with a painless, hard lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast, along with palpable ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy.
items.explanation: Hard, painless mass with lymph node involvement in a middle-aged woman is suggestive of malignancy.

items.stem: A woman in her early 20s presents with a 2 cm, firm, freely mobile lump in the breast.
items.explanation: Young women often present with mobile, well-circumscribed benign lumps like fibroadenoma.

theme_label: Theme 2: Breast Conditions – Diagnosis and Investigations
options: ANDI (Aberration of normal development and involution)

items.stem: A 26-year-old breast-feeding mother presents as an emergency with pain, swelling in the right breast and fever for 2 days.
items.explanation: The acute presentation during lactation with fever, pain, swelling and signs of inflammation suggests a breast abscess, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. These infections often occur within weeks postpartum and may need aspiration or surgical drainage with antibiotics. Other options such as a galactocele (H) would not present acutely with fever or signs of infection.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman underwent a screening mammogram and was recalled for further assessment. She was found to have fine linear branching micro-calcifications.
items.explanation: Micro-calcifications, especially linear or branching types, may represent ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Vacuum-assisted biopsy provides a larger tissue sample to accurately assess calcifications. Core biopsy (E) may not be sufficient for subtle calcifications. MRI (K) is more for invasive lobular carcinoma or multicentric disease assessment.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman woke up to find a lump in the right breast with pain. She is very anxious.
items.explanation: Sudden onset of a painful lump is suggestive of a breast cyst, often benign and hormonally related. Cysts can be tender and fluctuate with menstrual cycles. It is unlikely to be fibroadenoma (G) which is painless and slow-growing. A malignant lump (E) would not present suddenly with pain.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with breast pain and lumpiness in both breasts. It is particularly worse before her periods.
items.explanation: Cyclical pain and lumpiness in both breasts point toward benign hormonal changes, described under ANDI. These changes are common during reproductive years and usually do not require invasive treatment. Cyst (D) or fibroadenoma (G) would be localized rather than diffuse bilateral discomfort.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman attends the breast clinic with a strong family history of breast cancer. Two of her sisters, her mother and her maternal aunt’s daughter had breast cancer at an early age. She wants to know her risk of getting breast cancer.
items.explanation: A significant family history of early-onset breast cancer warrants BRCA testing. These genetic mutations carry a high lifetime risk and require genetic counseling. Imaging or biopsy is not indicated unless a lesion is found. MRI (K) may be considered after confirming carrier status.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presented with a painless mass in the right breast, which has been rapidly increasing in size. On examination she has a large mass in the right breast with skin stretched and shiny over it.
items.explanation: Rapid growth and a large size suggest a phyllodes tumour, especially in women over 40. These can be benign or malignant and require excision. Fibroadenoma (G) is more common in younger women and grows slowly. Breast cancer (E) tends to have a different clinical presentation and texture.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman feels a hard lump that is painless and gradually increasing in size over the past 4 months. Her mammogram shows a spiculated mass in the right breast.
items.explanation: A spiculated mass is highly suspicious for malignancy. Core needle biopsy is essential to confirm the diagnosis and assess receptor status. FNAC would be inadequate for full histological diagnosis. Vacuum-assisted biopsy (M) is used more for microcalcifications.

items.stem: A 26-year-old young woman presents with a painless mass in the left breast. She stopped breastfeeding 1 month ago, following which she noticed this lump.
items.explanation: A galactocele typically develops after cessation of breastfeeding as a milk-retention cyst. It is painless and often resolves after aspiration. An abscess (C) would present with pain and signs of infection. Fibroadenoma (G) does not have a temporal link to lactation.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with enlarging breasts which are embarrassing him.
items.explanation: Pubertal gynaecomastia is common and usually resolves. It is bilateral, subareolar, and non-tender. It can be physiological or due to hormonal imbalance or drugs. Male breast cancer (J) is rare in this age group and usually presents as a firm unilateral lump.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has been diagnosed with a lobular carcinoma in the right breast.
items.explanation: Lobular carcinoma is often multicentric and bilateral. MRI is the most sensitive modality for assessing its extent and contralateral disease. Mammogram and ultrasound may miss multifocal involvement. Biopsy (E) is done earlier for diagnosis.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman presented with a greenish black nipple discharge on both sides.
items.explanation: Greenish-black bilateral discharge in a postmenopausal woman suggests duct ectasia. This is due to ductal dilatation and secretory stasis, common with age. Malignancy would likely present with unilateral bloody discharge or a mass.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a discrete lump in the breast. The lump is painless and moves freely within the breast.
items.explanation: A mobile, well-circumscribed, non-tender lump in a young woman is classic for fibroadenoma – often called a “breast mouse.” Phyllodes (L) are less mobile and grow more rapidly. Cancer is unlikely at this age with such benign features.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man presents with a painless mass just under the nipple and areola on the right side of 3 months duration.
items.explanation: A unilateral, subareolar, painless mass in a man is suspicious for breast cancer, especially at this age. Gynaecomastia (I) would be bilateral and more diffuse. Male breast cancer is rare but carries a prognosis similar to that in women when matched stage for stage.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman presents with a breast lump in the upper outer quadrant. On examination the lump is hard and irregular. There is axillary lymphadenopathy.
items.explanation: Carcinoma of breast is suspected in a 75‐year‐old woman because a hard, irregular mass with axillary lymphadenopathy is highly suggestive of malignancy; the clinical findings correlate with the aggressive nature of carcinoma in elderly patients.

items.stem: A 53-year-old woman presents with nipple retraction and a greeny-yellow discharge. Ultrasound shows dilated breast ducts.
items.explanation: Duct ectasia is the likely diagnosis in a 53‐year‐old with nipple retraction and a greenish-yellow discharge, with ultrasound findings of dilated ducts indicating a benign inflammatory process affecting the ductal system.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman presents with a smooth, non-tender, highly mobile mass on the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Fine needle aspiration shows benign breast epithelial cells (C2).
items.explanation: Fibroadenoma is indicated by the presentation of a smooth, non-tender, and highly mobile mass in a young 21‐year‐old woman combined with FNAC showing benign epithelial cells, reflecting its typical benign pathology.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with a worsening eczema-like rash overlying the areola and nipple. The rash does not itch. On examination a palpable mass can be felt under the rash.
items.explanation: Paget’s disease is considered in a 70‐year‐old woman presenting with a persistent eczema-like, non-pruritic rash over the nipple and an underlying palpable mass; this clinical picture is classic for Paget’s disease with associated underlying carcinoma.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents a fortnight postpartum with a painful, enlarged left breast. On examination she is pyrexial and her breast is tender and inflamed. There are no palpable masses.
items.explanation: Mastitis is the diagnosis in a 26‐year‐old postpartum woman with a painful, enlarged, tender breast and pyrexia; these findings represent the acute infectious inflammation commonly seen during the postpartum period.

options: Wide local excision, sentinel node biopsy plus tamoxifen
Wide local excision, axillary node clearance and chemotherapy

items.stem: A 92-year-old woman presents with oestrogen receptor positive stage III invasive ductal carcinoma.
A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with ductal carcinoma-in-situ involving all quadrants of the breast.
A 60-year-old patient presents with a 2-cm invasive ductal carcinoma of the outer quadrant of the right breast. The tumour is oestrogen receptor positive.
A 32-year-old patient presents with a 2.5-cm invasive ductal carcinoma. She has a palpable axillary lymph node which reveals cancer cells on cytology. The tumour is oestrogen receptor negative.
A 17-year-old female presents with multiple bilateral cystic swellings, which she admits to having for years. These are causing her considerable discomfort, especially premenstrually.
items.explanation: Fibrocystic disease causes bilateral cyclical cystic breast changes.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a single 4 cm firm, smooth lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. On examination, it is noted that the lump is not adherent to the overlying skin and is freely mobile within the breast.
items.explanation: Fibroadenoma is a firm, mobile, well-circumscribed benign breast lump.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman attends the breast clinic with a rapidly growing irregular mass in her right breast. On examination, it is 6 cm in diameter. Core biopsy later reveals mixed epithelial and connective tissue elements.
items.explanation: Phyllodes tumour is a rapidly enlarging biphasic breast mass.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman complains of dry, cracked skin around the right areola. On examination, there is a discrete firm nodule underlying the affected area.
items.explanation: Paget disease presents with eczematous nipple changes and underlying carcinoma.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman went to her general practitioner complaining of a swelling in the left breast. On examination, you notice dimpling of the skin in the left breast and a firm 3 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant.
items.explanation: Peau d’orange reflects lymphatic obstruction in inflammatory breast cancer.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman attends the breast clinic complaining of a sudden pain and swelling in her right breast. On examination, a single, fluctuant swelling is palpable. Fine-needle aspiration reveals clear fluid.
items.explanation: Fluctuant swelling with clear fluid on aspiration indicates a breast cyst.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents 5 weeks after the birth of her second child with a painful left breast. On examination, there is a 4 cm area of inflammation and erythema lateral to the nipple with an associated underlying lump.
items.explanation: Painful, inflamed lump postpartum is a breast abscess.

items.stem: A 52-year-old obese woman comes to the breast clinic with an irregular 2 cm firm lump in her left breast. On questioning, she admits to recent trauma to the area. Core biopsy of the lesion is reported as B2.
items.explanation: History of trauma and benign histology suggests fat necrosis.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man complains of a soft swelling around his left nipple that has increased in size over the last year. He has no significant past medical history but admits to being a frequent user of cannabis. His body mass index is 21. On examination, there is no discharge, skin changes, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
items.explanation: Soft swelling under the nipple in a male indicates gynaecomastia.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of pain in her left breast. On examination, you feel an indurated, tender, cord-like structure running down the anterior surface of the breast.
items.explanation: Tender cord-like structure is Mondor disease (superficial thrombophlebitis).

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with lumpiness and tenderness in both breasts worsening premenstrually; ultrasound shows multiple small cysts and biopsy shows fibrosis and epithelial hyperplasia.
items.explanation: Fibrocystic changes are benign; no further tests.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a sudden, painless 1 cm soft lump in her right breast.
items.explanation: Ultrasound is first-line for a young woman’s breast lump.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman with a hard 2 cm UOQ breast lump and axillary nodes; mammogram inconclusive due to augmentation.
items.explanation: MRI clarifies lesions when mammography is inconclusive in augmented breasts.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with a 4 cm left breast lump; FNAC reveals dysplastic cells.
items.explanation: Core biopsy provides definitive histology for dysplasia.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a longstanding breast cyst; aspiration yields blood-stained fluid.
items.explanation: Blood-stained cyst fluid requires cytological analysis.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of unilateral, painless, blood-stained discharge from the left nipple. On examination, no lumps are palpable on either side and there is no axillary lymphadenopathy. Cytology of the discharge reveals no malignant cells.
items.explanation: Intraductal papilloma is the most common benign cause of bloody nipple discharge.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had multiple visits to her general practitioner over the last 6 months complaining of early morning headaches unresponsive to analgesia. On this occasion, she also admits to having a milky discharge from both nipples. A β-hCG urine test is negative and she has not had any children before.
items.explanation: Prolactinoma causes galactorrhea and headaches from pituitary enlargement.

items.stem: A 45-year-old smoker presents to her general practitioner with a 6-month history of pain and a cheesy discharge from her left nipple associated with some inflammation of the areola. A mass can be felt under the areola, but no other lumps were palpable.
items.explanation: Duct ectasia presents with cheesy discharge and subareolar inflammation.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman is referred to you by her general practitioner with a 7-month history of amenorrhoea. She also complains of a whitish discharge from her nipples bilaterally. Her body mass index is 42 and she has no neurological symptoms. Breast examination is otherwise normal. She is worried as her mother has recently been diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer.
items.explanation: Lactating breast indicates benign hormonal-related discharge.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of a firm 3 cm lump in her right breast, with associated nipple inversion, a bloody discharge and axillary lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was reported as C5.
items.explanation: Features of lump, inversion, bloody discharge, and positive cytology indicate breast cancer.

options: Wide local excision and axillary clearance
Wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman is found to have a 5 cm invasive ductal carcinoma in the upper outer quadrant. You have explained that she may need a mastectomy, but she is keen to preserve the breast.
items.explanation: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy downstages tumour for conservation.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman has a 6.5 cm central invasive breast tumour. She is otherwise fit and well.
items.explanation: Modified radical mastectomy for large central tumours.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman has recently had a wide local excision and axillary clearance for a 2 cm breast carcinoma. Histology showed clear excision margins, a grade I oestrogen receptor-negative tumour and no positive axillary lymph nodes. She returns to the outpatient clinic and wants to know what further treatment she will be having.
items.explanation: Radiotherapy reduces local recurrence after conservation.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman who has recently had a 3 cm invasive breast tumour resection has returned to clinic. The histology report states that the tumour is oestrogen receptor-negative but is overexpressing HER2.
items.explanation: Trastuzumab targets HER2-positive disease.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has just had a radical mastectomy and radiotherapy for a large invasive breast tumour. Histology showed an oestrogen receptor-positive tumour. Apart from suffering a left deep vein thrombosis during the postoperative recovery period, she is well.
items.explanation: Aromatase inhibitors are standard in postmenopausal ER-positive cancer.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with a 3 cm firm lump in the left breast that is fixed to the overlying skin.
items.explanation: CA15-3 is used for monitoring breast cancer; its elevation is commonly seen in patients with invasive breast carcinoma that may involve skin fixation.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man complains of new constipation. He has a history of passing fresh blood mixed with his stools and has recently lost weight.
items.explanation: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a marker for colorectal cancer, fitting his presentation of blood in the stool, constipation and weight loss.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with difficulty passing urine and dribbling at the end of the stream.
items.explanation: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is used in the detection and management of prostate cancer, which is consistent with his urinary symptoms.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 1 cm flat, brown lesion on her left leg. On examination, the lesion is irregularly pigmented and occasionally itches and bleeds.
items.explanation: S-100 is frequently elevated in malignant melanoma, corresponding to the irregular, pigmented lesion that bleeds occasionally.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with jaundice that has been worsening over the previous weeks. She denies having any pain. On examination, the gallbladder is palpable.
items.explanation: CA 19-9 is associated with pancreatic head adenocarcinoma; its elevation accounts for the painless jaundice and palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier’s sign).

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the breast clinic with a history of lumpiness and tenderness in both breasts that is worse in the days prior to menstruation. An ultrasound scan reveals multiple small cysts bilaterally, and a tissue sample shows fibrosis and epithelial hyperplasia.
items.explanation: In a 34‐year-old with cyclical breast pain, bilateral small cysts with fibrosis and hyperplasia on tissue evaluation confirm a benign fibrocystic change; thus no further investigation is needed.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 1 cm soft lump in her right breast that appeared suddenly last week. The lesion is painless and there is no other abnormality on examination.
items.explanation: In a young 28‐year-old woman with a small, soft, and mobile lump appearing acutely, ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate likely benign lesions such as fibroadenoma.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the breast clinic with a hard 2 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast associated with axillary lymphadenopathy. She has a history of bilateral breast augmentation for cosmetic reasons. A mammogram is performed, but the resulting image is hazy and the radiologist cannot confidently delineate any lesions.
items.explanation: In a 42‐year‐old woman with a suspicious hard mass and axillary lymphadenopathy whose mammogram is obscured by cosmetic implants, MRI is used to provide superior soft tissue contrast and further delineate the lesion.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman attends the breast clinic with a 4 cm lump in her left breast. A fine-needle aspiration was performed and the cells sent for cytology. The resulting report notes the presence of dysplastic cells.
items.explanation: In a 52‐year‐old with a sizeable 4 cm mass where fine‐needle aspiration shows dysplastic cells, a core biopsy is indicated as it offers better tissue architecture for an accurate histological diagnosis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman complains of a lump in her right breast that hasbeen present for some time. An ultrasound scan reveals a breast cyst, and this is aspirated under ultrasound guidance. The aspirate is found to be blood-stained.
items.explanation: In a 45‐year‐old with a breast cyst that yields a blood‐stained aspirate, aspirate cytology is performed to assess for atypical or malignant cells that may be masked within the cyst fluid.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman is seen in the breast clinic with a lump in her right breast for 1 month. She has a 1cm discrete, mobile lump in the lower outer quadrant of the right breast which is non-tender.
items.explanation: Fibroadenoma is a benign breast lump seen in young women under 30; discrete, mobile, painless.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has suffered a painful lump in the right breast for 3 weeks. Over the last few months she has had irregular periods and hot flushes. There is a 2cm discrete, moderately tender lump in the lower inner quadrant of her right breast with normal-looking breast skin. Ultrasound scan shows a well-defined lesion and needle aspiration yielded 12 mL of a green-yellow fluid.
items.explanation: Breast cysts are common in perimenopausal women; aspiration yields green-yellow fluid.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has found an asymptomatic lump in the central portion of her right breast. Past medical history includes diabetes mellitus and a fractured collar bone in a road traffic collision 3 months ago. There is a semimobile irregular lump in the central portion of the right breast with overlying skin haemosiderin deposition. There is no evidence of axillary lymphadenopathy.
items.explanation: Fat necrosis may follow trauma; haemosiderin deposition indicates tissue injury.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had 5 weeks of redness and swelling around the right nipple. There is no past medical history but she is a heavy smoker. There is periareolar skin inflammation with a small palpable tender mass just behind the nipple.
items.explanation: Periductal mastitis occurs in smokers; presents with periareolar inflammation and tender subareolar mass.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has noted that in the last few months both nipples have gradually retracted. She is also complaining of significant nipple discharge that is thick and yellow/green in colour. Both nipples are retracted and slit-like with no palpable lumps or lymphadenopathy.
items.explanation: Duct ectasia involves duct dilatation in involution; causes cheesy discharge and slit-like nipple retraction.

options: Wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy
Wide local excision and axillary node clearance

items.stem: An 84-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of a lump in her left breast. She has ischaemic heart disease and previous deep vein thrombosis, with shortness of breath on minimal exertion. Triple assessment reveals a grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma which is oestrogen receptor positive.
items.explanation: Anastrozole is first-line hormonal therapy for an elderly patient unfit for surgery.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with a small area of microcalcification in the left breast measuring approximately 12 mm under the national breast cancer screening programme. Stereotactic core biopsies confirm low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ.
items.explanation: Wire-guided wide local excision is required to remove a small, impalpable area of DCIS.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman is diagnosed with a palpable invasive ductal carcinoma. She undergoes a wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy. Histology confirms a 10 mm grade 1 invasive ductal carcinoma completely excised with no lymph node involvement. The tumour is oestrogen receptor negative.
items.explanation: External beam radiotherapy reduces recurrence after breast-conserving surgery.

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman is 3 years post mastectomy and axillary node clearance for a lymph node positive, grade 3 breast cancer. She has developed spinal metastases causing back pain without cord compression.
items.explanation: External beam radiotherapy provides rapid pain relief for bone metastases.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of a large lump in the right breast. There is an 8 cm mass and palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Core biopsy confirms invasive ductal carcinoma and FNAB of nodes is positive.
items.explanation: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy downstages large tumours and treats micrometastases.

items.stem: A therapeutic agent highly recommended in the treatment of lymph-node-positive HER2-positive breast cancer.
A selective oestrogen-receptor modulator drug useful in the treatment of breast cancer but associated with risks of endometrial cancer and pulmonary embolism.
An aromatase inhibitor useful in the treatment of early breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
A therapeutic agent useful in the treatment of breast cancer but known to cause left ventricular failure and pulmonary toxicity.
A therapeutic agent useful in the treatment of breast cancer but known to cause bladder cancer.
items.explanation: - Trastuzumab (Herceptin) (B) is for HER2+ breast cancer; can cause cardiotoxicity and some pulmonary issues. - Tamoxifen (C) is a SERM with risk of endometrial cancer and thromboembolism. - Anastrozole (D) is an aromatase inhibitor in postmenopausal women. - Trastuzumab again (B) known for cardiac dysfunction risk. - Cyclophosphamide (A) can cause hemorrhagic cystitis and bladder toxicity.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with a highly mobile lump in her breast. Fine-needle aspiration shows no malignancy.
A 28-year-old woman, four weeks postpartum, presents to her GP with a tender lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. On examination it is ill-defined, erythematous and hot to touch.
items.explanation: i Mastitis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old very anxious woman presents with a hard, irregular lump in her breast. On examination it is craggy and well-defined. Fine-needle aspiration shows no evidence of malignancy. On further questioning, she reveals that she was involved in a car crash 6 months previously.
items.explanation: d Fat necrosis.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a yellow-brown discharge from her nipples. On examination her discharge appears to be coming from multiple ducts. Examination is otherwise normal and mammography is unremarkable.
items.explanation: c Duct ectasia.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a lump in her breast which is painless. On examination it is well demarcated, fluctuant and transilluminable.
items.explanation: b Cyst (E) is a “breast mouse,” mobile and benign. - Mastitis (i) is common in lactation, can lead to abscess if untreated. - Fat necrosis (d) can mimic malignancy, often after trauma. - Duct ectasia (c) shows colored nipple discharge from multiple ducts near menopause. - Breast cyst (b) is fluctuant, transilluminable, well-defined.

sub: Ministerial Evaluation Exam - Head and Neck
stem: A 40-year-old female presents with an acute onset of fever, pain, and swelling at her right cheek. On examination, there is tenderness and swelling at the area of the right parotid gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acute fever and parotid tenderness indicate sialadenitis.
_raw_ans: 1. C. Parotid gland sialadenitis. Acute fever and parotid tenderness indicate sialadenitis.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
options: There are three pairs of minor salivary glands.
Minor salivary glands contribute 10% of overall saliva flow.
Most minor salivary gland tumours are benign.
Presumed benign tumours of the minor salivary glands >1 cm should be managed with excisional biopsy.
Malignant minor salivary gland tumours are managed with primary surgical resection.
explanation: B and E are correct because minor salivary glands produce about 10% of saliva and malignant tumours require primary surgical resection; the other options are incorrect.
_raw_ans: 2. B. Minor salivary glands contribute 10% of overall saliva flow, E. Malignant minor salivary gland tumours are managed with primary surgical resection B and E are correct because minor salivary glands produce about 10% of saliva and malignant tumours require primary surgical resection; the other options are incorrect.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
options: The sublingual glands occupy the anterior floor of mouth.
The sublingual glands drain both directly into the mouth and into the submandibular duct.
Tumours of the sublingual glands are rarely malignant.
The term ranula is applied to mucous retention cysts of the sublingual gland.
A plunging ranula is the term used to describe a ranula that extends beyond the floor of mouth and into the neck.
explanation: A, B and E are correct based on gland location, drainage pattern and the definition of a plunging ranula; options C and D are incorrect.

A plunging ranula is the term used to describe a ranula that extends beyond the floor of mouth and into the neck A, B and E are correct based on gland location, drainage pattern and the definition of a plunging ranula; options C and D are incorrect.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
options: The two lobes of the submandibular gland communicate around the posterior belly of the digastric muscle.
80% of salivary calculi occur in the submandibular duct.
Calculi identified posterior to the point where the duct crosses the lingual nerve should be removed via a transoral approach.
The marginal mandibular nerve is at risk during removal of the gland.
The lingual nerve is divided during removal of the gland to facilitate dissection of the deep lobe of the gland.
explanation: B and D are correct; A, C and E are false due to anatomical inaccuracies.
_raw_ans: 4. B. 80% of salivary calculi occur in the submandibular duct, D. The marginal mandibular nerve is at risk during removal of the gland B and D are correct; A, C and E are false due to anatomical inaccuracies.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
options: 80% of submandibular gland tumours are benign.
Submandibular gland masses can be differentiated from lymph nodes by bimanual palpation.
Facial nerve weakness is a sign suggestive of malignancy.
Open surgical biopsy is indicated to confirm malignant disease prior to surgery.
Radiation is the primary modality of treatment for most submandibular gland malignancies.
explanation: B and C are correct; option A is false since only about 50% are benign and D and E are not standard practice.
_raw_ans: 5. B. Submandibular gland masses can be differentiated from lymph nodes by bimanual palpation, C. Facial nerve weakness is a sign suggestive of malignancy B and C are correct; option A is false since only about 50% are benign and D and E are not standard practice.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
options: 80% of the parotid gland lies deep to the facial nerve.
During parotidectomy, the greater auricular nerve should be included in the skin flap to preserve function.
The facial nerve is identified using landmarks including the tragal pointer and the posterior belly of digastric.
If a branch of the facial nerve must be sacrificed during dissection, immediate grafting should be performed.
Frey’s syndrome results from inappropriate innervation of sweat glands with parasympathetic fibres within the parotid bed.
explanation: C and E are correct; options A, B and D are incorrect based on surgical anatomy.
_raw_ans: 6. C. The facial nerve is identified using landmarks including the tragal pointer and the posterior belly of digastric, E. Frey’s syndrome results from inappropriate innervation of sweat glands with parasympathetic fibres within the parotid bed C and E are correct; options A, B and D are incorrect based on surgical anatomy.

stem: Which of the following statements is true?
options: Viral infection of the parotid glands affects both glands symmetrically.
Dehydrated patients are at risk from bacterial parotitis.
Recurrent parotitis of childhood tends to result in abscess formation.
HIV might present with multiple parotid cysts.
Chronic trauma to the parotid duct may result in obstruction.
explanation: B, D and E are correct; A and C are not consistently true.
_raw_ans: 7. B. Dehydrated patients are at risk from bacterial parotitis, D. HIV might present with multiple parotid cysts, E. Chronic trauma to the parotid duct may result in obstruction B, D and E are correct; A and C are not consistently true.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
options: The most common tumour of the parotid gland is a pleomorphic adenoma.
Tumour excision for benign disease involves enucleation of the lesion.
Malignant tumours should be excised with a cuff of normal tissue including the facial nerve.
Symmetrical swelling of the parotid glands may be due to excess alcohol intake.
Sjogren’s syndrome is associated with B cell lymphoma.
explanation: A, D and E are correct; B and C are incorrect regarding surgical management.
_raw_ans: 8. A. The most common tumour of the parotid gland is a pleomorphic adenoma, D. Symmetrical swelling of the parotid glands may be due to excess alcohol intake, E. Sjogren’s syndrome is associated with B cell lymphoma A, D and E are correct; B and C are incorrect regarding surgical management.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with a submandibular calculus, having presented with a tender lump below the jaw on eating. Which structure is likely to be obstructed?
explanation: Submandibular calculi typically obstruct Warthin’s duct, leading to pain and swelling during meals.
_raw_ans: 9. A. Warthin’s duct Submandibular calculi typically obstruct Warthin’s duct, leading to pain and swelling during meals.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a month-long history of intermittent, left-sided pain and swelling in the anterior neck under the left jaw. His symptoms are associated with meal times and regress shortly after completing each meal. In recent days however, the pain appears to have become more intense and the swelling more firm. On examination a firm lump is palpable in the left submandibular region, bimanual palpation of which causes the patient to complain of a foul taste in his mouth. The most appropriate diagnostic investigation will be
explanation: A sialogram is used to evaluate salivary duct obstruction.
_raw_ans: 10. D. Sialogram A sialogram is used to evaluate salivary duct obstruction.

stem: A 54-year-old builder attends your outpatient clinic with his wife, reporting an 8-month history of a lump on the left side of his face, in front of his ear. It is painless and does not trouble him. He has attended on the insistence of his wife, who is worried that it may be growing larger. On examination, the swelling appears to lie anterior to the angle of the jaw on the left side. It is non-tender and approximately 5 cm in diameter with a clear edge. The skin is easily moved on top of it and the lump itself feels rubbery to touch. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy or facial droop evident on examination. An aspirate is taken which shows cells of many different types. A decision is made at a follow-up appointment to excise the lump under anaesthesia. This is likely to be
explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign parotid tumor, presenting as a rubbery and mobile mass.
_raw_ans: 11. A. Pleomorphic adenoma Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign parotid tumor, presenting as a rubbery and mobile mass.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with his mother to the general practice at which you are based, with a 3-week history of bilateral cheek swelling. The family is newly registered and medical records have not yet been transferred to the practice. His mother informs you that the young boy has not received any of his childhood vaccinations, as she has been worried about their possible detrimental effects. The clinical suspicion is of mumps parotitis. Which class of infectious agent is responsible for mumps?
explanation: Mumps is caused by an RNA virus from the paramyxovirus family.
_raw_ans: 12. A. RNA viruses Mumps is caused by an RNA virus from the paramyxovirus family.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents with a lump on the left side of her neck which has been slowly enlarging over the last few months. On examination, there is a 2 cm firm, painless, mobile lump near the angle of the left jaw. She is still able to move her facial muscles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Most common benign parotid tumour, usually painless, no facial nerve involvement.
_raw_ans: 13. B. Pleomorphic adenoma Most common benign parotid tumour, usually painless, no facial nerve involvement.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents to the GP with a painful, enlarging lump just in front of his right ear, which has been present for 2 months. He woke this morning to find that the right side of his face was drooping. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Malignant parotid tumour often presents with rapid growth and facial nerve involvement.
_raw_ans: 14. E. Salivary gland carcinoma Malignant parotid tumour often presents with rapid growth and facial nerve involvement.

stem: After undergoing total gastrectomy, the patient presents with chest pain and sore throat. What could be the cause, and how should it be managed?
options: GERD; manage with lifestyle modifications and proton pump inhibitors
explanation: Post-gastrectomy, GERD is common and is managed with lifestyle changes and PPIs.
_raw_ans: 1. C. GERD; manage with lifestyle modifications and proton pump inhibitors Post-gastrectomy, GERD is common and is managed with lifestyle changes and PPIs.

stem: A 54-year-old man with recurrent problems with acid reflux despite changes to his diet and reduction of his alcohol intake. An endoscopy is performed which reveals Barrett’s oesophagus. Which of the following is the optimum management for this patient in regards to symptom control and disease monitoring?
options: Long term PPI and endoscopy every year
Long term PPI and endoscopy every five years
Trial of PPI and endoscopy every five years
explanation: Barrett’s oesophagus requires acid suppression and periodic surveillance with endoscopy.
_raw_ans: 2. C. Long term PPI and endoscopy every five years Barrett’s oesophagus requires acid suppression and periodic surveillance with endoscopy.

stem: Shortly after an esophagoscopy, a 30-year-old patient develops shortness of breath, chest pain, and fever. A contrast study shows extravasation of contrast into the left chest cavity. The most appropriate course of action is:
options: Perform a cervical esophagostomy, gastrostomy, and insert a chest tube.
Perform Immediate left thoracotomy and repair the esophageal tear.
Insert a nasogastric tube and begin high dose antibiotic therapy
Deploy an endoscopic intra-esophageal stent to plug the hole.
Stop ingestion of food, insert a chest tube and begin high dose antibiotic therapy.
explanation: and E is correct 18, The development of respiratory distress, chest pain, and fever with contrast extravasation into the left chest cavity post‐esophagoscopy indicates esophageal perforation; both surgical repair with cervical diversion (option A) and chest tube drainage with antibiotics (option E) are appropriate interventions.

A and E is correct 18, The development of respiratory distress, chest pain, and fever with contrast extravasation into the left chest cavity post‐esophagoscopy indicates esophageal perforation; both surgical repair with cervical diversion (option A) and chest tube drainage with antibiotics (option E) are appropriate interventions.

explanation: The gastro‐oesophageal junction is about 40 cm from the incisors; the oesophagus is lined by non‐keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and its diaphragmatic opening lies at T10. Note that its true length is around 25 cm and it has three natural constrictions.

stem: The following statements are true except:

The normal length of the LOS is 3 to 4 cm.
The three phases of swallowing, oral, pharyngeal and oesophageal, are involuntary.
Pharyngeal diverticulum occurs because of the incoordination of the pharyngeal phase of deglutition.
The pressure in the LOS is 10–25 mmHg.

Dysphagia associated with cough is a symptom of impending tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
Dysphagia in the oral and pharyngeal phases of swallowing indicates a neurological rather than a mechanical problem.
Odynophagia is always of cardiac origin.
Regurgitation and reflux are the same and caused by dysphagia.

stem: For the Zenker’s diverticulum described above, what is the most important aspect of treatment?
options: (D) elevation of the head of the bed
explanation: cricopharyngeal muscle myotomy Myotomy is key to relieve the underlying neuromotor dysfunction.

stem: A 55-year-old man with 10 years of heartburn, chronic cough, and regurgitation—whose endoscopy shows Barrett’s esophagus with high-grade dysplasia—would most likely have been prevented by which early treatment?
explanation: Early antireflux surgery may prevent progression to Barrett’s esophagus.
_raw_ans: 11. C. Nissen fundoplication Early antireflux surgery may prevent progression to Barrett’s esophagus.

stem: For the same patient with Barrett’s esophagus and high-grade dysplasia, what is recommended?
options: double dose proton-pump inhibitor and repeat endoscopy in 3 months
proton-pump inhibitor and H₂ blocker, followed by repeat endoscopy in 3 months
antibiotic treatment for Helicobacter pylori with proton-pump inhibitor
explanation: Esophagectomy is indicated for high-grade dysplasia in Barrett’s esophagus.
_raw_ans: 12. E. esophagectomy Esophagectomy is indicated for high-grade dysplasia in Barrett’s esophagus.

stem: The blood supply to the oesophagus is derived from which three vessels?
options: Inferior thyroid artery, descending aorta, left gastric artery
Internal carotid, descending aorta, oesophageal artery
Lateral thoracic artery, phrenic artery, right gastric artery
Pharyngeal artery, long thoracic artery, phrenic artery
Ascending aorta, common hepatic artery, left gastric artery
explanation: After excluding unsuitable vessels, option A correctly lists the main suppliers to the oesophagus.
_raw_ans: 13. A. Inferior thyroid artery, descending aorta, left gastric artery After excluding unsuitable vessels, option A correctly lists the main suppliers to the oesophagus.

stem: A 58-year-old patient presents with a 6-week history of increasing difficulty swallowing. He first noticed problems when eating meat which became stuck ‘behind his heart’, but this gradually began to include other foods. He is now struggling with thick fluids and has noticed some unintentional weight loss. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Endoscopy is the gold standard investigation to assess suspected oesophageal cancer.
_raw_ans: 14. C. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy Endoscopy is the gold standard investigation to assess suspected oesophageal cancer.

stem: A 27-year-old patient presents with a 3-month history of increasing difficulty in swallowing – beginning with fluids and later with solids – accompanied by regurgitation and unintentional weight loss; a chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Achalasia, due to failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax, is the most likely cause.
_raw_ans: 15. D. Achalasia Achalasia, due to failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax, is the most likely cause.

stem: CREST syndrome is an autoimmune condition associated with atrophy and fibrosis of the oesophageal musculature resulting in dysphagia and reflux‐type symptoms. Which of the following is not a feature of CREST syndrome?
explanation: An erythematous malar rash is not a characteristic feature of CREST syndrome.
_raw_ans: 16. B. Erythematous malar rash An erythematous malar rash is not a characteristic feature of CREST syndrome.

stem: The gastro-oesophageal sphincter does not rely on a ring of contractile muscle but on several mechanisms to prevent reflux. Which of the following does not contribute to its function?
options: Smooth muscle of the lower oesophageal sphincter
explanation: The left crus does not contribute to the maintenance of sphincter tone.
_raw_ans: 17. A. Left crus of diaphragm The left crus does not contribute to the maintenance of sphincter tone.

stem: A 58-year-old builder with a long history of retrosternal chest pain and a hiatus hernia is found on endoscopy to have grade 2 oesophagitis. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Acid suppression with a PPI is the first-line treatment for oesophagitis associated with reflux.
_raw_ans: 18. B. Proton pump inhibitor Acid suppression with a PPI is the first-line treatment for oesophagitis associated with reflux.

stem: Which of the following is not a lifestyle change that might reduce reflux-type symptoms?
options: Raise the head of the bed at night
explanation: Abdominal exercise may worsen reflux rather than improve it.
_raw_ans: 19. B. Abdominal exercise Abdominal exercise may worsen reflux rather than improve it.

stem: A 65-year-old patient with symptoms of oesophagitis and endoscopic findings of Barrett’s oesophagus with low grade dysplasia is best managed by
options: Staging CT chest abdomen and pelvis
High dose PPI and repeat endoscopy
explanation: High-dose PPI therapy with surveillance is recommended for Barrett’s oesophagus with low grade dysplasia.
_raw_ans: 20. D. High dose PPI and repeat endoscopy High-dose PPI therapy with surveillance is recommended for Barrett’s oesophagus with low grade dysplasia.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with increasing difficulty swallowing over the last few months. He has been working in Mexico for the last two years. He is otherwise well and denies any other symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Trypanosoma cruzi infection can cause megaoesophagus presenting with progressive dysphagia.
_raw_ans: 21. A. Chagas disease Trypanosoma cruzi infection can cause megaoesophagus presenting with progressive dysphagia.

stem: A 56-year-old woman complains of episodes of severe retrosternal chest pain postprandial, with a bitter taste in her mouth, but no difficulty swallowing. Examination is unremarkable. Which investigation is most useful?
explanation: GORD is best diagnosed by prolonged oesophageal pH monitoring.
_raw_ans: 22. A. 24-hour lower oesophageal pH GORD is best diagnosed by prolonged oesophageal pH monitoring.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents to the surgical outpatient clinic with increasing dysphagia for solids and liquids, retrosternal chest pain on eating, regurgitation of undigested food and weight loss. Oesophageal and gastric biopsy at endoscopy was normal. Oesophageal manometry showed impaired relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and barium swallow revealed a dilated proximal oesophagus with distal narrowing. Which of the following surgical procedures would be indicated?
explanation: Achalasia is treated surgically by incising the LES (Heller myotomy).
_raw_ans: 23. C. Heller myotomy Achalasia is treated surgically by incising the LES (Heller myotomy).

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with acute lower chest and upper abdominal pain following an episode of vomiting. On examination, he has marked tenderness in the epigastrium and you note the presence of subcutaneous emphysema. ECG shows a sinus tachycardia with no ST segment changes, and a chest X-ray demonstrates mediastinal air. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Forceful vomiting caused transmural oesophageal rupture leading to mediastinal air.
_raw_ans: 24. A. Boerhaave syndrome Forceful vomiting caused transmural oesophageal rupture leading to mediastinal air.

stem: 28-year-old woman has dysphagia with low retrosternal ‘sticking’ and an occasional sensation of choking. A video barium swallow shows this appearance in the oesophagus (see Figure 6.1). Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Achalasia (failure of relaxation of the distal oesophageal musculature associated with degeneration of the myenteric plexus) is among the most common causes of dysphagia in the younger population.
_raw_ans: 25. A. Achalasia Achalasia (failure of relaxation of the distal oesophageal musculature associated with degeneration of the myenteric plexus) is among the most common causes of dysphagia in the younger population.

stem: 72-year-old man has had a sensation of retrosternal burning that is worse at night and after meals for the last 4 months. It partially responds to ‘over the counter’ antacid treatment. Which is the single most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation?
explanation: This man most likely has gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. The differential diagnosis includes oesophageal or gastric malignancy, functional disease, and peptic ulcer disease and the first investigation should be direct visualization of the oesophagus and stomach. A barium swallow would exclude tumours or stricturing but would not assess the mucosal integrity so well or allow biopsies to be taken. Twenty-four-hour pH studies may be useful to evaluate the severity or timing of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease but are not useful for diagnosis.
_raw_ans: 26. D. OGD This man most likely has gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. The differential diagnosis includes oesophageal or gastric malignancy, functional disease, and peptic ulcer disease and the first investigation should be direct visualization of the oesophagus and stomach. A barium swallow would exclude tumours or stricturing but would not assess the mucosal integrity so well or allow biopsies to be taken. Twenty-four-hour pH studies may be useful to evaluate the severity or timing of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease but are not useful for diagnosis.

stem: A 41-year-old man complains of regurgitation of saliva and of undigested food. An esophagram reveals a dilated esophagus and a bird’s-beak deformity. Manometry shows a hypertensive lower esophageal sphincter with failure to relax with deglutition. Which of the following is the safest and most effective treatment of this condition?

It is thought that the pathogenesis of anal fissures involve spasm of the internal anal sphincter with associated changes in anal blood flow and poor healing. items.stem: A 45-year-old female with a history of CBD stones presents with acute upper abdominal pain, jaundice, and high-grade fever.
items.explanation: The triad of pain, jaundice, and fever with CBD stones supports acute cholangitis.

items.stem: A 50-year-old heavy drinker male presents with anal pain, distended abdomen, guarding, rigidity, and absent bowel sounds.
items.explanation: Guarding, rigidity, and absent bowel sounds in a distended abdomen suggest a perforated viscus.

items.stem: A 70-year-old male presents with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, blood-stained stool, a tender soft abdomen, and tachycardia.
items.explanation: Severe pain, vomiting, blood-stained stool, and tachycardia point toward mesenteric ischemia.

items.stem: A 16-year-old male presents with high-grade swinging fever, chills, and upper abdominal pain, is jaundiced, and has a history of bloody diarrhea.
items.explanation: The presentation of upper abdominal pain, swinging fever, chills, jaundice, and a history of bloody diarrhea suggests a liver abscess.

items.stem: A 29-year-old lady presents with right upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, fever, and a history of 40kg weight loss post-bariatric surgery.
items.explanation: Right upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with nausea, vomiting, and significant weight loss post-bariatric surgery indicates acute cholecystitis.

items.stem: A 34-year-old male presents with vague upper abdominal pain, nausea, a single episode of vomiting, and loss of appetite; later he develops blisters along his right lower chest.
items.explanation: The appearance of blisters following vague upper abdominal pain is characteristic of herpes zoster.

items.stem: A 43-year-old alcoholic male presents with vague abdominal pain for 3 months, weight loss, new-onset diabetes, and a history of similar severe attacks.
items.explanation: A chronic history of pain, weight loss, and new-onset diabetes in an alcoholic suggests chronic pancreatitis.

items.stem: A newly married lady presents with upper abdominal pain, nausea, and vaginal discharge; ultrasound reveals right hydrosalpinx.
items.explanation: Upper abdominal pain with vaginal discharge and right hydrosalpinx supports the diagnosis of Fitz-Hugh Curtis syndrome.

items.stem: A 24-year-old male is found to be HCV positive on preparation for thyroid surgery. The best antiviral agent with near 100% cure is:
items.explanation: DAA drugs directly target the replication of the Hepatitis c virus.

items.stem: A 29-year-old female with a history of bloody diarrhea 2 weeks earlier now presents with upper abdominal pain, jaundice, and rigor. US revealed an 8 cm cystic mass in the liver. Drainage revealed dark brown-red thick drainage fluid. The best adjuvant treatment option would be:
items.explanation: Metronidazole is commonly used for abdominal infections (And their complicated abscess).

items.stem: A 32-year-old male underwent appendectomy for perforated gangrenous appendicitis. Which drug should be given to the patient in addition to Levofloxacin to prevent sepsis:
items.explanation: Levofloxacin + Metronidazole are commonly used in acute appendicitis. Metronidazole covers anaerobic bacteria while levofloxacin covers aerobic bacteria.

items.stem: A 36-year-old obese lady with BMI of 43 underwent mesh repair for large ventral hernia. Postoperatively, she has severe necrotizing fasciitis with MRSA infection. She is allergic to penicillins & carbapenems. The best drug to treat MRSA in this patient would be:
items.explanation: Linezolid is used as an alternative to carbapenems and penicillin in patients who have drug sensitivity.

items.stem: A 41-year-old female will have an elective surgery. Three to five doses of this antibiotic is all that needed to prevent infection:
items.explanation: Second-generation cephalosporins, such as cefoxitin or cefotetan are commonly used as a prophylactic antibiotic prior to surgery.

items.stem: A 43-year-old male presents with recurrent acute pancreatitis. The best drug to counteract infection with deep penetration into pancreatic parenchyma is:
items.explanation: Meropenem is a broad-spectrum antibiotic with excellent penetration into pancreatic tissue.

items.stem: A 54-year-old male has exploratory laparotomy for perforated diverticulitis. In spite of adequate antibiotic coverage and abscess drainage, the patient is still toxic. Swab from his drainage revealed CRE or carbapenem-resistant enterococci. The best treatment now is:
items.explanation: Tigecycline is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that is effective against multidrug-resistant organisms, including CRE.

items.stem: An 18-year-old male is undergoing mesh repair for right inguinal hernia. The best drug prophylaxis to prevent infection is:
items.explanation: Cloxacillin is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin that provides effective coverage against a wide range of bacteria, including those commonly associated with surgical site infections.

items.stem: A 21-year-old female presents with progressive dysphagia over the past one year. She gave a history of long duration hospitalization after suicidal ingestion of a corrosive agent one year ago.
items.explanation: Ingestion of corrosive agent leads to progressive fibrosis and narrowing of the esophagus resulting in a complete stricture.

items.stem: A 33-year-old slim lady presents with progressive dysphagia. Workup with barium swallow and endoscopy revealed a hugely distended tortuous esophagus with smooth esophageal mucosa.
items.explanation: Findings are consistent with Megaesophagus.

items.stem: A 43-year-old alcoholic judge presents after self-induced vomiting with severe central chest pain, tachypnea, and tachycardia. CXR shows pneumomediastinum.
items.explanation: Self-induced vomiting in alcoholics may result in a Mallory-Weiss tear progressing to a ruptured esophagus known as Boerhaave syndrome.

items.stem: A 46-year-old obese male with a long history of using antacids for dyspepsia and heartburn presents with new onset dysphagia. Endoscopy reveals erythematous lower esophageal mucosa with goblet cells on histopathological biopsy.
items.explanation: Chronic acid reflux causes metaplastic change in the lower esophagus resulting in Barret’s esophagus.

items.stem: A 69-year-old lady presented with progressive dysphagia and recent hoarseness of voice.
items.explanation: Progressive dysphagia with compression effects (hoarseness of voice) is suggestive of Esophageal carcinoma.

items.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with vague right-sided lower abdominal pain, with nausea and loss of appetite & low-grade fever. Examination is near normal. WBC count is 14,000. US revealed free fluid in right iliac fossa and pelvis.
items.explanation: Presentation with vague right lower quadrant pain, low-grade fever, and free fluid is suggestive of Acute appendicitis.

items.stem: A 21-year-old female has colicky central & lower abdominal pain with diarrhea (7 times) in the past 24 hours with tenesmus. The abdomen is soft and not tender. Two of her children have similar conditions 2 days earlier.
items.explanation: Colicky pain and diarrhea with family involvement indicate Acute enterocolitis.

items.stem: A 23-year-old male presents with vague upper abdominal pain. Abdominal examination is normal. Sclera shows slight yellowish discoloration.
items.explanation: Upper abdominal pain with jaundice suggests Acute hepatitis.

items.stem: A 25-year-old female presents with acute central abdominal pain with bilious vomiting. Examination shows a distended abdomen with normal shaped gridiron scar. Bowel sounds are exaggerated.
items.explanation: Bilious vomiting with abdominal distension and exaggerated bowel sounds indicate Acute intestinal obstruction.

items.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with severe right upper abdominal pain over the past 7 days. Abdominal exam is completely normal apart from some rash over the right loin that appeared few days after pain. US of abdomen is normal. WBC count is 7,000.
items.explanation: The presence of a rash following severe pain in a normal exam is indicative of Herpes Zoster.

items.stem: A 36-year-old female presents with excruciating epigastric pain over the past 24 hours that radiates to the back. Examination revealed tender upper abdomen with guarding. US is nearly normal apart from several tiny gallstones with normal wall thickness of gallbladder. WBC count is 13,000.
items.explanation: Excruciating epigastric pain radiating to the back with guarding is consistent with Acute pancreatitis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old female with BMI of 52 presents with acute upper abdominal pain with jaundice and high-grade swinging fever. She declared a history of common bile duct stones the month earlier.
items.explanation: Jaundice with high-grade fever and a history of bile duct stones are characteristic of Acute cholangitis.

items.stem: A 59-year-old heavy smoker male presents with exquisite diffuse abdominal pain. Abdomen is distended with generalized tenderness & rigidity. Bowel sounds are absent.
items.explanation: Perforated viscus Diffuse abdominal pain with rigidity and absent bowel sounds points toward a Perforated viscus.

items.stem: A 70-year-old male has severe abdominal pain with twice vomiting over the past 24 hours. His stool is blood-stained. Examination shows mildly tender soft abdomen. His pulse is 110 completely irregular.
items.explanation: Mesenteric ischemia Severe pain with vomiting, blood-stained stool, and irregular pulse suggest Mesenteric ischemia.

options: CT scan abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

A 34-year-old male presents with heavy bleeding per rectum with clots. His pulse is thready (120 beats/min), and blood pressure is 70/40. The best initial test is:
A 40-year-old female presents with dyspepsia. CT scan of the abdomen revealed a cystic mass of the body of the pancreas. The best test to differentiate cystic neoplasm from pseudocysts is:
A 42-year-old male presents with obstructive jaundice. She had a history of gallstones for 3 years. The best test to reach the cause of jaundice, as well as it can be therapeutic, is:
A 44-year-old male presents with recurrent symptoms after he had fundoplication for GERD 5 years ago. The best test to detect esophageal shortening is:
A 57-year-old female presents with bleeding per rectum with her stool. DRE revealed large piles. The next test would be:

A 70-year-old male presents with jaundice and itching. Further workup revealed inoperable cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor). ERCP stenting to relieve jaundice failed. The next logical step would be:
It is a mandatory follow-up test for patients with ulcerative colitis.

A 25-year-old man presents to the surgical clinic with a 3-month history of passing loose, bloody motions up to 10/day associated with fever and weight loss. Stool analysis did not show bacteria or parasites.
items.explanation: Bloody diarrhea, fever, and weight loss in a young adult are typical of ulcerative colitis, an inflammatory bowel disease. Stool analysis not showing bacteria or parasites is consistent with the diagnosis of ulcerative colitis.

items.stem: A 35-year-old 7-month pregnant lady complains of progressively protruding painless anal mass with passage of drops of blood with, and shortly after defecation. She has no change in bowel habit.
items.explanation: Hemorrhoids are common in pregnancy due to the increased pressure on the pelvic veins.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of per rectal bleeding with passage of clots. He is medically fit apart from chronic constipation. Six months ago, he was hospitalized for an attack of left-sided lower abdominal pain with fever, for which he received antibiotics and antispasmodics.
items.explanation: Chronic constipation and recent episode of left-sided abdominal pain with fever suggest diverticular disease. The presence of clots in the stool indicates active bleeding from the colon, which is a potential complication of diverticular disease.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman presents to the surgical clinic with a 3-week history of passing fresh blood and mucus per rectum. She denies a change in bowel habit but does reveal weight loss of at least 5 kg over the past month.
items.explanation: Severe weight loss, and elderly patient suggests malignancy. Colorectal cancer is usually associated with stool mixed with blood, but it can sometimes present with fresh blood and mucus.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man presents with frequent nosebleeds and heavy bleeding after dental extraction.
A 25-year-old woman complains of difficulty swallowing and pain behind the sternum.
A 30-year-old man presents with melena and hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals an arterial bleeding lesion in the stomach.
A 35-year-old man presents with spontaneous bruising and prolonged bleeding after a minor cut.
A 40-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent nosebleeds and telangiectasias on her face, lips, and fingers.

A 45-year-old sales executive presents with an episode of hematemesis amounting to about 500 ml in volume. He has a recent history of a gnawing pain in the upper abdomen, which radiates to the back and is relieved by eating. His weight is stable.

A 50-year-old office worker developed nausea and vomiting after a party during which he drank 10 pints of beer. Initially, he brought up gastric contents, but later he noticed a considerable amount of blood in the vomitus.
A 50-year-old woman with a history of heavy menstrual bleeding presents with easy bruising and petechiae on the skin.
A 60-year-old man presents with anemia and epigastric discomfort. Endoscopy reveals small punctate lesions in the gastric mucosa.
A 60-year-old vagrant presents with recurrent hematemesis but is hemodynamically stable. He has palmar erythema, spider naevi, splenomegaly, and ascites.
A 70-year-old retired man is admitted with a history of weight loss, poor appetite, and upper abdominal pain. He has had a few episodes of hematemesis, although the amount of blood loss is minimal.
A 43 old pregnant lady present with painless left groin swelling that disappears on lying in bed. On exam, there are bilateral tortuous veins in her legs.

36 year old lady with history of sleeve gastrectomy 8 months ago presents with tender swelling below her right groin crease. It is associated with central colicky abdominal pain with bilious vomiting.

A 48-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of a lump in the Rt. groin. On examination, the lump is above and medial to the pubic tubercle. There is an expansile impulse on coughing and the lump reduces spontaneously on lying down.

A 56-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with a 3-month history of pigmented lesion (male) on her right shin that has been increasing in size. She also complains of weight loss. Examination reveals three firm round swellings below the inguinal ligament.
A 63 year farmer presents with backache, fever, night sweats and a lump in his examination, there is tenderness in the thoracolumbar spine and fluctuating groin swelling.
