items.stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and with vomiting. On examination, there is tenderness and guarding in the epigastrium. His pulse is 118 beats/min and his blood pressure is 96/68 mmHg.
items.explanation: Serum amylase is the initial test to confirm acute pancreatitis.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis presents with acute severe abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, the abdomen is rigid and bowel sounds are absent.
items.explanation: Erect chest X-ray identifies free intraperitoneal air in suspected perforation.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset right iliac fossa pain with nausea and vomiting. She was admitted last year with similar symptoms, which turned out to be torsion of an ovarian cyst. Examination reveals tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa.
items.explanation: Laparoscopy provides direct visualisation and treatment of pelvic pathology.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of severe central abdominal pain occurring 20 minutes after eating. He is reluctant to eat nowadays and has dropped a waist size. He has a medical history of intermittent claudication. Examination of the abdomen is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Mesenteric angiography is the investigation of choice for chronic mesenteric ischaemia.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man with a long history of gastro-oesophageal reflux presents with worsening dysphagia to solids, epigastric discomfort, and weight loss. An urgent endoscopy shows a mass lesion in the lower third of the oesophagus.
items.explanation: CT scan assesses the extent and staging of an oesophageal mass.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man presents with abdominal pain and distension. On examination, the pain is worse in the lower abdomen. An abdominal X-ray shows a single loop of dilated bowel that turns back on itself.
items.explanation: A twisted sigmoid colon loop on X-ray is characteristic of sigmoid volvulus.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a 24-hour history of central abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, she has a midline laparotomy scar but no other abnormality.
items.explanation: Postoperative adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with a 12-hour history of colicky abdominal pain and distension. An abdominal X-ray shows multiple loops of dilated small bowel and gas in the biliary tree.
items.explanation: Pneumobilia with SBO indicates gallstone ileus.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man underwent a semi-elective bowel resection for a caecal tumour 2 days ago. He is now vomiting and has not passed flatus or stool since the operation. On examination, his abdomen is distended but non-tender and bowel sounds are absent.
items.explanation: Absent bowel sounds and distension post-laparotomy reflect paralytic ileus.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought by her parents to the emergency department with a 12-month history of indigestion, nausea, and stomach upsets. She has a history of psychiatric problems and is under regular follow-up. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. A barium swallow shows an irregular, round filling defect in the duodenum.
items.explanation: A duodenal filling defect on barium study in a psychiatric patient suggests a bezoar.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has a long-standing hernia above and medial to the pubic tubercle that does not descend into the scrotum. The hernia is easily reducible and the patient is asymptomatic.
items.explanation: Observation is appropriate for an asymptomatic, reducible hernia.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman has a hernia in her left groin that is below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. On examination, the hernia is tender, erythematous, and irreducible, and the patient is complaining of colicky abdominal pain and vomiting.
items.explanation: Emergency repair is required for a tender, irreducible strangulated hernia.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has a hernia that is above and medial to the pubic tubercle and descends into the scrotum on standing. On examination, the hernia is reducible and the patient is asymptomatic.
items.explanation: Elective repair prevents complications of an asymptomatic inguinoscrotal hernia.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has a hernia that is below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. On examination, the patient is well and the hernia is painless but irreducible.
items.explanation: Urgent repair is advised for a painless but irreducible femoral hernia.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man has a scrotal hernia that has only been present for a fortnight. On examination, the hernia is irreducible but painless.
items.explanation: Prompt repair is indicated for a recent irreducible scrotal hernia.

items.stem: A 25-year-old mature student decides to enter a drug trial to fund his education. Routine blood tests on admission show an elevated bilirubin concentration in the absence of any other abnormality.
items.explanation: Isolated bilirubin elevation without other abnormalities indicates hepatic jaundice.

items.stem: A 39-year-old man develops jaundice after commencing rifampicin and isoniazid for tuberculosis.
items.explanation: Hepatotoxic drugs like rifampicin and isoniazid cause hepatic jaundice.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman is started on a blood transfusion after a lower gastrointestinal bleed secondary to angiodysplasia. Shortly into the transfusion, she develops fever, shortness of breath, and jaundice.
items.explanation: Hemolytic transfusion reaction leads to pre-hepatic jaundice.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and jaundice. On further questioning, she admits to having pale stools and dark urine.
items.explanation: Pale stools and dark urine indicate obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man returns from travelling around Southeast Asia and develops diarrhea and vomiting. A couple of days later, he suffers abdominal pains and notices that his eyes are becoming yellow.
items.explanation: Travel-acquired hepatitis causes hepatic jaundice.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl presents with central abdominal pain that localizes to the right iliac fossa. She also complains of a loss of appetite over the last 24 hours and nausea. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.8°C and is tender in the right iliac fossa.
items.explanation: Lanz incision is used for appendicectomy in the right iliac fossa.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman is undergoing elective caesarean section for a breech presentation.
items.explanation: Pfannenstiel incision is standard for caesarean section.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with known peptic ulcer disease presents with sudden-onset, severe epigastric pain. On examination, he has a tender, rigid abdomen and absent bowel sounds.
items.explanation: Midline laparotomy provides access for emergency peritonitis and perforated ulcer.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Unfortunately, the surgeons are unable to clearly delineate the anatomy of the area due to the presence of adhesions.
items.explanation: Kocher incision offers exposure for difficult gallbladder surgery.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman is about to undergo a Whipple procedure for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
items.explanation: Rooftop incision provides upper abdominal access for Whipple procedure.

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted to the emergency department with a history of abdominal pain, passing blood per rectum, and haematemesis. An urgent upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy are performed, but no active bleeding is noted. The patient is showing signs of hypovolaemic shock and is still passing melaena. Her haemoglobin drops by 4 g/dL over 4 hours.
items.explanation: Angiography localizes and allows embolization in ongoing GI bleeding when endoscopy fails.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with haematemesis. After initial management, she is sent for an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. The endoscopist sees a bleeding gastric ulcer with a vessel at the base.
items.explanation: Adrenaline injection achieves haemostasis in bleeding gastric ulcer.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman presents with fresh rectal bleeding. She also admits to a history of left-sided abdominal pain that is relieved by passing stools. Examination is unremarkable and the patient is haemodynamically stable.
items.explanation: Colonoscopy visualizes colonic source in stable lower GI bleeding.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with fresh blood loss per rectum. There is no haematemesis or melaena. He has no history of similar problems. On examination, his pulse is 138 and blood pressure is 80/42.
items.explanation: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy excludes upper GI source in unstable patients.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of passing blood per rectum. She complains of seeing small amounts of bright red blood on the toilet paper and in the pan. The patient is otherwise well.
items.explanation: Proctosigmoidoscopy evaluates distal anorectal causes in chronic bright red bleeding.

options: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of vague abdominal pain and worsening jaundice. She also complains of passing pale motions. The patient underwent a total colectomy for familial adenomatous polyposis at the age of 20. There is no abnormality on abdominal examination.
items.explanation: Duodenal carcinoma causes obstructive jaundice in FAP patients.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of jaundice associated with fatigue, itching, and dark urine. She has a history of early-onset rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, she appears very jaundiced and has multiple xanthelasmas around her eyes. Abdominal examination is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Primary biliary cirrhosis presents with pruritus, fatigue, and xanthelasmas.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a 1-month history of worsening jaundice and itching. He has lost 2 stone in weight over this time but denies experiencing any pain. On examination, the abdomen is soft and a mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant.
items.explanation: Carcinoma head of pancreas causes painless obstructive jaundice with RUQ mass.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man attends the emergency department with a productive cough and malaise. His routine bloods on admission show a bilirubin level of 45 µmol/L. The remainder of his liver function tests are normal.
items.explanation: Isolated hyperbilirubinemia with normal enzymes indicates Gilbert syndrome.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man is brought to hospital by his wife as he has developed jaundice over the last few days. He is slightly confused and is unable to give a clear history. On examination, he has a distended, tense abdomen and dilated superficial veins around his umbilicus. His liver is not palpable.
items.explanation: Portal hypertension signs in acute jaundice suggest alcoholic liver disease.

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl requests a colonoscopy after her older brother was recently diagnosed with colon cancer at the age of 21. Her mother died at the age of 28 from a caecal tumour. The colonoscopy shows multiple polyps throughout the colon. Histology shows these to be benign.
items.explanation: Adenomatous polyps in FAP are benign but premalignant.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man undergoes an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy following an episode of haematemesis. He is found to have multiple polyps in his duodenum, which are later found to be benign. It is noticed that he has multiple freckles around his lips.
items.explanation: Hamartomatous polyps with mucocutaneous pigmentation indicate Peutz-Jeghers.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of diarrhoea and muscle weakness. A colonoscopy shows a 2 cm sessile growth that has multiple projections.
items.explanation: Villous adenoma is a large sessile polyp with malignant potential.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with known ulcerative colitis undergoes a routine colonoscopy. A number of small projections can be seen throughout the bowel. These are confirmed as benign.
items.explanation: Pseudopolyps occur in ulcerative colitis from mucosal regeneration.

items.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents with one episode of per rectum bleeding. A lower gastrointestinal endoscopy detects the presence of a single, large lesion that appears to be on a ‘stalk’.
items.explanation: Juvenile polyps are pedunculated benign lesions in children.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man presents with a lump in his groin. On examination, there is a mass in the scrotum that disappears on lying down. There is no pain or erythema associated with the lump and the patient is asymptomatic. When the patient coughs, an impulse can be felt over the hernia.
items.explanation: A reducible hernia can be pushed back into the abdomen and shows a cough impulse.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a lump in the lower midline of his abdomen. On examination, you note that the lump is in the lower end of a midline laparotomy scar. The lump is 4 cm in size, and the contents cannot be returned to the abdomen by pressure; there is no cough impulse. The lump is neither painful nor erythematous.
items.explanation: An incarcerated hernia cannot be reduced.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a small lump in the groin, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. She also complains of vomiting and colicky abdominal pain. On examination, the lump is 1 cm in diameter, painful, and erythematous. There is no cough impulse.
items.explanation: A strangulated hernia presents with pain, erythema, and systemic signs of ischemia.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man who has a known direct inguinal hernia presents to the emergency department because his hernia has become painful over the last few hours. On examination, the hernia is irreducible, tender, and erythematous. The patient denies any colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, or constipation.
items.explanation: A Richter hernia involves only a portion of the bowel wall, leading to tenderness and irreducibility.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with a previous epigastric hernia presents with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, she is pyrexial and tachycardic and has a diffusely painful, rigid abdomen with no bowel sounds. Her hernia is noted to be erythematous and irreducible.
items.explanation: A perforated hernia with a rigid, painful abdomen and systemic signs indicates bowel perforation.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after vomiting large amounts of fresh blood. On examination, he is drowsy with a heart rate of 120/min and blood pressure of 92/50 mmHg. An urgent full blood count shows haemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, platelets 160 × 10⁹/L, mean cell volume 106, and an INR of 2.3.
items.explanation: Massive bleeding in an unstable patient suggests variceal hemorrhage.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with three episodes of vomiting that contained altered blood. He has recently started a busy job, has not had time to eat well, and also complains of a 6-month history of upper abdominal pain that is relieved by eating. He regularly takes ibuprofen.
items.explanation: NSAID use with epigastric pain relieved by food indicates peptic ulceration.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student presents with blood-stained vomiting. He was on a pub crawl last night and spent the latter hours vomiting and retching over a bucket.
items.explanation: A history of forceful retching in a young man points to a Mallory–Weiss tear.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man presents vomiting copious amounts of fresh blood. On examination, his pulse is 138/min and blood pressure is 68/42 mmHg. A per rectum examination demonstrates melaena and fresh blood. His only past medical history is an abdominal aortic aneurysm repair last year. he denies any medical history.
items.explanation: A history of AAA repair with massive bleeding suggests an aorto-enteric fistula.

items.stem: An 83-year-old man attends the emergency department after vomiting small amounts of fresh blood. He complains of a 3-month history of aching epigastric pain and a poor appetite with a weight loss of over 2 stone. He denies difficulty swallowing, and on examination, enlarged supraclavicular lymph nodes are found.
items.explanation: Chronic epigastric pain with weight loss and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy indicates carcinoma of the stomach.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of lower abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. Her abdomen is tender with guarding in the left iliac fossa, and her temperature is 38.2°C.
items.explanation: Lower abdominal pain with guarding and fever indicates an infective process treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman complains of a long history of abdominal bloating. She feels full after eating small amounts and tends to vomit soon after eating. She has a history of diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Endoscopy shows a dilated stomach with some stale food but no evidence of ulceration or obstruction.
items.explanation: Gastroparesis is managed with a prokinetic agent such as metoclopramide.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man attends the emergency department with a short history of epigastric pain and vomiting. On examination, there is some epigastric tenderness but no guarding. Upper endoscopy reveals inflammation and ulceration in the stomach, and a CLO test is positive.
items.explanation: A positive CLO test confirms H. pylori infection, which is treated with triple therapy.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of lower abdominal pain, dysuria, and vomiting. On examination, there is guarding in the left iliac fossa. A per rectum examination is normal, but there is evidence of a yellow vaginal discharge.
items.explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease is managed with ofloxacin and metronidazole.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with previously well-controlled ulcerative colitis presents with a 2-day history of severe lower abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. She is pyrexial on examination.
items.explanation: A severe ulcerative colitis flare is managed with steroids.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with intermittent severe retrosternal chest pains that occur soon after eating and are accompanied by dysphagia. She complains of no other symptoms. An ECG shows no acute abnormality and cardiac enzymes are normal.
items.explanation: Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes intermittent chest pain and dysphagia with normal cardiac workup.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of dysphagia and odynophagia. this initially occurred with solids, but he is now finding it difficult to drink liquids. Over the past months, he has lost 12 kg in weight. Examination is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) and weight loss are red flags for oesophageal carcinoma.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man, who has recently arrived in the country from Brazil, presents with a 5-month history of dysphagia for solids and liquids. He is otherwise fit and well, and examination demonstrates no other abnormality. A chest X-ray shows an air–”uid level behind the heart.
items.explanation: Chagas disease causes achalasia-like dysphagia with radiographic air–fluid level.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of increasing difficulty in swallowing. You notice that his speech is a little slurred, and his wife tells you that this is a new development. On examination, his tongue is wasted and shows fasciculations.
items.explanation: Bulbar palsy presents with dysphagia, dysarthria, and tongue fasciculations.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with retrosterwnal pain and dysphagia. He is currently on a course of prednisolone for an exacerbation of inflammatory bowel disease. On examination, you notice multiple white lesions in his mouth that rub off easily.
items.explanation: Oral thrush in an immunosuppressed patient indicates oesophageal candidiasis.

options: Laying open of the fistula tract

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman presents with a history of fresh rectal bleeding after defaecation. On examination, with a proctoscope, haemorrhoids are seen within the anal canal. The patient denies any prolapse of these haemorrhoids.
items.explanation: Injection sclerotherapy treats internal haemorrhoids without prolapse.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents with pruritus ani. On examination, she has an obvious prolapsed rectum.
items.explanation: DeLorme procedure repairs full-thickness rectal prolapse.

items.stem: A 22-year-old female with known inflammatory bowel disease presents with a constant discharge from the anus. On examination, two external openings are seen at the posterior margin of the anus, both of which are discharging faeculent material. An MRI scan shows a high-lying anal fistula that passes through the puborectalis muscle.
items.explanation: Seton insertion manages complex anal fistulae in IBD to preserve continence.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of pain around his anus, difficulty sitting down and fever. On examination, there is a 1 cm tender, erythematous lump adjacent to the anal margin. No other abnormality is evident.
items.explanation: Incision and drainage is definitive for anal abscess.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 7-day history of severe stinging pain in the anus on defaecation, associated with fresh blood on the toilet paper. Examination reveals a tight anal tone and a lone skin tag on the posterior margin of the anus.
items.explanation: Topical diltiazem reduces sphincter spasm in fissure healing.

items.stem: A hernia that has two parts, each lying on either side of the inferior epigastric artery.
items.explanation: Pantaloon hernia has sacs on both sides of the inferior epigastric vessels.

items.stem: A hernia that passes through the greater sciatic foramen.
items.explanation: Gluteal hernia protrudes through the greater sciatic foramen.

items.stem: A hernia that contains a ‘W’ loop of intestine within its sac.
items.explanation: Maydl’s hernia contains a ‘W’-shaped loop of bowel.

items.stem: A hernia that arises from the triangle of Petit.
items.explanation: Lumbar hernia arises through the triangle of Petit.

items.stem: A hernia that contains the appendix within its sac.
items.explanation: Amyand’s hernia contains the appendix in the sac.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of left iliac fossa pain and nausea. Further questioning reveals that she is also suffering pain on micturation. On examination, there is tenderness and guarding in the left iliac fossa as well as some tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Her temperature is 37.6°C.
items.explanation: PID presents with lower abdominal pain, dysuria, and LIF tenderness.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis presents with acute severe abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, the abdomen is rigid and bowel sounds are absent.
items.explanation: Rigid abdomen and absent bowel sounds indicate perforated peptic ulcer.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with an 8-month history of abdominal discomfort that is improved following defaecation. She complains of a regular change in her bowel habit, alternating between constipation and loose motions. On examination, her abdomen is soft and nontender. There are no obvious masses, and bowel sounds are present.
items.explanation: Chronic discomfort with normal exam and altered bowel habit suggests IBS.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of severe epigastric pain that radiates to his back and is improved on leaning forwards. On examination, he is jaundiced, with guarding in his epigastrium, but there is no evidence of haemorrhage. Observations are stable. Routine bloods are sent off, and the amylase returns at 248 IU/L.
items.explanation: Recurrent epigastric pain, jaundice, and elevated amylase point to chronic pancreatitis.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman undergoes a laparotomy for a perforated diverticulum. A few days later, she develops pain in the left upper quadrant that radiates to the shoulder, nausea, vomiting and rigors. Her temperature is 38.9°C.
items.explanation: Postoperative LUQ pain with shoulder radiation and fever suggests subphrenic abscess.

theme_label: Theme 62: DIAGNOSIS OF BILIARY TRACT DISEASE

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman presents with worsening jaundice and weight loss. An abdominal ultrasound shows dilatation of the common bile duct, and a subsequent magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatogram (MRCP) confirms an irregular stenosing lesion in the common bile duct.
items.explanation: Irregular biliary stenosis with weight loss suggests cholangiocarcinoma.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of abdominal pain. On examination, she is clinically jaundiced and tender in the right upper quadrant, but no masses are palpable. An ultrasound scan confirms the presence of biliary stones and intrahepatic duct dilatation. An MRCP shows a gallstone within the gallbladder pressing on the common bile duct.
items.explanation: Impacted gallstone compressing CBD is characteristic of Mirizzi syndrome.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with known gallstones presents with a 12-month history of indigestion attacks and flatulence. Symptoms occur after meals and can last up to an hour. On examination, she is obese but shows no signs of jaundice or anaemia. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender.
items.explanation: Recurrent dyspeptic symptoms from gallstones indicate chronic cholecystitis.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man with ulcerative colitis presents with a 4-week history of worsening jaundice. He denies any pain, fevers or nausea. On examination, his abdomen is soft. An abdominal ultrasound shows dilatation of the intrahepatic biliary tree but a normal common bile duct.
items.explanation: Intrahepatic duct dilatation in UC patient indicates primary sclerosing cholangitis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 48-hour history of right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. On examination, she is clinically jaundiced and her temperature is 38.5°C. An abdominal ultrasound shows multiple stones in the gallbladder and a common bile duct diameter of 9 mm.
items.explanation: RUQ pain, fever, and jaundice with duct dilatation define ascending cholangitis.

items.stem: An 86-year-old woman with intermittent bright-red rectal bleeding, normal barium enema and colonoscopy.
items.explanation: Painless intermittent bleeding in elderly suggests angiodysplasia.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with 2 days of loose, blood-stained motions, abdominal tenderness, and vomiting.
items.explanation: Loose, blood-stained stools with tenderness and vomiting indicate infective colitis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with a single episode of fresh rectal bleeding, 6 months of worsening constipation and LIF pain relieved by defaecation.
items.explanation: Fresh bleeding with left-sided discomfort relieved by defaecation suggests diverticular disease.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with 3 weeks of alternating constipation and diarrhoea, occasional fresh blood, haemorrhoids on exam.
items.explanation: Change in bowel habit with bleeding in older patient raises suspicion for colorectal cancer.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl with 4 weeks of RIF pain, occasional blood and mucus, palpable RIF mass.
items.explanation: RIF pain with blood, mucus, and palpable mass suggests Crohn’s disease.

items.stem: A term baby is born with large amounts of visible intestine emerging from of his abdomen. The external gut is covered with a thin membrane.
items.explanation: Exomphalos is a congenital midline hernia with viscera in a membranous sac.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a lower midline mass that is 8 cm in size. He has a history of an emergency laparotomy for toxic megacolon secondary to ulcerative colitis. On examination, the mass is soft, non tender and reducible.
items.explanation: Incisional hernia occurs at a previous surgical scar.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with two groin lumps, one on each side. On examination, the lumps have a cough impulse and are reducible but do not extend into the scrotum.
items.explanation: Direct inguinal hernias are medial to epigastric vessels and do not descend into the scrotum.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with colicky abdominal pain and an abdominal lump. On examination, the lump is in the midline just above the umbilicus and is tender to touch.
items.explanation: Paraumbilical hernias occur adjacent to the umbilicus and can be tender.

items.stem: A 39-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a ‘tearing’ pain in his upper abdomen after trying to lift weights at home. On examination, you find a 2 cm lump at the site of the pain in the midline of the abdomen, halfway between the xiphisternum and the umbilicus.
items.explanation: Epigastric hernias occur between xiphisternum and umbilicus, often symptomatic with strain.

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl presents with a 1-week history of right lower quadrant pain, nausea and anorexia. In the last 24 hours, she has become more unwell, developing spiking fevers and rigors. On examination, she appears mildly jaundiced. Her liver is enlarged and tender to palpation.
items.explanation: Pyogenic abscess causes fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a long history of vague abdominal pain. She denies any other symptoms, but she mentions that she was admitted to hospital last year with a bleed in her brain. On examination, there is massive, nodular hepatomegaly.
items.explanation: Polycystic disease leads to massive nodular liver enlargement.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man attends his general practice with a history of excessive thirst and urinary frequency. On examination, he appears to be tanned, although he denies going abroad over the winter months. The liver is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.
items.explanation: Haemochromatosis presents with bronze skin, diabetes, and hepatomegaly.

items.stem: A 39-year-old man from India presents with a 2-week history of aching abdominal pain and weight loss. His past medical history includes eczema and a fractured femur in a car crash 20 years ago for which he received a blood transfusion. On examination, his abdomen is tender in the right hypochondrium and is mildly distended with a fluid thrill. His liver is enlarged and nodular.
items.explanation: HCC presents with nodular liver, weight loss, and portal hypertension.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset severe upper abdominal pain. She takes the oral contraceptive pill, but has no other medical history. On examination, she is slim but has a distended abdomen that is positive for shifting dullness. The liver is palpable three finger breadths below the costal margin.
items.explanation: Budd-Chiari presents with ascites and hepatomegaly in hypercoagulable states.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of left upper quadrant pain, which is worse on inspiration, malaise and fevers. He also complains of a cough productive of green sputum. Abdominal examination is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Supine CXR assesses diaphragm and lung bases for referred pain.

items.stem: A 56-year-old sheep farmer presents to his general practitioner with a 2-month history of abdominal aches and worsening jaundice. He denies weight loss or any other symptoms. On examination, a smooth mass can be felt in the right upper quadrant. An abdominal X-ray shows flecks of calcification in the right upper quadrant, separate to the liver and gallbladder.
items.explanation: CT scan characterizes abdominal masses and calcifications.

items.stem: An 84-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of severe, colicky, central abdominal pain. On arrival, she is pale and sweaty, with an irregularly irregular pulse of 125/min and a blood pressure of 105/68 mmHg. There is diffuse tenderness on abdominal examination, and per rectum exam reveals fresh blood.
items.explanation: Mesenteric angiography localizes ischaemia in acute GI bleeding.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of severe epigastric pain that radiates to his back and is improved on leaning forward. On examination, he is jaundiced, with guarding in the epigastrium. There is no evidence of bruising. Observations are stable. Routine bloods are sent off and the amylase returns at 132 IU/L.
items.explanation: Faecal elastase tests pancreatic exocrine function in chronic pancreatitis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with sudden-onset tight epigastric pain that radiates up to his neck. He is also nauseated and is sweating. On examination, the abdomen is soft and non-tender. Bowel sounds are present and a per rectum exam is unremarkable. The pain is only relieved by morphine.
items.explanation: Troponin rules out MI in atypical epigastric pain.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of pruritus ani and occasional fresh blood on the toilet paper. He denies pain on defaecation. On examination, there is evidence of ulceration at the anal margin.
items.explanation: Anal ulceration and bleeding in an elderly patient suggest carcinoma.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a long history of intermittent pain in the rectum. The pain tends to occur at night. He denies passing any blood or mucous per rectum. Examination is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Brief, recurrent nocturnal pain with normal exam indicates proctalgia fugax.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman complains of a stinging pain that occurs on defecation. This has been occurring for over a month. Rectal examination is very painful and there is a skin tag at the anal verge.
items.explanation: Painful defaecation and skin tag are classic for anal fissure.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset anal pain that occurred while straining at the toilet. On examination, a smooth, dark lump can be seen at the anal verge.
items.explanation: Sudden painful dark lump at anal verge is a perianal haematoma.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man presents with a long history of pruritus ani. On examination, large pink, confluent lesions are seen around the anus.
items.explanation: Warty confluent lesions around anus are condylomata acuminata.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman presents with dysphagia that is equally apparent with solids and liquids. She also complains of regurgitation of food, which usually occurs on lying flat. She otherwise feels well, but admits to losing 5 kg in weight over the past 3 months. A chest X-ray shows an air–fluid level behind the heart, a double right heart border and absence of the gastric air bubble.
items.explanation: Manometry is diagnostic gold standard for achalasia.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with occasional retrosternal chest pain that is worse on bending and lying flat. The pain is not relieved by analgesia. He also experiences a night cough. An electrocardiogram shows no acute changes, and troponin levels after 12 hours are negative.
items.explanation: 24-hour pH monitoring confirms GERD.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of lethargy, occasional blurred vision and difficulty swallowing that is worse at the end of the day. She has no pain on swallowing and denies any other symptoms. Examination is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Tensilon test confirms myasthenia gravis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the general practitioner with a 2-month history of dysphagia and worsening shortness of breath on exertion. On examination, you notice that she has multiple telangiectasias on her face and tight skin around her fingers causing fixed flexion deformities.
items.explanation: Anti-centromere antibody is positive in CREST syndrome.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with pain in his throat after swallowing a penny coin earlier in the day. An X-ray confirms the presence of a foreign body in the duodenum.
items.explanation: Serial X-rays track passage of ingested foreign bodies.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a tender, erythematous swelling in the left groin. On examination, you find an irreducible, hard lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
items.explanation: Femoral hernia presents as irreducible lump below pubic tubercle.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with a groin swelling that descends into the scrotum on standing. On examination, the swelling does not transilluminate and you cannot get above it, but it is reducible.
items.explanation: Indirect inguinal hernia follows canal into scrotum and is reducible.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of heartburn and night cough. She denies any other symptoms. On examination, you note that she is obese, but no other abnormality is evident.
items.explanation: Hiatus hernia causes reflux symptoms without palpable mass.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man, who has a history of a laparotomy following a perforated peptic ulcer, presents with a tender mass underlying the caudal end of his midline scar. At operation, the hernial sac is found to contain a Meckel diverticulum.
items.explanation: Littré hernia contains Meckel’s diverticulum in sac.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with a lump in his abdomen that is associated with a dull ache. On examination, the lump is 2 cm in size and below the umbilicus. It is located lateral to the rectus muscles.
items.explanation: Spigelian hernia occurs lateral to rectus below umbilicus.

theme_label: Theme 70: MANAGEMENT OF BILIARY TRACT DISEASE

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department with a 5-day history of upper abdominal pain, nausea and worsening jaundice. She has experienced bouts of similar pains before, but has never previously had jaundice. On examination, she is apyrexial and there is mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant, but no masses are palpable. An abdominal ultrasound confirms the presence of a large gallstone in the common bile duct.
items.explanation: ERCP removes CBD stones in obstructive jaundice.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman complains of her first episode of severe epigastric pain, which occurred 2 hours after eating fish and chips. On further questioning, she admits feeling nauseated. There are no other symptoms. Her observations include pulse 96, blood pressure 126/80 and temperature 37°C.
items.explanation: Ultrasound is first-line for suspected biliary colic.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of worsening epigastric discomfort. On examination, the abdomen is soft, but she is tender in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant. Her pulse is 96, blood pressure 130/85 and temperature 38.5°C.
items.explanation: Acute cholecystitis managed with antibiotics then elective cholecystectomy.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman with known gallstones presents with a 3-day history of severe right upper quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting. On examination, her temperature is 39.1°C. There is tenderness and a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant. A full blood count shows a haemoglobin 11.8 g/dL and leukocytes 27 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: Percutaneous drainage indicated in high-risk acute cholecystitis with mass.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman presents with a 24-hour history of right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. On examination, she is jaundiced and her temperature is 38.5°C. An abdominal ultrasound shows multiple stones in the gallbladder and a common bile duct diameter of 9 mm.
items.explanation: ERCP extracts stones and decompresses CBD in choledocholithiasis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with known diverticular disease of the sigmoid colon presents with sudden-onset abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, the abdomen is rigid. An erect chest X-ray confirms air under the diaphragm.
items.explanation: Hartmann procedure for perforated diverticulum with peritonitis.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with rectal bleeding and a feeling of incomplete emptying after defaecation. A per rectum examination reveals a tumour 1 cm from the anal margin.
items.explanation: APR for low rectal tumour near anal margin.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman who presented with rectal bleeding is found to have a non-obstructing tumour of the sigmoid colon.
items.explanation: Sigmoid colectomy for non-obstructing sigmoid cancer.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with weight loss and rectal bleeding. An urgent colonoscopy reveals a non-obstructive tumour at the caecum.
items.explanation: Right hemicolectomy for caecal tumour with lymphadenectomy.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman who was found to have anaemia on her last admission to hospital has a lower gastrointestinal endoscopy arranged. She is found to have a high rectal tumour.
items.explanation: Anterior resection for high rectal tumour preserving sphincter.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents to the general practitioner with worsening dysphagia for solids. On examination, you notice that her tongue is smooth and she has deformed nails. Routine blood tests show a haemoglobin level of 9.0 g/dL (normal range 11.5–16.0 g/dL), with a mean cell volume of 70 fL (normal range 76–96 fL).
items.explanation: Oesophageal web in Plummer-Vinson causes dysphagia.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with dysphagia and a night cough – symptoms he has suffered for 6 months. He has recently been admitted to hospital with a chest infection. On examination, there is a soft swelling in the anterior triangle of the neck that gurgles on palpation.
items.explanation: Pharyngeal pouch presents with gurgling neck swelling.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with dysphagia and worsening shortness of breath. On examination, her pulse is irregularly irregular. She has a flushed face, and auscultation reveals a mid-diastolic murmur.
items.explanation: The combination of atrial fibrillation, a flushed face and a mid-diastolic murmur suggest mitral stenosis. In context with the dysphagia, there is likely to be extrinsic oesophageal compression from an enlarged left atrium.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman presents with occasional retrosternal pain and acid reflux. She denies other symptoms and examination is unremarkable. A chest X-ray shows an air–fluid level behind the heart.
items.explanation: Hiatus hernia causes reflux and CXR air–fluid level.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man presents with sudden-onset pain in his chest and neck with dysphagia. On examination, he appears unwell. An ECG shows no acute changes and cardiac enzymes are normal. A chest X-ray shows gas in the mediastinum.
items.explanation: Boerhaave syndrome shows mediastinal gas after rupture.

items.stem: An 18-year-old woman is seen with a 48-hour history of lower abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. On examination, there is tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa and no masses are palpable. A routine urinary β-hCG test is negative.
items.explanation: Appendicitis causes RIF pain with guarding.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset abdominal pain that she describes as moderately severe. She has a history of recurrent nose bleeds. On examination, you notice multiple telangiectasias around her mouth. Abdominal examination is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome presents with vascular malformations causing bleeding.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man attends his general practice with a 3-month history of central, aching abdominal pain. The pain occurs soon after eating and can last up to half an hour. Because of this, the patient has avoided eating and has lost a stone in weight.
items.explanation: Mesenteric angina causes postprandial pain and weight loss.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man who is currently undergoing treatment for a testicular tumour presents with a 2-day history of cramping abdominal pain, nausea, anorexia and diarrhoea. He denies any infectious contacts or eating ‘dodgy’ food. A stool culture comes back as negative.
items.explanation: Acute radiation enterocolitis occurs during radiotherapy.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband with a sudden-onset, severe abdominal pain. On examination, there is guarding over the lower abdomen. The patient’s pulse is 125, blood pressure 86/56 and temperature 36.5°C.
items.explanation: Ectopic pregnancy presents with shock and lower abdominal guarding.

items.stem: An 86-year-old woman presents with bright-red rectal bleeding. She had two previous similar episodes in the last month. The patient denies abdominal pain or any other symptoms. A barium enema and colonoscopy are performed, but no abnormality is detected.
items.explanation: In an elderly patient with painless, recurrent bright‐red bleeding and negative imaging, angiodysplasia (a vascular malformation often seen in the elderly) is the likely source of bleeding.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of increased frequency of motions. She describes these motions as loose and blood-stained. The patient also complains of generalized abdominal tenderness and vomiting. On examination of the abdomen, there is no guarding or masses. A digital rectal examination is unremarkable.
items.explanation: Acute onset of loose, blood-stained motions with generalized tenderness and vomiting points toward infective colitis, where inflammatory changes in the colonic mucosa cause the symptoms.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a single episode of fresh rectal bleeding. She denies having any abdominal pain, fever, weight loss or history of rectal bleeding. On further questioning, you ascertain a 6-month history of worsening constipation and left iliac fossa pain that is relieved by defecation.
items.explanation: Chronic left iliac fossa pain with a history of constipation and a single bleeding episode suggests diverticular disease; diseased diverticula in the colon can erode vessels causing fresh bleeding.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man attends his general practice with a 3-week history of alternating constipation and diarrhoea. He used to open his bowels once daily. On further questioning, he admits to passing fresh blood occasionally per rectum. A digital rectal exam reveals haemorrhoids but nothing else.
items.explanation: An older patient with a history of alternating bowel habits and rectal bleeding—even when haemorrhoids are found on exam—raises concern for colorectal cancer, necessitating further evaluation.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with a 4-week history of right iliac fossa pain that has become worse over the last couple of days. She admits to the occasional passage of blood and mucus over this period. On examination, a mass can be palpated in the right iliac fossa.
items.explanation: A young patient presenting with right iliac fossa pain, a palpable mass, and occasional passage of blood and mucus is characteristic of Crohn’s disease, where transmural inflammation causes local mass formation and luminal ulceration.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman has had 3 days of increasing epigastric pain, nausea, and fever. She is tender in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Investigations reveal a WBC of 17 × 10⁹/L, a CRP of 25 mg/L, and an aspartate transaminase of 67 IU/L.
items.explanation: Ultrasound scan is the investigation of choice for suspected acute cholecystitis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has had epigastric pain developing jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine for 1 week. An ultrasound scan has shown gallstones in the gallbladder and a common bile duct diameter of 10 mm.
items.explanation: MRCP is non-invasive and best for imaging a dilated bile duct in obstructive jaundice.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman is seen in clinic following an attack of acute pancreatitis. A recent ultrasound scan has demonstrated gallstones in the gallbladder and a probable stone in the common bile duct. She is being considered for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
items.explanation: ERCP allows diagnosis and removal of common bile duct stones prior to surgery.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man has had intermittent episodes of colicky epigastric pain, abdominal distension, and vomiting for 2 weeks. His abdomen is distended, tympanitic, but there is no evidence of tenderness or peritonism.
items.explanation: CT scan of the abdomen is most appropriate to evaluate possible bowel obstruction.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has had persistent and increasing epigastric pain with a loss of appetite and some pain after eating for 5 weeks. Abdominal examination is normal.
items.explanation: OGD provides direct visualization and biopsy for persistent epigastric pain.

items.stem: A patient with recurrent episodes of epigastric and right upper quadrant pain after eating, typically lasting 30 min to 1 h.
items.explanation: Painful biliary colic is due to gallstones in the gallbladder (neck/Hartmann’s pouch).

items.stem: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy the surgeon should identify and divide this structure which forms the inferior side of Calot’s triangle.
items.explanation: The cystic duct forms the inferior border of Calot’s triangle and must be divided.

items.stem: During an ERCP the endoscopist identifies and passes a cannula into this structure to take the required images.
items.explanation: The ampulla of Vater is cannulated during ERCP for imaging of the biliary tree.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has obstructive jaundice due to Mirizzi’s syndrome. There is external compression of this structure.
items.explanation: Mirizzi’s syndrome compresses the common hepatic duct externally.

items.stem: A patient admitted with pancreatitis undergoes an ERCP to remove stones from this structure.
items.explanation: Stones are removed from the common bile duct during ERCP.

unparsed: C. Common bile duct
D. Common hepatic duct
E. Cystic duct
F. Gallbladder

items.stem: A 37-year-old man has 9 months of worsening epigastric pain, weight loss, and loose stools despite acid reduction; gastroscopy shows multifocal ulceration of the stomach and duodenum without masses.
items.explanation: Gastrinoma causes excess gastric acid leading to multifocal peptic ulceration (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome).

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has 4 months of 5 kg weight loss and anorexia with 10 days of painless jaundice.
items.explanation: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma presents with painless jaundice and weight loss from a head-of-pancreas mass.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has 18 months of episodic lethargy, sweating, and aggressive behaviour precipitated by hunger and relieved by eating.
items.explanation: Insulinoma causes fasting hypoglycaemia with symptoms relieved by glucose (Whipple’s triad).

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has 12 months of prolonged watery diarrhoea, lethargy, and dehydration with hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia.
items.explanation: VIPoma produces secretory diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, and dehydration due to excess VIP.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man drinks 35 units of alcohol per week, has hepatitis C, and has 2 months of anorexia, weight loss, and epigastric fullness.
items.explanation: Hepatocellular carcinoma arises in chronic liver disease, causing anorexia, weight loss, and epigastric fullness.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has abdominal discomfort and loose stools after food with a weight loss of 5kg over 12 months and has developed poor skin and hair texture. She has haemoglobin of 8.3g/dL and ferritin of 7mg/dL.
items.explanation: The clinical features in this young woman are suggestive of coeliac disease; the most appropriate investigation is an OGD with duodenal biopsy.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man is under surveillance for Barrett’s metaplasia.
items.explanation: Surveillance for Barrett’s metaplasia is best achieved with an OGD with oesophageal biopsy.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has had progressive, intermittent right iliac fossa pain with variable loose stools and weight loss of 10kg for 2 years.
items.explanation: D. Colonoscopy — Best to assess suspected Crohn’s disease causing chronic RIF pain, weight loss, and diarrhea, with biopsy capability.  4.E. CT colonography — Frail elderly with COPD/CKD and anemia with RIF mass; safer, less invasive colonic evaluation than colonoscopy.

items.stem: An 84-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic renal impairment on long-term oral steroids has a palpable right iliac fossa mass. Her haemoglobin is 7.7g/dL and ferritin 9mg/dL.
A 63-year-old man admitted with upper abdominal pain and melaena for 24h. His heart rate is 108bpm and blood pressure is 98/45mmHg.
items.explanation: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding with melaena is best evaluated by an OGD with gastric biopsy.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with a 25-pack-year history of smoking takes regular ibuprofen for headaches. He has had 2 weeks of constant, worsening epigastric pain radiating to the middle of his back and has 6h of passing dark red and black stools with 2h of vomiting clotted red blood.
items.explanation: This patient has a severe upper GI bleed. In the absence of any alcohol history the diagnosis is most likely to be a bleeding peptic ulcer. Although gastric ulcers (either in the body or the antrum) may bleed very profusely as here, the lack of haematemesis and the back pain suggest the other likely cause of acute severe upper GI haemorrhage which is a duodenal ulcer with bleeding from the gastroduodenal artery. This is located deep to the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has several years of worsening difficult, painful swallowing which is worse with fluids than solids, and has recently developed nocturnal coughing and wheezing.
items.explanation: The patient has dysphagia. The progressive nature, her age, and the fact that fluids are more troublesome than solids point to a diagnosis of achalasia. This is characterized by failure of relaxation of the distal oesophagus.

items.stem: A 53-year-old man undergoes an OGD to investigate dyspepsia. Helicobacter pylori is suspected as the cause and biopsies are taken from this location.
items.explanation: *Helicobacter pylori* are most commonly found beneath the mucus layer in the pre-pyloric antrum of the stomach. A rapid urease test may be done on biopsies from this area although it is not the most accurate test for the presence of the organism; serum antibody status gives information on previous or current exposure but a CO₂ breath test is most sensitive for the active presence of the condition.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man has abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and diarrhoea. A serum tissue transglutaminase test is positive. An OGD is performed to establish a diagnosis and multiple biopsies are taken from this site.
items.explanation: The diagnosis is coeliac disease; the clinical picture is typical and the tissue transglutaminase is very strongly suggestive of the diagnosis. Biopsies from the duodenum are required to confirm the presence of villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intra-epithelial (T) lymphocytes. These should be multiple and taken from as far distal in the second part of the duodenum as possible since the first part often fails to demonstrate clear evidence of the disease. It is not usually possible to reach the fourth part of the duodenum (site H) during normal OGD.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has been vomiting violently for 3h after a take-away meal and the last three episodes of vomiting have been accompanied by streaks of fresh red blood.
items.explanation: The presentation is typical for a Mallory–Weiss tear of the upper GI tract lining. Although it may occur in the fundus of the stomach, the mucosa is more robust here and the most likely location is the distal oesophagus at the gastro-oesophageal junction.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had several years of progressive dysphagia and a ‘bird’s beak’ appearance on barium swallow. Balloon dilatation has failed and she requires surgery.
items.explanation: Failed balloon dilatation in a patient with a ‘bird’s beak’ appearance (achalasia) necessitates a cardiomyotomy (Heller’s operation).

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has longstanding proven gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and has severe persistent and debilitating symptoms despite maximal medical therapy.
items.explanation: Severe reflux disease refractory to medical therapy is best managed with an anti-reflux fundoplication.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has ongoing melaena in hospital. He has a proven proximal duodenal ulcer and has continued bleeding despite two episodes of endoscopic treatment.
items.explanation: A bleeding proximal duodenal ulcer that is refractory to endoscopic treatment requires duodenotomy and repair.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with no other medical co-morbidity has a carcinoma of the body of the stomach staged as T2 N0.
items.explanation: Gastric carcinoma is potentially curable by radical resection provided there is no evidence of metastatic disease. This includes anything more than local lymph node disease. With a staging of T2 the primary is confined to the stomach and N0 indicates no known nodal disease. Thus palliation, such as bypass, is only indicated for those not fit for resection. Being in the body of the stomach it is most likely that radical total gastrectomy is required rather than partial gastrectomy.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with invasive adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas involving the superior mesenteric vessels.
items.explanation: Carcinoma of the pancreas may be amenable to curative surgery depending on location and involvement of local structures. Tumours of the head may be resectable by pancreaticoduodenectomy but involvement of the major vessels effectively renders the tumour incurable. Since the tumour is involving the head, the most likely complication is gastric outlet or duodenal obstruction and a gastrojejunal bypass may be necessary to treat it. Obstruction of the common bile duct may occur but bypasses such as hepaticojejunostomy are rarely necessary with endoscopic and radiological stenting techniques.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man undergoes an operation for suspected appendicitis. However, an inflamed Meckel’s diverticulum is found and excised. Histopathological examination identifies another pathology within the diverticulum in addition to the inflammation.
items.explanation: Meckel’s diverticula can be associated with ‘peptic’ ulceration due to the presence of gastric acid-secreting mucosa but the perforation occurs in the normal ileal wall adjacent to the diverticulum. The small bowel is the commonest site of neuroendocrine tumours, the most common of which is a carcinoid tumour, and aberrant tissue, such as a Meckel’s diverticulum, may show a predilection for such tumours.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with small volume haematemesis following a prolonged episode of vomiting during an evening of binge drinking.
items.explanation: Forceful vomiting during binge drinking can result in a Mallory–Weiss tear, which is a traumatic laceration.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man with a history of smoking has a 2h history of acute onset epigastric and chest pain. His abdomen is non-tender and his pulse rate is 100bpm.
items.explanation: In a smoker with acute epigastric and chest pain but a benign abdominal exam, myocardial infarction must be considered.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with months of progressive dysphagia, weight loss of 4kg, and anorexia.
items.explanation: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss in an older patient is highly suggestive of adenocarcinoma.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man who smokes ten cigarettes/day has retrosternal burning pain after meals especially when lying down. He has some pain on swallowing with a sensation of food becoming ‘stuck’ in his throat.
items.explanation: Retrosternal burning pain with dysphagia in a smoker is most consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

items.stem: Associated with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and absent bowel movement.
items.explanation: A classic presentation of bowel obstruction.

items.stem: A patient presenting with generalized abdominal tenderness with evidence of free gas on an erect chest X-ray.
items.explanation: Free gas on an erect chest X-ray is diagnostic of a perforation.

items.stem: Associated with colicky abdominal pain in the left flank with radiation to the groin. Abdominal signs are usually minimal. The pain may be so severe as to interrupt one’s breath.
items.explanation: Typical presentation of renal colic.

items.stem: A medical student presents with severe upper abdominal tenderness and a serum amylase greater than four times the normal limit.
items.explanation: An abnormal amylase together with abdominal tenderness is a key feature of pancreatitis.

items.stem: Associated with sudden-onset severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back. A chest X-ray demonstrates evidence of a widened mediastinum.
items.explanation: The diagnosis is a dissecting aortic aneurysm in view of symptomatology and a widened mediastinum.- Bowel obstruction (H) typically features colicky pain, vomiting, and no bowel movements. - Perforated viscus (J) often shows free gas under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray. - Renal colic (C) presents with flank pain radiating to the groin. - Pancreatitis (B) presents with high serum amylase and severe epigastric pain. - Dissecting aortic aneurysm (F) can show a widened mediastinum on X-ray and tearing chest pain.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted with severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back. He has nausea and vomiting and is clearly dehydrated. He returned from holiday in Ayia Napa earlier today.
A 33-year-old woman is admitted with a 24-hour history of nausea, vomiting and absolute constipation. Her abdomen is tympanic with increased high-pitched bowel sounds.

A 57-year-old man is admitted with onset of abdominal pain initially in the left upper quadrant. He has been self-medicating with ibuprofen after spraining his left ankle playing squash. On examination the abdomen is rigid with no bowel sounds.
A 24-year-old woman is admitted with fever, rigors and severe back pain radiating to her left groin.

A 10-year-old boy is admitted with right iliac fossa pain of several hours’ duration. Initially, he has guarding and rebound tenderness. Pressing in the right iliac fossa also elicits the same pain. He rapidly progresses to having a tense abdomen.
items.explanation: - Acute pancreatitis (A) often follows alcohol excess or gallstones; dehydration and severe epigastric/back pain are classic. - Small bowel obstruction (I) presents with absolute constipation, vomiting, and high-pitched bowel sounds. - Perforated peptic ulcer (F) is suggested by sudden abdominal rigidity, typically associated with NSAID use. - Acute pyelonephritis (B) features flank pain, fever, and urinary findings. - Perforated appendix (E) presents with right iliac fossa pain progressing to peritonitis.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with altered bowel habit, crampy abdominal pain and blood mixed in with his stools.
A 40-year-old woman presents with a long history of indigestion, worse recently, black tarry stools and feeling lightheaded.
A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP following childbirth, worried about the fresh, painless red blood on the toilet paper.
A 22-year-old medical student presents to A&E with haematemesis and chest pain following celebrations on passing his finals.
A 17-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis presents to A&E vomiting profuse volumes of fresh blood.
items.explanation: .- Colonic carcinoma (B) may present with altered bowel habit, blood in stools, abdominal pain. - Duodenal ulcer (E) can cause melaena and syncope/lightheadedness. - Haemorrhoids (G) often cause fresh painless bleeding, especially post-childbirth. - Mallory-Weiss tear (I) follows heavy bouts of retching/vomiting. - Oesophageal varices (J) can cause profuse haematemesis, often in portal hypertension/liver disease.

items.stem: Associated with abdominal pain, notable distension and vomiting. It may result in perforation of the bowel.
Seen commonly in newborn babies where, typically, the left side of the chest is occupied by the bowel.
A hernia occurring through a part of the abdominal wall between the lateral border of the rectus abdominis and linea semilunaris, typically diagnosed by ultrasound.
A combined indirect and direct hernia whereby the hernial sac protrudes on either side of the inferior epigastric vessels.
A lump located near the groin which protrudes straight on coughing and is not controlled by pressure over the deep ring.
items.explanation: - Richter hernia (G) involves only part of the bowel wall, risking perforation. - Diaphragmatic hernia (J) in newborns often shows abdominal contents in the chest. - Spigelian hernia (I) protrudes through the Spigelian fascia. - Pantaloon hernia (B) is both indirect and direct around inferior epigastric vessels. - Direct inguinal hernia (A) often protrudes straight forward and is not controlled by pressure over the internal ring.

items.stem: A condition known to cause severe gastroduodenal ulceration due to excessive gastrin secretion.
A tumour of the lower third of the oesophagus thought to be the result of longstanding reflux disease.
A motility disorder of the oesophagus characterized by a “rat tail” segment at the lower oesophageal sphincter.
Associated with severe epigastric discomfort particularly at night and relieved by food.
A condition associated with iron-deficiency anaemia and swallowing difficulties.
items.explanation: .- Zollinger-Ellison (D) causes excessive gastrin leading to multiple or severe ulcers. - Adenocarcinoma (G) of the lower oesophagus often follows Barrett’s oesophagus. - Achalasia (A) shows failure of the LES to relax, “rat tail” on barium swallow. - Duodenal ulcer (F) is classically nocturnal, relieved by food. - Plummer-Vinson (I) involves iron-deficiency anaemia, dysphagia, and oesophageal webs.

items.stem: Associated with vomiting and the passage of redcurrant-like stool in children.
A bluish tender perianal swelling often resulting from constipation and straining.
Typically affects the right colon and associated with severe rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy may reveal the presence of dilated tortuous vessels and “cherry red” areas.
A pan-intestinal inflammatory disorder associated with deep ulcers in the mucosa to give a cobblestone-like appearance.

items.explanation: - Intussusception (B) in children can have redcurrant jelly stools. - Perianal haematoma (C) is a tender bluish swelling from straining. - Angiodysplasia (F) affects the right colon, can cause large bleeds. - Crohn disease (E) is transmural, can affect any GI segment. - Ischaemic colitis (J) often presents with sudden severe left-sided pain, rectal bleeding, and typical radiographic changes.
