items.stem: A patient presenting with recurrent pain in the right upper quadrant radiating to the tip of the scapula. There is no associated pyrexia.
A tumour presenting typically with painless jaundice, known to result commonly from primary sclerosing cholangitis.
A patient presenting with tenderness and guarding in the right upper quadrant with evidence of hyperaesthesia below the right scapula and pyrexia.
A patient presenting with abdominal pain, fever and jaundice as a result of Escherichia coli infection.
A female patient presenting with anorexia, ascites and abdominal discomfort with a background history of cirrhosis and long-term use of the oral contraceptive pill.
items.explanation: .- Biliary colic (G) causes RUQ pain radiating to the scapula without fever. - Cholangiocarcinoma (D) often presents with painless jaundice, sometimes linked to PSC. - Cholecystitis (F) features RUQ tenderness, fever, positive Murphy sign. - Cholangitis (A) has Charcot’s triad: pain, fever, jaundice. - Hepatoma (E) can be associated with cirrhosis, OCP use, and presents with abdominal discomfort and ascites.

items.stem: A 19-year-old male who was previously fit and well presents with generalized abdominal pain for 3 days which is worsening, weight loss, diarrhoea and dysuria. He is most tender in the right iliac fossa. He has no appetite and has been feverish.
A 35-year-old man presents with 5 months of colicky abdominal pain, weight loss and bloody diarrhoea with mucus. He has also been suffering from lower back pain for the last few months.
A 37-year-old man presents with acute sudden right testicular pain which radiates to the right groin, and has blood +++ in his urine.

A 35-year-old man presents with red blood mixed in his stool and weight loss over the last 6 months. He had a colonoscopy 5 years ago, but is an infrequent attender to his GP. His father died of colorectal cancer aged 46.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of left iliac fossa pain and a significant (PR) bleed of bright red blood which fills the pan. She has had alternating diarrhoea and constipation over the last year.
items.explanation: - Acute appendicitis (A) can present with dysuria if the appendix is pelvic. - Ulcerative colitis (I) features bloody diarrhoea; can be associated with back pain (e.g. sacroiliitis). - Renal colic (G) may present with testicular or groin pain and haematuria. - Familial adenomatous polyposis (E) has strong family history of early colon cancer. - Acute diverticulitis (B) can cause left lower quadrant pain and rectal bleeding in older patients.

items.stem: A 64-year-old labourer presents to his GP with increasing pain in his groin. He has had a lump for several years which usually disappears on lying. It no longer does so. On examination you can feel a mass in the right groin arising above the inguinal ligament. It is irreducible but bowel sounds are present.

A 57-year-old woman is referred to the surgeon who performed her laparoscopic cholecystectomy 2 years previously. She has developed a bulge, which on examination is in the midclavicular line in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. It disappears on lying down and “gurgles.”

A 92-year-old frail lady is admitted to hospital with severe abdominal pain, colicky in nature, with nausea and vomiting. A nasogastric tube is passed, but on abdominal X-ray, no bowel distension is seen. Close inspection of the film reveals the diagnosis.
A 31-year-old man presents to his GP with a mass in his left groin. It disappears on lying, is above the inguinal ligament and reappears on coughing. His brother had the same problem.
A 29-year-old woman presents to her GP with an abdominal mass following the birth of her first child. During her pregnancy, she had had an everted umbilicus and this has worsened after giving birth.
items.explanation: - Incarcerated hernia (D) is irreducible but not necessarily strangulated. - Incisional hernia (E) occurs at previous surgical sites. - Obturator hernia (G) often presents with obstruction but no obvious external lump. - Inguinal hernia (F) can be familial and appears above the inguinal ligament. - Umbilical hernia (K) often worsens after pregnancy or with increased intra-abdominal pressure.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of constipation and constant pain in the left iliac fossa. The pain has suddenly become much worse and she has collapsed and been admitted to casualty. On examination she has a tachycardia and is hypotensive. There is severe lower abdominal pain with guarding throughout the mid- and lower abdomen.
A 50-year-old obese woman presents with epigastric pain. On examination, her temperature is 38.5°C. She is tender in the upper abdomen and Murphy sign is positive.

A 22-year-old woman presents with pain in the right iliac fossa. The patient is anorexic, has not vomited, but had some dysuria and frequency. Her temperature is 37.5°C. The patient is flushed and has localized guarding in the right iliac fossa and suprapubic region.

A 72-year-old man presents with increasing constipation. He has colicky lower abdominal pain and has not passed flatus for 24 hours. Examination reveals a distended abdomen which is tympanitic on percussion.

A 60-year-old man presents with a 48-hour history of sudden-onset epigastric pain radiating through to the back after an alcoholic binge. Examination reveals the patient to be apyrexial, tachycardic and normotensive. The patient is diffusely tender, with guarding in the epigastrium. An erect chest X-ray is normal, but the blood gas analysis reveals hypoxia.
items.explanation: - Perforated sigmoid diverticular disease (H) presents with left-sided pain, sudden deterioration, peritonitis. - Acute cholecystitis (B) shows RUQ tenderness, fever, positive Murphy sign. - Acute appendicitis (A) can present with mild urinary symptoms. - Large bowel obstruction (F) leads to distension, absolute constipation, colicky pain. - Acute pancreatitis (D) causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, often after alcohol excess.

items.stem: An 80-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of abdominal distension and pain. He is vomiting faeculent fluid. He has not been feeling well for 3 months and has lost 2 stone in weight. Clinical examination reveals visible peristalsis in the midabdomen, distension and a mass in the right iliac fossa.

A 68-year-old woman presents with colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. Examination shows that she is dehydrated, with abdominal distension and a lower midline scar from a perforated appendix. Plain abdominal film shows multiple distended small bowel loops and the presence of air in the biliary tree.

A 60-year-old man undergoes emergency lumbar disc decompression. Postoperatively, he is immobile. He becomes increasingly constipated and develops a distended abdomen. Plain abdominal films show a grossly distended colon down to the pelvic brim.

A 78-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of vomiting faeculent fluid. He has a grossly distended abdomen and a palpable mass in the right groin. The mass is firm, slightly tender and lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

An 88-year-old woman with dementia is referred by her GP because she seems to be in pain and unwell. She has a long history of constipation. On examination, she has a grossly distended tympanitic abdomen which is nontender. The plain abdominal X-ray shows a large distended loop of colon.
items.explanation: - Carcinoma caecum (B) can cause subacute obstruction, weight loss, palpable RIF mass. - Gallstone ileus (E) shows pneumobilia and small bowel obstruction. - Pseudo-obstruction (G) (Ogilvie’s) can cause massive colonic dilation. - Strangulated femoral hernia (I) presents with obstructive symptoms, tender groin lump below/lateral to the pubic tubercle. - Sigmoid volvulus (H) often in elderly with chronic constipation; “coffee bean” sign on X-ray.

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman suffering with osteoarthritis of the hip is admitted with haematemesis and melaena. She has been taking ibuprofen in increasing amounts to control her hip pain.

A 77-year-old man presents with his fourth episode of acute rectal bleeding. The blood is a mixture of fresh blood and clots. On this occasion, the bleeding has been severe enough to require a 4-unit blood transfusion. A barium enema is undertaken and is normal.
A 56-year-old man presents with anaemia and weight loss. Examination reveals a mass in the right iliac fossa and hepatomegaly.
A 50-year-old alcoholic presents with melaena. On examination the patient is drowsy and hypotensive. Examination of the abdomen shows splenomegaly.

A 58-year-old man is admitted with acute onset of left iliac fossa pain. Recently, he has noticed he has had some vague abdominal pain and felt more constipated. On examination he is pyrexial, pale and has localized peritonism in the left iliac fossa. His abdomen is distended. Investigations show a haemoglobin (Hb) of 7 g/dL (hypochromic, microcytic) and a WCC of 18 x 10^9/L.
items.explanation: - Posterior duodenal ulcer (G) often erodes the gastroduodenal artery → haematemesis/melaena. - Angiodysplasia (A) can cause recurrent painless lower GI bleeding in older patients, with normal barium enema. - Caecal carcinoma (C) presents with weight loss, RIF mass, anaemia. - Oesophageal varices (F) cause severe upper GI bleed in portal hypertension. - Sigmoid carcinoma (I) may present with altered bowel habit, rectal bleeding, anaemia.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain. The pain is most severe when he is hungry and often wakes him from sleep at night. The pain is relieved by eating and by taking milk and snacks. The patient has gained half a stone in weight since his symptoms started.
A 19-year-old student experiences worsening dysphagia for 3 months. She has lost a stone in weight and has had two courses of antibiotics for a persistent chest infection.

A 55-year-old vagrant man has had a long history of recurrent episodes of epigastric pain. He presents with weight loss and severe vomiting. On admission, he is noted to be dehydrated and abdominal examination demonstrates a succussion splash.

A 65-year-old man presents with a long history of indigestion self-treated with antacids, but progressive dysphagia and weight loss for 3 weeks. On examination, the patient is anaemic and is markedly cachectic.

A 27-year-old man is admitted to the casualty with frank haematemesis. He has been on his stag weekend and after consuming large amounts of alcohol, has been vomiting repeatedly, and has some epigastric pain.
items.explanation: .- Duodenal ulcer disease (B) causes pain relieved by food, often leading to weight gain. - Achalasia (A) leads to progressive dysphagia, risk of aspiration. - Pyloric stenosis (J) often from chronic ulcer scarring → vomiting, succussion splash. - Oesophageal adenocarcinoma (H) arises from Barrett’s oesophagus, presents with dysphagia, weight loss. - Mallory-Weiss tear (G) follows repeated retching/vomiting causing a mucosal tear.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with flatulent dyspepsia, fatty food intolerance and right upper quadrant pain.

A 65-year-old man is diagnosed with oesophageal adenocarcinoma. The surgeon wishes to stage the local extent of the tumour and to assess whether there is local lymph node spread or invasion of the thoracic aorta.
A 70-year-old man presents with painless obstructive jaundice. He has undergone assessment by ultrasonography, showing a mass in the head of the pancreas. The surgeon wishes to stage the tumour.
An 80-year-old man presents with intermittent cervical dysphagia and has a soft swelling on the left side of his neck. He coughs and splutters after eating and often aspirates liquids.
A 59-year-old man has carcinoma of the stomach. He is suitable for surgical resection but the surgeon wants to exclude peritoneal seedlings before undertaking a laparotomy.
items.explanation: .- Abdominal ultrasound (A) is first-line for gallbladder and RUQ issues. - Endoscopic ultrasound (G) accurately stages oesophageal cancer locally. - CT scan (E) stages pancreatic cancer. - Barium swallow (C) evaluates a suspected pharyngeal pouch. - Laparoscopy (I) checks for peritoneal spread in gastric cancer.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman presents to her GP with a history of fatigue for 3 months, and 4 days of colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. Examination shows that she is pale and dehydrated, with a mass in the right iliac fossa.

A 72-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of increasing discomfort in her lower abdomen. She has not opened her bowels for 5 days but has passed flatus. On examination, she looks pale and dehydrated and the abdomen is distended and tympanitic. There is an irregular nontender mass in the left iliac fossa region.

A 25-year-old woman presents with acute onset of generalized abdominal pain. She has been unwell for about 2 months and has lost half a stone in weight. On examination, she looks unwell, has a pyrexia and a tender mass felt in the right iliac fossa with diffuse tenderness in the lower abdomen.

A 67-year-old man is seen in the outpatient clinic following an episode of severe colicky upper abdominal pain which has settled to leave some discomfort. He has a history of ‘indigestion’ after fatty food and alcohol intake of at least 4 units a day. On examination, he is slightly jaundiced, apyrexial and, on abdominal examination, has a smooth, nontender mass in the right hypochondrium.

A 45-year-old woman complains to her GP of tiredness and a dragging sensation in the lower abdomen. She has noticed that her clothes do not fit as well. On examination, she is anaemic and her abdomen is distended with a mass consistent with the size of an 18-week pregnancy in the suprapubic region.
items.explanation: .- Caecal carcinoma (B) can present with chronic blood loss, mass in RIF, subacute obstruction. - Sigmoid carcinoma (J) may present with altered bowel habit, distension, left-sided mass. - Crohn disease (C) can form an inflammatory RIF mass with fever. - Mucocoele of the gallbladder (G) is distension of the gallbladder (stone in neck) without infection. - Uterine fibroids (L) often present with a large pelvic mass and anaemia.

items.stem: An 80-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of a lump in the left groin. It has been associated with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and abdominal distension. Examination reveals a red, tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. The abdomen is distended, with high-pitched ‘tinkling’ bowel sounds.

A 75-year-old lady presents with a 3-month history of a right groin lump. It becomes painful when she walks, but disappears when she rests. Examination reveals a right groin lump with cough impulse. It reduces to a point above and medial to the pubic tubercle. She also has long-standing varicose veins.

A 70-year-old woman presents with a pretibial laceration but also mentions that she has a 4-week history of a lump in the right groin. It is completely painless but has gradually increased in size during this period. She had a melanoma excised from her right calf 2 years previously. Examination reveals a firm, nontender, irregular lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
An 80-year-old woman with recent onset of a leg ulcer presents with a painless lump in her right groin. She has recently had a femoral angiogram. On examination, there is a 3 x 2 cm pulsatile lump.
items.explanation: - Femoral hernia (C) is below/lateral to the pubic tubercle, can present with obstruction/strangulation. - Inguinal hernia (D) is above/medial to the tubercle, typically has a cough impulse. - Malignant lymphadenopathy (G) may occur following melanoma spread. - False aneurysm (A) can occur post-femoral artery puncture (angiogram).

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with fresh rectal bleeding, diarrhoea, profuse mucous discharge, tenesmus and lethargy. Investigations show that she is anaemic (Hb 10 g/dL) and has a potassium of 2.2 mmol/L.

A 50-year-old woman presents with a short history of painful, fresh rectal bleeding. She has a history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). On examination, she has a single indurated painful ulcer in the perianal region.
A 5-year-old girl’s mother brings her to the GP because of increasing problems with constipation and she has noticed some fresh blood on her clothes.

An 80-year-old man is admitted as an emergency with acute onset of profuse, painless, dark red rectal bleeding. He is normally fit and well and has no history of bowel problems. On examination, he is pale, cold, clammy, hypotensive and his abdomen is nontender.
items.explanation: .- Rectal villous adenoma (J) can cause mucus discharge, bleeding, hypokalaemia. - Anal carcinoma (A) presents as a painful indurated ulcer, often linked with HPV. - Anal fissure (B) often due to constipation/straining, bright red blood on wiping. - Angiodysplasia (D) can cause sudden painless lower GI bleeding in elderly.

stem: A 9-month-old child appears to have had a history of 48 hours of colicky abdominal pain described by his parents as episodes of crying and drawing his legs up to the abdomen. Additionally, he has passed some mucus-like blood from the rectum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The classic triad of intussusception includes colicky abdominal pain, red currant jelly stool (mucus-like blood), and vomiting.

stem: What is the most reasonable treatment for intussusception in this child?
explanation: Barium enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic in cases of uncomplicated intussusception.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?

The ribs are more horizontal and flexible.
The liver and bladder are intra-abdominal.
The infant’s head constitutes 20% of the surface area.
The infant has a large tongue, the larynx is high, and minimal access surgery (MAS) can be used at all ages.

The urinary bladder is an intra-abdominal organ in infants and children.
An infant’s head accounts for 20% of the body surface area.
Gluconeogenesis in infants is as good as in adults.
The infant’s immune system is immature.

Attention to thermoregulation is very important.
Postoperative management requires extreme care because of an inadequate stress response.

Blunt trauma is more common than penetrating trauma.
Splenic injury in the majority should be treated by splenectomy.

case: E. Minimal access surgery (MAS) can be used at all ages.

stem: Which of the following statements about inguinoscrotal swellings are false?
options: A hydrocele is a patent processus vaginalis, as is a hernia.
Hernia can be direct or indirect.
In incarcerated hernia, reduction should be attempted by taxis followed by operation 24 hours later.
A hydrocele always needs an operation.

stem: Which of the following statements are true for undescended testis?

The operation is recommended at the age of 2 years.
When a testis is impalpable and therefore intra-abdominal, laparotomy should be done.
Laparoscopy is the gold standard procedure for an intra-abdominal testis.

stem: Which of the following statements are true with regard to acute scrotal pain?

stem: What is the operation for congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis called?
explanation: Ramstedt’s operation is a pyloromyotomy that carefully splits the hypertrophied pyloric muscle while preserving the mucosa, and is the standard treatment for pyloric stenosis.

stem: A 5-week-old infant presents with a 1-week history of progressive nonbilious vomiting, decreasing urine output, but remains eager to feed. On examination, a visible peristaltic wave is noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: pyloric stenosis Progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting in weeks-old infant suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

stem: The diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is best confirmed by which of the following?
options: (B) careful clinical examination with palpation of an epigastric mass

stem: An infant with pyloric stenosis is evaluated for possible electrolyte derangements. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely?
options: (A) Na 145, K 3.0, Cl 110, CO2 17, urine pH 8.0
(B) Na 130, K 3.0, Cl 80, CO2 36, urine pH 4.0
(C) Na 135, K 4.0, Cl 104, CO2 23, urine pH 7.0

_raw_ans: 13. B) Na 130, K 3.0, Cl 80, CO2 36, urine pH 4.0 Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria is classic.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this infant with pyloric stenosis?

(C) change the infant’s formula and feeding regimen

stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with a 24-hour history of low-grade fever, anorexia, vomiting, and loose stools. On exam, there is fullness in the right upper quadrant and passage of a stool with blood mixed in. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: A neonate with bile-stained vomiting, abdominal distention, and dilated loops of bowel on plain radiographs with a small-caliber colon on contrast enema is evaluated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: A 1-day-old infant has persistent vomiting and no stools. An abdominal film shows a ‘double bubble’ sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: A 3-day-old term infant with progressive vomiting and abdominal distention—who passed meconium only after a glycerin suppository—requires which essential intervention before transfer?

blood and urine cultures, followed by initiation of broad spectrum antibiotics

stem: Upon arrival at the pediatric hospital, what is the best approach to establish a diagnosis?

stem: 6-week-old boy is brought to hospital with projectile and persistent vomiting. Weight gain has been poor. The child appears listless and quiet. A lump is palpable in the upper abdomen. Pulse is 100bpm, serum electrolytes are sodium 132mmol/L and potassium 3.2mmol/L. A provisional diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is made. Which is the single most appropriate initial intervention?

Administration of IV 0.9% sodium chloride (weight adjusted)
explanation: Hypertrophy of the pylorus can cause a gastric outlet obstruction leading to persistent projectile vomiting. This usually becomes apparent in the first 2 months of life. The vomit is high in potassium and chloride and the child may develop hypochloraemic alkalosis. A nasogastric tube will be very difficult to insert and will do nothing to correct any underlying electrolyte imbalances, neither will making the child nil by mouth. A test feed is helpful for diagnosis but the diagnosis may be assumed.

items.stem: A 2-year-old boy has been sent in as an emergency with vomiting for 24 hours. According to the parents, the vomitus was greenish to start with but over the past few hours has consisted of dirty brownish fluid. There has been no bowel action. On examination the child looks toxic and is dehydrated - sunken eyes, depressed fontanelles, loss of skin turgor. There is a tympanitic abdomen with a red, irreducible swelling in the left groin not noticed by the parents.
items.explanation: This scenario describes a classic presentation of an incarcerated inguinal hernia in a child. Bilious to feculent vomiting suggests a progressing intestinal obstruction, and the presence of an irreducible groin swelling confirms the diagnosis of an incarcerated hernia. The toxic appearance and dehydration imply that the hernia may be progressing toward strangulation. The tympanitic abdomen reflects bowel obstruction with gas accumulation. Prompt fluid resuscitation, nasogastric decompression, and emergency surgical intervention are crucial.

items.stem: Jonathan, a 5-week-old boy, has been vomiting intermittently for 2 weeks. This has become incessant for the past 24 hours. The vomitus is clear fluid. The infant seems hungry and takes its feed only to bring it up within a short while. The mother noticed some twitching of muscles. The baby is dehydrated. The paediatrician felt a lump in the upper abdomen when Jonathan was being fed by his mother.
items.explanation: Jonathan’s presentation is typical of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: non-bilious, forceful vomiting in a young infant, often after feeding, with persistent hunger and signs of dehydration. The palpable “pyloric tumor” in the epigastrium is a key diagnostic feature. Muscle twitching may indicate hypokalaemia due to metabolic alkalosis. Ultrasound or contrast studies can confirm the diagnosis. The definitive treatment is Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy.

items.stem: Mary-Ann, a 10-month-old girl, has been brought in with occasional vomiting for a couple of days. The parents noticed that the vomitus is sometimes green and at other times brownish. They feel that Mary-Ann is in pain intermittently, because she screams, flexing her knees and elbows, denoting spasms. They noticed that the nappy has bloodstained mucus. On examination she looks ill and dehydrated, and the right side of the abdomen feels empty.
items.explanation: Mary-Ann’s case strongly suggests intussusception, with hallmark features including intermittent colicky pain (flexing knees), vomiting (which may become bilious), and “red currant jelly” stool (bloodstained mucus). The right iliac fossa may feel empty due to telescoping of the bowel (Dance’s sign). This is a surgical emergency requiring urgent diagnosis (ultrasound showing target sign) and reduction either via air enema or surgery.

items.stem: George, a 10-year-old boy has been brought in with abdominal pain, vomiting, pyrexia and diarrhoea for the past 24 hours or so. He has been off his food for a couple of days. He has pyrexia of 39°C, tachycardia, looks toxic and has marked lower abdominal tenderness, rigidity and rebound tenderness, and the abdominal wall does not move with respiration.
items.explanation: George’s clinical picture is classic for acute appendicitis with complications, likely perforation and generalised peritonitis. High fever, tachycardia, and peritoneal signs (rigidity, rebound tenderness, lack of abdominal wall movement with respiration) all suggest a significant intra-abdominal inflammatory process. Diarrhoea is not uncommon in pelvic appendicitis. Children are prone to rapid progression and perforation due to a poorly developed omentum. This is a surgical emergency.

items.stem: Kerry, a 5-year-old girl, has been brought in by her parents with generalised abdominal pain, which has been recurrent over 6 months or so. On this occasion she looks ill, out of sorts and anorexic, and she has been vomiting. She has marked urinary frequency. On examination she has a temperature of 100°C, looks toxic, listless and dehydrated and has generalised abdominal and bilateral loin tenderness.
items.explanation: Kerry’s presentation is suggestive of a urinary tract infection, especially given the history of urinary frequency, systemic signs (fever, lethargy, vomiting), and bilateral loin tenderness. UTIs in young children may present with vague abdominal symptoms. The chronicity also suggests a possible underlying anatomical abnormality such as vesicoureteric reflux, which predisposes to pyelonephritis and renal damage. Investigations include urinalysis, ultrasound, and possibly a micturating cystourethrogram.

items.stem: Millie, a 10-year-old girl, has been admitted with generalised abdominal pain, vomiting and anorexia for 2 days. She has missed school a few times because of similar attacks of abdominal pain in the past, which has subsided on its own within 24 hours. On this occasion it has persisted. Examination revealed a well-looking introspective child with generalised abdominal tenderness without any rigidity or rebound tenderness, with the abdominal wall moving freely with respiration.
items.explanation: Millie’s recurrent episodes of abdominal pain without signs of peritonitis, and her well appearance on examination, point towards nonspecific abdominal pain. This is a common diagnosis in children with acute abdomen, accounting for up to 50% of cases. Psychosocial factors, stress, or constipation may play a role. There are no red flags like focal tenderness, fever, or urinary symptoms.

items.stem: A 2-month-old Down’s syndrome baby has been brought in with gradual abdominal distension and intermittent bilious vomiting with a history of delayed passage of meconium. The parents feel that the baby is unduly constipated. Examination shows a baby that has not been thriving normally, with a hugely distended abdomen and gross dehydration.
items.explanation: This is classic for Hirschsprung’s disease, especially with delayed meconium passage, chronic constipation, abdominal distension, and signs of failure to thrive. It’s caused by aganglionosis of the distal bowel, leading to functional obstruction. Common in children with Down syndrome, the diagnosis is confirmed by contrast enema and rectal biopsy.

items.stem: A prenatal ultrasound scan alerted the paediatricians to a congenital abnormality affecting the abdomen and chest. The premature neonate has been born with severe respiratory compromise and is on ventilatory support in the neonatal ICU.
items.explanation: Severe respiratory distress at birth with prenatal detection suggests congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The abdominal contents herniate into the chest, compressing the lungs, causing pulmonary hypoplasia. Initial management includes ventilatory support; surgery is delayed until stabilization.

items.stem: A neonate is born with frothy saliva and episodes of cyanosis. Any attempt to feed makes the symptoms worse. A fine orogastric tube is arrested. A plain x-ray shows that the tube is curled up in the chest and there is gas in the abdomen. The condition was suspected on prenatal ultrasound.
items.explanation: This presentation is textbook for tracheo-oesophageal fistula, especially the most common type (Type C): blind upper oesophageal pouch with distal tracheal communication. The inability to pass an orogastric tube and the x-ray findings confirm the diagnosis.

items.stem: A mother who suffered from polyhydramnios has given birth to a baby who has Down syndrome. The baby has bilious vomiting. The plain abdominal x-ray shows a ‘double-bubble’ appearance, and the condition was suspected on prenatal ultrasound.
items.explanation: Duodenal atresia classically presents with bilious vomiting and the “double-bubble” sign on x-ray. Strongly associated with Down syndrome and polyhydramnios due to impaired swallowing in utero. Surgical correction via duodenoduodenostomy is required.

items.stem: A neonate has bile-stained vomiting with passage of blood-stained stools. The baby is very sick, and a contrast meal shows the bowel mostly on the right side with a subhepatic caecum.
items.explanation: Malrotation often presents with bilious vomiting and can lead to volvulus and bowel ischemia. The contrast meal showing the abnormal bowel position (e.g., DJ flexure on the right, subhepatic caecum) is diagnostic. Requires urgent surgical correction to prevent necrosis.

items.stem: A 2-week-old neonate who was born with jaundice has exhibited increasing yellowish discoloration of skin and conjunctiva ever since birth. There are some superficial skin bruises.
items.explanation: Persistent jaundice beyond 2 weeks of life, especially if worsening, should raise suspicion for biliary atresia. The presence of bruising suggests coagulopathy from fat-soluble vitamin (K) deficiency due to cholestasis. Early diagnosis and surgical intervention (Kasai procedure) are essential.

items.stem: A few days after birth, a neonate has developed abdominal distension, blood-stained stools and bilious vomiting. The baby is toxic with septic shock.
items.explanation: This is a hallmark presentation of NEC, particularly in premature infants. Symptoms include feeding intolerance, bilious aspirates, bloody stools, and signs of sepsis or shock. Diagnosis is clinical and radiological (pneumatosis intestinalis), and management includes bowel rest, antibiotics, and possibly surgery.

items.stem: A 7-month-old child is brought to A&E crying inconsolably and drawing his legs up. He has had one episode of vomiting and has been passing bloody stools. On examination a small mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant.
items.explanation: Intussusception is the telescoping or invagination of a segment of bowel into an adjoining segment. It typically presents between 6 and 9 months with severe intermittent abdominal pain, drawing up of the legs, vomiting and ‘redcurrant jelly’ stools. Management begins with rehydration, electrolyte correction and nasogastric decompression, followed by an attempt at non-surgical reduction via air or contrast enema, with surgery reserved for failed reduction or perforation.

items.stem: A 6-week-old child is brought to A&E by his mother as she has been concerned about severe forceful vomiting shortly after feeding. He is reported to be constantly hungry. There is no history of diarrhoea. On examination the child looks dehydrated and malnourished. Gastric peristalsis is visible.
items.explanation: Pyloric stenosis (infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis) results from hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the pyloric muscular layers. It presents in early infancy with projectile vomiting, visible gastric peristalsis and often an olive-shaped epigastric mass. After stabilization with rehydration and electrolyte correction, the condition is treated with surgical pyloromyotomy.

items.stem: A newborn has failed to pass meconium in the first 48 hours and is reluctant to feed. On examination the abdomen is distended. Plain abdominal radiography shows distended loops of bowel with absence of air in the rectum.
items.explanation: Hirschsprung’s disease is due to the congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon, resulting in functional obstruction. Characteristic features include abdominal distension and failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life. Definitive diagnosis is via rectal biopsy, and treatment involves surgical resection or bypass of the aganglionic segment.

items.stem: A newborn with trisomy 21 has suffered several episodes of bilious vomiting from a few hours since birth. On examination the baby has a scaphoid abdomen. Plain abdominal film shows a large gastric bubble proximal to an air-filled first part of duodenum.
items.explanation: Duodenal atresia presents shortly after birth with bile-stained vomiting and a scaphoid abdomen. A characteristic ‘double bubble’ sign on radiography and its association with trisomy 21 guide diagnosis. Management involves stabilization with fluid and electrolyte correction, nasogastric decompression and surgical repair (duodenoduodenostomy).

items.stem: A 42-year-old alcoholic presents with hæmatemesis.
items.explanation: For the 42-year-old alcoholic with hæmatemesis, OGD examines the oesophagus, stomach and proximal duodenum to identify bleeding varices, which are managed with banding or injection sclerotherapy.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a history of weight loss and diarrhoea, noting blood mixed with his stools.
items.explanation: In the 65-year-old man with weight loss, diarrhoea and blood in stools, colonoscopy is conducted to visualize a right-sided colonic lesion and obtain tissue samples; CT is used for staging.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of worsening constipation and rectal bleeding.
items.explanation: The 74-year-old woman with chronic constipation and rectal bleeding is evaluated using flexible sigmoidoscopy to detect a left-sided colonic carcinoma.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of diverticular disease presents with suspected diverticulitis and shows no improvement after 24 hours of conservative management.
items.explanation: In the 65-year-old man with suspected diverticulitis not responding to conservative management, a CT abdomen scan is essential to assess for complications.

theme_label: Theme 6: MANAGEMENT OF PAEDIATRIC SURGICAL CONDITIONS

items.stem: A 7-month-old baby presents with a 2-day history of intermittent abdominal pain and crying episodes. On examination, there is a mass in the upper abdomen. The doctor notices that the baby has passed blood and mucus motions in his nappy.

A 3-week-old boy presents with a history of projectile vomiting that occurs a few minutes after every feed. There is no bile or blood in the vomit. His mother says that despite the vomiting, the baby is still hungry for feeds.
items.explanation: Pyloromyotomy treats hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

items.stem: A 3-day-old baby presents with a distended abdomen and bile-stained vomit. He is known to have cystic fibrosis. On examination, there are no masses in the abdomen and the rectum is empty.
items.explanation: Gastrografin enema relieves meconium ileus in cystic fibrosis.

items.stem: An 11-year-old boy presents with a 24-hour history of right iliac fossa pain. He has no other complaints apart from a cold that started last week. On examination, his temperature is 37.5°C and he has cervical lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests show a white cell count of 4.7 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: Observation is appropriate for non-specific RIF pain with mild signs.

items.stem: A 7-day-old infant who was born preterm presents with bile-stained vomiting, abdominal distension and bloody diarrhoea. He is tachycardic and tachypnoeic on examination. An abdominal X-ray shows distended bowel loops with some intramural air.
items.explanation: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are essential for necrotizing enterocolitis.

theme_label: Theme 7: DIAGNOSIS OF PAEDIATRIC SURGICAL CONDITIONS

items.stem: A newborn baby presents with bile-stained vomiting and abdominal distension on its third day of life. An abdominal X-ray reveals gas in the stomach and the first part of the duodenum, but nowhere else in the abdomen.
A 2-day-old baby presents with abdominal distension and bile-stained vomiting. It is noted that she has failed to pass meconium. An abdominal X-ray shows enlarged small and large bowel loops.
items.explanation: Delayed meconium and distension suggest Hirschsprung disease.

items.stem: A baby is born with its liver and some small intestine herniating through a defect in the anterior abdominal wall adjacent to the umbilicus.
items.explanation: Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect with uncovered bowel.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with a 2-day history of right iliac fossa pain, nausea and vomiting, anorexia, and diarrhoea. On examination, the boy is tender in the right iliac fossa, with no masses palpable. His temperature is 37.8°C.
items.explanation: RIF pain with systemic features indicates appendicitis.

items.stem: A 6-year-old girl presents with an episode of painless rectal bleeding. She complains of no other symptoms and she otherwise feels well. Rectal examination shows no obvious abnormality.
items.explanation: Meckel diverticulum is a common cause of painless rectal bleeding in children.

stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of liver cirrhosis and well known on the general medical ward after recurrent admissions for drainage of ascites. He presents with confusion, fever (38.5°C), ascites and abdominal pain. Which of the following investigations is most important to establish the diagnosis?
options: Stool culture and microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites
explanation: Ascitic fluid analysis is crucial in diagnosing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhotic patients.
_raw_ans: 1. E. Ascitic fluid white cell count Ascitic fluid analysis is crucial in diagnosing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhotic patients.

stem: A 30-year-old driver sustained an abdominal trauma after a road traffic accident. He was transferred to the emergency department in a haemodynamically unstable state. He was resuscitated with an intravenous fluid and a blood transfusion, after which vital signs became normal. An abdominal CT scan revealed a capsular laceration of 6 cm in depth in the liver. Which of the following grades of liver injury does this patient suffer from?
explanation: Grade III liver injury: A 6 cm deep capsular laceration exceeds the 3 cm threshold of AAST Grade II, thus meeting criteria for Grade III (moderate parenchymal disruption) requiring careful observation; In splenic injury with a tear confined to the capsule and in a hemodynamically stable patient, non‐operative management (with cross–match, ICU monitoring, serial CT imaging) is preferred, so explorative laparotomy is least indicated; In elderly patients with a femoral hernia—which carries a high risk of strangulation—prompt surgical repair is advised rather than conservative management
_raw_ans: 2. c. Grade3 Grade III liver injury: A 6 cm deep capsular laceration exceeds the 3 cm threshold of AAST Grade II, thus meeting criteria for Grade III (moderate parenchymal disruption) requiring careful observation; In splenic injury with a tear confined to the capsule and in a hemodynamically stable patient, non‐operative management (with cross–match, ICU monitoring, serial CT imaging) is preferred, so explorative laparotomy is least indicated; In elderly patients with a femoral hernia—which carries a high risk of strangulation—prompt surgical repair is advised rather than conservative management

stem: A 35-year-old man is involved in a motor vehicle collision where he was thrown against the steering column. He sustains a blunt trauma injury to his left upper abdomen. explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening problem requiring immediate treatment. A lung wound that behaves as a ball or flap valve allows escaped air to build up pressure in the intrapleural space. This causes collapse of the ipsilateral lung and shifting of the mediastinum and trachea to the contralateral side, in addition to compression of the vena cava and contralateral lung. Sudden death may ensue because of a decrease in cardiac output, hypoxemia, and ventricular arrhythmias. To accomplish rapid decompression of the pleural space, a large-gauge needle should be passed into the intrapleural cavity through the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line just above the third rib. This may be attached temporarily to an underwater seal with subsequent insertion of a chest tube after the life-threatening urgency has been relieved. Tension pneumothorax produces characteristic x-ray findings of ipsilateral lung collapse, mediastinal and tracheal shift, and compression of the contralateral lung. Occasionally, adhesions prevent complete lung collapse, but the tension pneumothorax is evident because of the mediastinal displacement.

stem: An 18-year-old man sustains a right-sided neck laceration after an assault. Which of the following is a relative, rather than an absolute, indication for neck exploration?
explanation: Acute signs of airway distress (stridor, hoarseness, dysphonia), visceral injury (subcutaneous air, hemoptysis, dysphagia), hemorrhage (expanding hematoma, unchecked external bleeding), and neurologic symptoms referable to carotid injury (stroke or altered mental status) or lower cranial nerve or brachial plexus injury require formal neck exploration. Pneumothorax would mandate a chest tube; the necessity for exploration would depend on clinical judgment and institutional policy. Additionally, all hemodynamically unstable patients with a penetrating neck wound should be explored, while management of asymptomatic, stable patients with neck injuries that penetrate the platysma is more controversial.

stem: Following blunt abdominal trauma, a 12-year-old girl develops upper abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. An upper gastrointestinal series reveals a total obstruction of the duodenum with a coiled spring appearance in the second and third portions. In the absence of other suspected injuries, which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
explanation: Duodenal hematomas result from blunt abdominal trauma, and they should be managed initially with observation in patients not undergoing laparotomy to rule out other associated injuries. They present as a proximal bowel obstruction with abdominal pain and occasionally a palpable right upper quadrant mass. An upper gastrointestinal series is almost always diagnostic, with the classic coiled spring appearance of the second and third portions of the duodenum secondary to the crowding of the valvulae conniventes (circular folds) by the hematoma. They can also be diagnosed with CT scans; no additional diagnostic workup is required. Observation is the initial management strategy in patients with no other injuries, since the vast majority of duodenal hematomas resolve spontaneously. However, in patients undergoing immediate laparotomy for other associated injuries, duodenal exploration with drainage of the hematoma is indicated. Also, patients whose obstructive symptoms do not resolve after 2 weeks should undergo exploration and evacuation of the hematoma in order to rule out a perforation or injury to the head of the pancreas.

explanation: Initial management of flail chest consists of adequate pain control and chest physiotherapy; intubation and mechanical ventilation are only indicated if respiratory compromise develops. Flail chest is diagnosed in the presence of paradoxical respiratory movement in a portion of the chest wall. At least 2 fractures in each of 3 adjacent rib or costal cartilages are required to produce this condition. The complications of flail chest are no longer believed to arise from this paradoxical motion, but rather the underlying pulmonary parenchymal injury with resultant hypoventilation can lead to atelectasis, pneumonia, and respiratory failure. Indications for mechanical ventilation include significant impedance to ventilation by the flail segment, large pulmonary contusion, an uncooperative patient (ie, owing to head injury), general anesthesia for another indication, and the development of respiratory failure. The indications for operative rib fixation are continuing to evolve, but immediate surgical stabilization would not be the initial management strategy for this patient. A right chest tube is only indicated if there is an associated pneumothorax and/or hemothorax. There is no role for a chest binder.

stem: A 23-year-old, previously healthy man presents to the ER after sustaining a single gunshot wound to the right chest. The entrance wound is 3 cm inferior to the nipple and the exit wound is just below the scapula. A chest tube is placed that drains 400 mL of blood and continues to drain 50 to 75 mL/h during the initial resuscitation. His blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg after 1 U packed red blood cells and 1 U fresh frozen plasma. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Chest x-ray reveals a reexpanded lung and no free air under the diaphragm. Which of the following is the best next step in his management?
explanation: Gunshot wounds to the lower chest are often associated with intra-abdominal injuries; any patient with a gunshot wound below the level of T4 should be subjected to abdominal exploration. The domes of the diaphragm are at the level of the nipples, and the diaphragm can rise to the level of T4 during maximal expiration. Exploratory thoracotomy is not automatically indicated because most parenchymal lung injuries will stop bleeding and heal spontaneously with tube thoracostomy alone. Indications for thoracic exploration for bleeding are 1500 mL of blood on initial chest tube placement or persistent bleeding at a rate of 200 mL/h for 4 hours or 100 mL/h for 8 hours. Peritoneal lavage is not indicated even when the abdominal examination is unremarkable. As many as 25% of patients with negative physical findings and negative peritoneal lavage will have significant intra-abdominal injuries in this setting. These injuries include damage to the colon, kidney, pancreas, aorta, and diaphragm. Local wound exploration is not recommended because the determination of diaphragmatic injury with this technique is unreliable.

stem: A 53-year-old man has a lump near his groin. It reduces on lying down and immediately reaches full size on standing. On coughing it protrudes straight and is not controlled by pressure over the deep ring. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bulges medially, not controlled by deep ring pressure.
_raw_ans: 47. B. Direct inguinal hernia Bulges medially, not controlled by deep ring pressure.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a lump in her groin. It is below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Femoral hernias present below and lateral to pubic tubercle.
_raw_ans: 48. C. Femoral hernia Femoral hernias present below and lateral to pubic tubercle.

stem: A 25-year-old woman complains of a painful swelling at the navel since birth. On exam there is an obvious swelling at the umbilicus. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Umbilical hernia Congenital defect at umbilical region, often present from birth.
_raw_ans: 49. A. Umbilical hernia Congenital defect at umbilical region, often present from birth.

stem: A 43-year-old man has epigastric pain and a tender, irreducible midline swelling. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Occurs in midline above umbilicus; often tender and irreducible.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has a lump at the lateral edge of the rectus sheath. Most likely diagnosis?

stem: A 65-year-old woman has 2 days of abdominal discomfort and vomiting, plus right-sided hip pain. An abdominal X-ray confirms small bowel obstruction. Emergency laparotomy is performed. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Elderly women; small bowel obstruction passing through obturator canal.
_raw_ans: 52. B. Obturator hernia Elderly women; small bowel obstruction passing through obturator canal.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy with sore throat, high-grade fever, and fatigue, which rapidly progresses to confusion post-splenectomy.
items.explanation: The presentation is indicative of Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI).

items.stem: A 52-year-old male develops shortness of breath immediately post-difficult splenectomy; breath sounds are absent on the left with hyperresonance.
items.explanation: Postoperative shortness of breath with absent breath sounds and hyperresonance suggests a pneumothorax.

items.stem: A 61-year-old male, 24 hours post-splenectomy, presents with low-grade fever and reduced left chest breath sounds.
items.explanation: Reduced breath sounds and low-grade fever post-splenectomy are characteristic of atelectasis.

items.stem: A 63-year-old patient, 5 days post-splenectomy, develops severe dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia with hemoptysis and a tender swollen left leg.
items.explanation: Severe dyspnea with tachypnea, hemoptysis and a swollen leg suggests pulmonary embolism.

items.stem: A 24-year-old presented with severe watery diarrhea that was unresponsive to antimicrobial and antispasmodic therapy. Ultrasound showed a 1.7 cm solid mass in the body of the pancreas with no liver metastasis.
items.explanation: VIPomas, also known as Verner-Morrison syndrome or pancreatic cholera, produce excessive vasoactive intestinal peptide leading to watery diarrhea.

items.stem: A 35-year-old mentally challenged male presented with recurrent syncopal episodes. His BMI is 42, and a CT scan showed a 2 cm mass in the body of the pancreas.
items.explanation: Insulinoma causes hypoglycemia which can result in recurrent syncopal episodes.

items.stem: A 42-year-old female presented with gallstones and greasy loose bowel movements, along with a recent history of diabetes mellitus. MRI revealed a 2.5 cm mass in the head of the pancreas.
items.explanation: Somatostatinoma presents with the triad of diabetes mellitus, cholelithiasis, and steatorrhea due to inhibitory effects on various gastrointestinal hormones.

items.stem: A 46-year-old male presented with migratory erythema with necrosis in his trunk and a 2-year history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus. An ultrasound revealed a 3 cm mass in the tail of the pancreas.
items.explanation: Glucagonoma is associated with necrolytic migratory erythema and uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.

items.stem: A 50-year-old male with a history of recurrent duodenal ulceration presented with hematemesis and melena despite adequate acid suppression. Somatostatin scintigraphy revealed a 1 cm mass in the duodenal wall adjacent to the pancreas.
items.explanation: Gastrinoma results in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome characterized by recurrent peptic ulcers and gastric acid hypersecretion.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl presents with central abdominal pain that localizes to the right iliac fossa. She also complains of a loss of appetite over the last 24 hours and nausea. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.8°C and is tender in the right iliac fossa.
items.explanation: The presentation of right iliac fossa pain, loss of appetite, and tenderness suggests a possible appendicitis. In cases of suspected appendicitis, a Gridiron incision (also known as McBurney incision) is commonly used. Lanz incision is only used in cases of complicated appendicitis for larger access.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Unfortunately, the surgeons are unable to clearly delineate the anatomy of the area due to the presence of adhesions.
items.explanation: The surgeon should switch to the open approach, with a Kocher incision which is used to access the gallbladder.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman is undergoing elective cesarean section for a breech presentation.
items.explanation: A Pfannenstiel incision, also known as a bikini incision, is commonly used for cesarean sections.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with known peptic ulcer disease presents with sudden-onset, severe epigastric pain. On examination, he has a tender, rigid abdomen, and bowel sounds are absent.
items.explanation: The presentation of sudden-onset severe epigastric pain, a tender rigid abdomen, and absent bowel sounds raises concern for a surgical emergency such as perforated peptic ulcer or acute abdomen. So a midline incision is needed for exploration.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman is about to undergo a Whipple procedure for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
items.explanation: Rooftop incision (Chevron incision or bilateral subcostal incision) is commonly used in Whipple procedure.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with generalised colicky abdominal pain with bilious vomiting for 48 hours. His symptoms have been intermittent. He has a distended abdomen with generalised tenderness without any rigidity or rebound tenderness. Following an operation for left hemicolectomy 3 years ago through a long midline incision, he has had several such episodes, some of them requiring admission.
items.explanation: A history of previous abdominal surgery with recurrent, intermittent symptoms is highly suggestive of adhesive small bowel obstruction, supported by the absence of peritoneal irritation.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man complains of malaise, bilateral backache, nausea and occasional vomiting for 2 months. Clinically there is nothing significant except for bilateral hydroceles, of which the patient was not aware. Routine blood tests reveal: Hb 10 g/dL, ESR 88, CRP 292, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 256 mmol/L, K 6.1 mmol/L, Na 135 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L and HCO₃ 18 mmol/L.
items.explanation: The combination of renal impairment, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, and bilateral hydroceles suggests a compressive retroperitoneal process, typical of idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman complains of an abdominal lump that she noticed in the bath 6 weeks ago. She experiences some generalised discomfort, and on examination she appears well with a smooth, fluctuant periumbilical mass that is freely mobile along a diagonal plane from the right subcostal to the left iliac fossa.
items.explanation: A freely mobile, smooth, and fluctuant periumbilical mass in an otherwise well patient is characteristic of a mesenteric cyst.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man underwent a laparoscopic closure of a perforated duodenal ulcer. His postoperative period during the first 4–5 days was uneventful; thereafter, he developed hiccoughs, pain in the right subcostal area and right shoulder tip, swinging pyrexia, toxicity, tachypnoea, and tenderness in the right upper quadrant with overlying skin oedema.
items.explanation: The onset of systemic toxicity, hiccoughs, right subcostal and shoulder tip pain after upper abdominal surgery strongly indicates the development of a right subhepatic abscess.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman, who arrived from the Indian subcontinent 1 year ago, complains of general malaise, cough, and low-grade evening temperatures for 6 months. She has experienced weight loss and on examination has central abdominal distension with a sensation of an encysted periumbilical mass.
items.explanation: Chronic constitutional symptoms, weight loss, and abdominal distension in a patient from a TB-endemic region point to tuberculous ascites with peritoneal involvement.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman complains of feeling generally unwell with weight loss for 6 months. She also reports discomfort over her entire left side of the abdomen accompanied by constipation. On examination, there is marked fullness in her left lumbar region and loin.
items.explanation: A deep-seated, slowly enlarging mass in the left abdomen accompanied by systemic symptoms is highly suggestive of a retroperitoneal liposarcoma.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man collapses with an expansile, pulsatile mass above the umbilicus.
items.explanation: 2. C. gastric carcinoma; 3. I. caecal carcinoma; 4. E. fibroids; 5. F. pancreatic pseudocyst1. K. Abdominal aortic aneurysm: an expansile, pulsatile mass suggests vascular dilation.

items.stem: A 75-year-old man presents with dyspepsia, weight loss and a firm, irregular epigastric mass with a palpable left supraclavicular node.
items.explanation: dyspepsia, weight loss and nodal involvement are concerning features.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with a firm, irregular mass in the right iliac fossa and severe microcytic anaemia.
items.explanation: presents with anaemia and a palpable right iliac fossa mass.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a progressively enlarging abdominal mass and heavy menstrual bleeding; the mass is knobbly and dull on percussion.
items.explanation: benign uterine tumors leading to heavy menstrual bleeding and an irregular mass.

items.stem: A 70-year-old alcoholic presents with a tender upper abdominal mass; CT reveals a thick-walled, rounded, fluid-filled mass adjacent to the pancreas.
items.explanation: a complication of pancreatitis seen as a fluid-filled mass on CT.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman has noticed a fullness in the left upper quadrant. On examination, the GP feels that there is a smooth moderately enlarged spleen. Past history includes rheumatoid arthritis and high blood pressure. Routine blood tests show normocytic anaemia and low WCC.
items.explanation: 2. H. Infectious mononucleosis; 3. A. malaria; 4. J. Budd–Chiari syndrome; 5. G. spherocytosis1. L Felty’s syndrome: Associated with rheumatoid arthritis, it presents with splenomegaly and neutropenia.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man presents with a week’s history of fever and sore throat. He developed a macular rash after receiving ampicillin On examination he has enlarged posterior cervical nodes, palatal petechiae and splenomegaly.
items.explanation: Typically follows Epstein–Barr virus infection; the rash after ampicillin is characteristic.

items.stem: A 21-year-old female backpacker returning from India presents with flu-like symptoms followed by a periodic fever. She is anaemic, jaundiced and has moderate splenomegaly.
items.explanation: A malaria: Periodic fever with anaemia in endemic regions is suggestive of malaria.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, vomiting and jaundice. On examination, tender hepatosplenomegaly and ascites are found. She has a history of recurrent miscarriages.
items.explanation: Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow causing tender hepatosplenomegaly, often linked with hypercoagulable states.

items.stem: A 16-year-old child is being investigated for gallstones. Routine blood tests show mild anaemia; clinically there is smooth, painless splenomegaly. A direct Coomb’s test is negative and blood film shows reticulocytes and spherocytes.
items.explanation: A defect in red cell membrane structure causing spherocyte formation with a negative Coomb’s test.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with episodes of faintness and tiredness. The symptoms worsen after exercise and are relieved by eating. On examination, he is pale and sweaty.

A 48-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of watery diarrhea, with up to 15 episodes a day. On examination, she is severely dehydrated; laboratory tests show a low potassium level and mild renal impairment, and her stool culture is negative.
items.explanation: Profuse watery diarrhea with dehydration suggests a VIPoma.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of thirst and urinary frequency, and she admits to losing 3 kg in weight. On examination, she has an erythematous, blistering rash over her buttocks.
items.explanation: Weight loss, rash, and hyperglycemia point to a glucagonoma.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man presents with coffee-ground vomiting. He describes intermittent epigastric pain and diarrhea over the last month. Endoscopy shows multiple, large ulcers and erosions over the stomach, duodenum, and proximal jejunum.
items.explanation: Multiple peptic ulcers indicate Zollinger–Ellison syndrome due to a gastrinoma.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a long history of foul-smelling, bulky stools that are becoming more frequent and severe. She also reports increased thirst and passing large amounts of dilute urine. On examination, she appears thin and wasted but there is no other abnormality..
items.explanation: Steatorrhea and diabetes-like symptoms indicate a somatostatinoma.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of left iliac fossa painand nausea. Further questioning reveals that she is also suffering pain on micturition. On examination, there is tenderness and guarding in the left iliac fossa as well as some tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Her temperature is 37.6°C.
A 68-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis presents with acute severe abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, the abdomen is rigid and bowel sounds are absent.
items.explanation: An elderly patient with a rigid abdomen and absent bowel sounds signals a perforated peptic ulcer causing generalized peritonitis

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with an 8-month history of abdominal discomfort that is improved following defaecation. She complains of a regular change in her bowel habit, alternating between constipation and loose motions. On examination, her abdomen is soft and nontender. There are no obvious masses, and bowel sounds are present.
items.explanation: Longstanding abdominal discomfort that improves with defaecation and fluctuating bowel habits is characteristic of irritable bowel syndrome without alarming physical findings

items.stem: A 44-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of severe epigastric pain that radiates to his back and is improved on leaning forwards. On examination, he is jaundiced, with guarding in his epigastrium, but there is no evidence of haemorrhage. Observations are stable. Routine bloods are sent off, and the amylase returns at 248 IU/L.
items.explanation: Recurrent severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and relief on leaning forward together with a modest amylase rise suggests chronic pancreatitis with repeating flare‐ups

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman undergoes a laparotomy for a perforated diverticulum. A few days later, she develops pain in the left upper quadrant that radiates to the shoulder, nausea, vomiting and rigors. Her temperature is 38.9°C.
items.explanation: Postoperative left upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder accompanied by fever and rigors is typical of a subphrenic abscess due to prior perforated diverticulum

items.stem: A 65-year-old diabetic man has a painless, smooth, firm mass in the right iliac fossa. He also has a radiocephalic fistula.
items.explanation: Radiocephalic fistula indicates haemodialysis; a transplanted kidney is palpable in the iliac fossa.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman has a haemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 72 fL, and ferritin of 6 mcg/L. There is a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa.
items.explanation: Right-sided colonic carcinoma commonly presents with iron deficiency anaemia and a RIF mass.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy with 1 week of vague abdominal pains, 24 h of swinging pyrexia, and a tender, firm mass in the right iliac fossa.
items.explanation: Appendiceal abscess presents in children with tender RIF mass and swinging pyrexia.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman with 48 h of vomiting, abdominal distension, and a new swelling in the left groin which appears to arise below the inguinal ligament.
items.explanation: Femoral hernia presents below the inguinal ligament with obstructive symptoms in elderly women.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with 5 weeks of intermittent left iliac fossa pain, anorexia, and anergia. He has lost 2 kg of weight and has had low-grade fevers for the last 3 nights. There is a tender mass in the left lower quadrant.
items.explanation: Diverticular abscess causes a septic presentation with a tender LLQ mass.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy undergoing an open excision of an appendix mass secondary to acute appendicitis.
items.explanation: The gridiron incision splits muscle fibres for open appendicectomy with minimal hernia risk.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with acute lower abdominal pain suspected of a ruptured ovarian and undergoing a diagnostic procedure to confirm the diagnosis.
items.explanation: A subumbilical incision is used for laparoscopic access and pneumoperitoneum.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman undergoing hysterectomy for intermenstrual bleeding secondary to large uterine leiomyomas (‘fibroids’).
items.explanation: Pfannenstiel incision provides transverse pelvic access for hysterectomy with minimal muscle division.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with a past history of aortic aneurysm surgery undergoing elective open surgery for symptomatic gallstones.
items.explanation: The Kocher right subcostal incision offers optimal exposure for gallbladder surgery.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man undergoing radical gastrectomy for gastric carcinoma.
items.explanation: The rooftop incision gives wide upper abdominal access for gastrectomy.

items.stem: The muscle aponeurosis first encountered in the dissection during an open appendicectomy using a right iliac fossa incision.
items.explanation: The external oblique aponeurosis is the first layer encountered in a right iliac fossa incision.

items.stem: The muscle most likely to be involved with retroperitoneal abscess (e.g. retrocaecal abscess) formation.
items.explanation: The psoas major lies retroperitoneally and is prone to abscess formation.

items.stem: The muscle of the anterior abdominal wall which has muscle fibres running medially and superiorly.
items.explanation: The internal oblique fibres run medially and superiorly from the iliac crest.

items.stem: The muscle with a thickened aponeurosis where it forms the inguinal ligament.
items.explanation: The external oblique’s inferior margin thickens to form the inguinal ligament.

items.stem: The muscle that must be divided during surgical retroperitoneal approaches to the kidney.
items.explanation: The transversus abdominis must be divided to access the retroperitoneum for kidney surgery.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with 48h of epigastric and right-sided abdominal pain, no jaundice, a temperature of 37.8°C, a pulse of 100bpm, and a white blood cell count of 14.7 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: The clinical picture in the first patient is most consistent with acute cholecystitis.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with 2h of severe central and left-sided abdominal pain radiating to the left flank and back. He is feeling faint with mild abdominal tenderness.
items.explanation: The combination of short-lived severe pain and haemodynamic upset (he is almost certainly hypotensive for his age and mildly tachycardic) suggests a non-inflammatory cause. Biliary or renal colic may be severe but the relative hypotension is uncharacteristic. Acute mesenteric ischaemia typically causes severe pain but often gives rise to no abdominal signs. The lack of a palpable, pulsatile mass should never be taken as evidence against an abdominal aortic aneurysm and the age and gender of the patient are typical of the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman with 3 days of increasing left lower abdominal pain, mild dysuria, and left iliac fossa and left flank tenderness. Her temperature is 37.7°C, pulse is 82bpm, blood pressure is 135/76mmHg, and her urine is positive for blood and protein.
items.explanation: Left lower quadrant pain with dysuria and urinary abnormalities is most consistent with acute sigmoid diverticulitis.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with 12h of intermittent colicky right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, and retching. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse is 82bpm, and blood pressure is 135/85mmHg.
items.explanation: Intermittent colicky right-sided pain with nausea is typical of biliary colic.

items.stem: An 81-year-old man with cognitive impairment is reported by his carers to have had 6h of progressively increasing lower abdominal, left iliac fossa, and suprapubic pain. There is mild lower abdominal tenderness, a temperature of 37.2°C, pulse of 88bpm, and blood pressure of 155/85mmHg.
items.explanation: In an elderly patient with cognitive impairment and lower abdominal pain, acute urinary retention should be considered.

stem: A 22-year-old previously healthy male complains of dysuria. Genital examination: there is urethral discharge. Urinalysis shows 30 to 40 white blood cells per high power field.
