items.stem: A 40-year-old man has come to A&E complaining of a sudden onset of very severe pain in his left loin of 4 hours duration, radiating to the front of the lumbar area and groin and the left testis. He has vomited a couple of times and has urinary frequency. On examination he is writhing in pain and cannot find a comfortable position.
items.explanation: This presentation is classical for ureteric colic. The pain’s severity, radiation to the groin and testis, urinary frequency, and the patient’s restlessness point towards a stone in the ureter. Ureteric stones often cause severe colicky pain due to peristaltic contractions against the obstruction. The diagnosis is confirmed by imaging (non-contrast CT or IVU). Other options such as pyonephrosis or carcinoma would not present so acutely or with this specific pain pattern.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man complains of haematuria associated with pain in his left loin radiating to the lower abdomen for about 2 months. He passes clots that are ‘worm-like’. On examination he has an enlarged left kidney, and scrotal examination reveals a varicocele of which he was unaware.
items.explanation: The triad of haematuria, loin pain, and a palpable mass is classic for renal cell carcinoma (hypernephroma). The presence of a left-sided varicocele indicates involvement of the left renal vein, suggesting tumour invasion. This tumour can also present with systemic signs like polycythaemia or hypertension, none of which are present here but the hallmark symptoms strongly suggest RCC.

items.stem: A 45-year-old female patient complains of nagging pain in her right loin and urinary frequency for several months. On examination she has tenderness in her loin over the kidney. Urine examination shows red blood cells and a growth of Proteus and staphylococci.
items.explanation: This presentation indicates a chronic urinary tract issue with urea-splitting organisms (e.g., Proteus), producing alkaline urine conducive to struvite (phosphate) stones like staghorn calculi. The persistent loin discomfort, haematuria, and infection strongly support this diagnosis. This condition needs careful assessment of renal function and potential surgical intervention.

items.stem: A fit 20-year-old young man had a game of rugby, following which he passed frank blood in his urine in the changing room. He felt some discomfort in his left loin. After returning home, his haematuria became worse and he noticed some fullness in his left loin. He then came to A&E. His blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg, his pulse was 110/minute and he had fullness in his left loin.
items.explanation: Haematuria following minor trauma often points to an underlying pathological kidney. The surprise of haematuria after minimal trauma suggests a structural abnormality like congenital hydronephrosis. These kidneys are enlarged and more prone to rupture or bleeding from minor impacts. Imaging would show dilated pelvicalyceal systems.

items.stem: A 60-year-old female patient was seen as an emergency with high temperature, rigors, and pain in her right loin. She had a blood pressure of 160/70 mmHg, bounding pulse of 90/minute, and extreme tenderness in her right loin.
items.explanation: The features here (fever, rigors, loin pain, high pulse pressure) point to sepsis originating from the kidney. Pyonephrosis refers to infected hydronephrosis, often resulting from obstructed infected urine. This is a surgical emergency and needs prompt drainage, antibiotics, and supportive care. Other diagnoses like renal carcinoma or ureteric stones do not typically present with such septic features.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man complains of left loin ache with intermittent painless haematuria in the form of clots, occasional high temperature and rigors, some dysuria, and frequency for 6 months. An IVU shows an irregular filling defect in the lower one-third of the left ureter. There is nothing to find on clinical examination. His Hb is 10.2 gm/dL.
items.explanation: The haematuria, systemic symptoms, and imaging finding of an irregular defect in the ureter are typical of transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) of the ureter. Chronicity, painless bleeding, and lower tract irritation suggest malignancy in the urothelial lining. The location (lower third) matches the common site of ureteral TCC.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent attacks of urinary tract infection. On every occasion this was successfully treated with antibiotics. In view of several such episodes in the past, she underwent an IVU, which showed the renal calyces to be pointing toward the vertebrae.
items.explanation: This is a classical description of a horseshoe kidney, a congenital fusion anomaly where the kidneys are joined at the lower poles. On IVU, calyces point medially (“flower vase” appearance). These kidneys are prone to recurrent infections and stone formation. No other diagnosis in the list would explain the recurrent UTIs with this imaging finding.

items.stem: A male child of 3 years has been brought by his mother, who noticed while bathing him that the right side of his abdomen felt larger than the left and was asymmetrical; she thought that there was probably a lump in his abdomen.
items.explanation: Wilms’ tumour is the most common renal malignancy in children, often presenting as an asymptomatic abdominal mass. Haematuria may occur if the tumour invades the collecting system. Other associated anomalies (e.g., aniridia, hemihypertrophy) support the diagnosis. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical. Imaging confirms the diagnosis before surgery and chemotherapy.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy has been brought in as an emergency by his parents as they noticed that he had bright red haematuria for the past 24 hours or so. About 6 hours prior to that he was climbing a tree and accidentally fell on his left side.
items.explanation: The timeline (fall followed by haematuria) and the age suggest blunt renal trauma. The kidney is a retroperitoneal organ vulnerable to deceleration or blunt force injury. Management involves imaging to assess the extent of injury and supportive care unless the patient is unstable or there is evidence of renal pedicle injury. No signs suggest infection or malignancy.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman complains of intermittent haematuria associated with a dull ache in her left loin. She has some dysuria and urine specimen showed E. coli infection. She has no physical findings. An IVU showed a persistent irregular filling defect in the left renal pelvis.
items.explanation: This older woman has a typical presentation of TCC of the renal pelvis: intermittent haematuria, E. coli UTI, and a filling defect in the renal pelvis seen on IVU. TCC is the most common malignancy of the urinary tract affecting the urothelium. It can be multifocal and requires cystoscopic and radiologic evaluation. The key differentiator from RCC is the location of the tumour and typical urothelial lining involvement.

items.stem: A 35-year-old male, a recent visitor from Egypt, attended the emergency department with painless terminal haematuria. He had a few similar episodes while at home in Egypt. Clinical examination revealed no abnormality. On flexible cystoscopy at the one-stop haematuria clinic, he was found to have scattered tubercles and islands of pale patches resembling sand.
items.explanation: This patient is from an endemic region (Egypt) for Schistosoma haematobium, which causes chronic granulomatous inflammation of the bladder. The cystoscopic findings of tubercles and pale patches are classic. Terminal painless haematuria is a hallmark symptom. Schistosomiasis may eventually lead to squamous metaplasia and bladder carcinoma if untreated.

items.stem: A 70-year-old male, a heavy smoker for more than 50 years, complains of painless, profuse and periodic haematuria for 6 weeks. The blood is uniformly mixed with the urine. He has frequency of micturition and some retropubic discomfort. Clinical examination reveals no abnormality.
items.explanation: This is a textbook presentation of bladder cancer. Risk factors include long-term smoking, and the key symptom is painless gross haematuria that is profuse and intermittent. The uniform mixing of blood with urine suggests a source higher up in the urinary tract, consistent with tumour bleeding. The diagnosis is confirmed by cystoscopy and imaging.

items.stem: A 70-year-old male complains of poor micturition stream, post-micturition dribbling and a feeling of insufficient emptying of his bladder. He has some dysuria. On occasions he has found that shortly after micturition he again passes a large amount of urine. Clinical examination reveals no abnormality.
items.explanation: The symptoms suggest bladder outlet obstruction (BOO), most likely due to benign prostatic enlargement, which can lead to diverticulum formation. The passage of more urine after initial voiding is due to residual urine trapped in the diverticulum. Diverticula are often incidental findings but can become symptomatic or lead to complications like infection or stones.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man complains of haematuria and painful micturition, and he occasionally finds that his micturition stream suddenly stops. He has learned to re-start his stream by changing position. Clinical examination reveals no abnormality.
items.explanation: The sudden interruption of urinary stream followed by restarting by repositioning is classic for a mobile bladder stone. These calculi can intermittently block the bladder outlet. Associated symptoms like haematuria and dysuria also support this diagnosis. The mechanical obstruction from the stone causes pain and stream abnormalities, often relieved by posture changes.

items.stem: A 35-year-old female patient, a recent visitor from the Indian subcontinent, complains of frequency of micturition and bilateral loin discomfort. She has evening pyrexia, general malaise and weight loss. Clinical examination reveals no abnormality. Urine examination carried out by her doctor shows sterile pyuria.
items.explanation: Sterile pyuria, chronic urinary symptoms, and constitutional features (fever, malaise, weight loss) in a patient from a TB-endemic region are highly suggestive of urinary tuberculosis. The infection usually descends from the kidneys and may eventually result in a small-capacity, non-compliant bladder (thimble bladder). Diagnosis is confirmed via early morning urine cultures for acid-fast bacilli.

theme_label: Theme 3: Prostate and Urinary Retention Diagnoses

items.stem: A 40-year-old man complains of feeling ill with pyrexia of 39°C, rigors with aches all over his body, and flu-like symptoms in general. He has rectal irritation, pain on defecation and perineal discomfort. He has pain on micturition and passes threads in his urine. Rectal examination reveals a tender, swollen prostate.
items.explanation: This patient presents with systemic symptoms (fever, rigors, flu-like malaise) and local perineal/rectal discomfort, characteristic of acute prostatitis. The presence of a tender, swollen prostate on rectal exam is diagnostic. Acute prostatitis is often due to E. coli or other uropathogens. Pain on defecation, micturition, and passage of threads (pus) in urine further support the diagnosis. Other prostate conditions like BPH or carcinoma wouldn’t cause this acute infectious profile.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man complains of poor stream, frequency of micturition both in the day and at night, hesitancy and intermittent stream, a feeling of incomplete emptying and terminal haematuria for about 4 months; recently he has had backache. Clinical examination shows no abnormality. On rectal examination he has a hard, nodular prostate with overlying fixed rectal mucosa.
items.explanation: This patient has lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), but the key features suggesting malignancy are the hard, nodular prostate and fixed rectal mucosa, which suggest extracapsular spread. The recent onset backache may indicate bony metastases, commonly seen in prostate cancer. In contrast to BPH, which presents with a smooth, symmetrical prostate, prostate cancer is typically irregular and firm on examination.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has come to the emergency department with severe acute pain in his lower abdomen not having passed urine for almost 10 hours. He has been on some medicines, which he bought across the counter for cold and flu. This has also made him constipated. On examination he is in severe pain from a large mass in his suprapubic region arising from the pelvis. The mass is dull to percussion.
items.explanation: This man has classic acute urinary retention—a painful inability to void, palpable bladder distension, and acute lower abdominal pain. The retention was likely triggered by anticholinergic cold medications and constipation, both of which reduce detrusor activity. Acute decompression with catheterisation is the immediate treatment. This condition is distinct from chronic retention, which is usually painless.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man complains of urgency, frequency and hesitancy of micturition with a feeling of incomplete emptying. He also has poor flow, intermittent stream and post-micturition dribbling. These symptoms have been going on for 2 years and are gradually getting worse. Clinical examination reveals no abnormality. On rectal examination he has an enlarged smooth prostate with overlying mobile rectal mucosa, and the median vertical groove is easily felt.
items.explanation: This patient has classic long-standing LUTS due to bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) from benign prostatic hyperplasia. Symptoms include poor stream, hesitancy, and dribbling. The rectal exam findings—a smooth, enlarged prostate with a palpable median sulcus—are characteristic of BPH. The absence of systemic symptoms or prostate irregularity helps exclude carcinoma or prostatitis.

items.stem: A 75-year-old male complains of general malaise, lethargy, abdominal distension and urinary incontinence. On examination he has a large painless mass in his suprapubic region arising from the pelvis and has continuous urinary dribbling. The mass is dull on percussion. He is a type 2 diabetic on oral medication.
items.explanation: This is a classic case of chronic urinary retention with overflow. The bladder is distended but painless, and the patient experiences incontinence due to overflow. The dull, suprapubic mass represents the enlarged bladder. Long-standing obstruction, often from BPH or neurogenic bladder (e.g., in diabetics), leads to this condition. Unlike acute retention, it is painless and often associated with systemic symptoms like lethargy.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man complains of deformity of his penis during erection. He has increasing difficulty in sexual intercourse. In the past he had urethritis, which was treated successfully with antibiotics.
items.explanation: Chordee is a fixed ventral curvature of the penis, often congenital but can also be secondary to scarring from chronic urethritis, as in this case. It causes deformity during erection and interferes with sexual activity. Unlike Peyronie’s disease, there are no palpable plaques or association with Dupuytren’s contracture here.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man complains of bloody, foul-smelling discharge from his penis. He has a hard ulcerated lesion under his prepuce. He also complains of lumps in his groin.
items.explanation: The ulcerated lesion under the prepuce, bloody discharge, and inguinal lumps (possibly metastatic or reactive nodes) strongly indicate penile cancer. Most cases are squamous cell carcinoma, often associated with poor hygiene or chronic inflammatory conditions like phimosis or BXO. A biopsy confirms diagnosis and guides staging and management.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man complains of progressive deformity of his penis, which is very pronounced during erection; this has been going on for the past 2 years. On examination, indurated plaques can be palpated around the penile shaft. On questioning he has thickening of his palmar fascia on both hands.
items.explanation: This case clearly points to Peyronie’s disease, a fibrotic disorder of the tunica albuginea. The penile plaques cause curvature during erection and are often associated with Dupuytren’s contracture (palmar fascia thickening). It differs from chordee in being acquired and plaque-related rather than congenital or urethritis-related.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man who is under treatment for leukaemia recently started developing penile erection without any reason. This is prolonged and painful and is now distressing him.
items.explanation: Priapism is a prolonged, painful erection unrelated to sexual stimulation. It is often linked to hematologic disorders such as leukaemia, sickle cell disease, or medications. Immediate urologic intervention is required to prevent ischemic damage to penile tissues.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man complains of itching around his glans penis and prepuce. Recently, he has developed purulent discharge from the subpreputial area. His glans and foreskin look red and inflamed. He is a type I diabetic on insulin.
items.explanation: The red, inflamed glans and foreskin with purulent discharge and itching indicate balanoposthitis. In diabetics, poor glycemic control predisposes to recurrent infections. Treatment involves local hygiene and broad-spectrum antibiotics. BXO would cause chronic, fibrotic changes rather than acute inflammation.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man was involved in a road-traffic accident in which he sustained polytrauma, chief among which was fracture of pelvis with fractured femoral shaft. After stabilisation according to the ATLS protocol, it became apparent that he has a distended bladder and is unable to pass urine.
items.explanation: Membranous urethral rupture is commonly associated with pelvic fractures. The distended bladder with urinary retention in the setting of trauma and pelvic injury strongly supports this diagnosis. Ascending urethrogram confirms the injury, and initial management includes suprapubic catheterisation.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man while performing on a Pommel Horse in a gymnastics competition, slipped and fell astride on the Pommel Horse. He complains of severe perineal pain in the penoscrotal junction where there is a haematoma. He has blood in his external urinary meatus.
items.explanation: Blunt perineal trauma with blood at the meatus, perineal bruising, and urinary retention is diagnostic for bulbous urethral rupture. This is typically due to falls astride objects. Emergency management includes suprapubic diversion and delayed urethral repair.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man complains of thickening of his foreskin over a period of 2 years. During this period he has had difficulty in retracting his foreskin, as a result of which he has been having difficulty in maintaining good hygiene. He finds that his urinary stream tends to spray around.
items.explanation: BXO is a chronic, sclerosing inflammatory condition of the foreskin, often leading to phimosis, hygiene issues, and meatal stenosis, causing spraying of the urinary stream. The long duration and progressive foreskin tightening distinguish it from acute balanoposthitis. It is considered a precancerous condition.

theme_label: Theme 5: Scrotal Swellings and Testicular Conditions
options: Torsion of the hydatid of Morgagni

items.stem: A 22-year-old man complains of acute pain in the top of his left testis for 16 hours. On examination the scrotum looks normal and the testis can be felt with care without undue tenderness. There is a small, blue, pea-sized tender mass on top of the testis.
items.explanation: This is a classic presentation of torsion of the hydatid of Morgagni—a vestigial remnant often found on the upper pole of the testis. It causes localized tenderness without generalized testicular pain, and the hallmark is a small, blue, tender lump. This condition is often confused with testicular torsion but is far less severe and easily treated with simple excision.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man complains of a swollen scrotum for almost 1 year. This is not painful but recently has caused discomfort. On examination he has a tense fluctuant lump in his right scrotum where the testis cannot be felt separately. The swelling transilluminates.
items.explanation: A vaginal hydrocele is a collection of fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. It is non-tender, transilluminates, and typically obscures palpation of the testis. It lies in front of and around the testis and is confirmed clinically or by ultrasound.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man complains of a painful left testis of 4 days’ duration. This is associated with fever and rigors. He has painful micturition and considerable frequency. On examination he looks unwell, has pyrexia of 39°C and has a swollen, red, oedematous and shiny left hemiscrotum; the testis and epididymis feel indurated and tender.
items.explanation: This patient presents with systemic and urinary symptoms in addition to local signs, characteristic of acute epididymo-orchitis. The tender, indurated epididymis, fever, and scrotal inflammation suggest a bacterial infection, often from STIs in younger men. Diagnosis is confirmed with ultrasound and urinalysis, and treatment involves antibiotics.

items.stem: An 18-year-old man complains of sudden onset of agonising pain in his right groin and suprapubic area of 6 hours’ duration. He has no urinary symptoms. On examination he is in agony, the right testis is drawn up and the scrotum is red. The testis is impossible to feel because of pain.
items.explanation: Sudden, severe testicular pain, high-riding testis, and scrotal erythema in a young male strongly suggest testicular torsion. This is a urological emergency, and prompt surgical exploration is necessary. Waiting for imaging (e.g. Doppler) can delay life-saving intervention and risk testicular necrosis.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man complains of feeling heavy in his left scrotum where he noticed a lump while in the shower. A few days before, he felt a lump in the periumbilical region of his abdomen. At the same time he noticed another lump on the left side of his neck. The abdominal and neck lumps do not give him any symptoms. On questioning he admits to coughing up some blood in his sputum 1 month ago. On examination he has a 2 cm irregular lump over his left supraclavicular area and a 5-cm irregular firm lump in his umbilical region. Examination of the left testis reveals a large lump, which is hard and heavy.
items.explanation: This case shows a testicular mass with widespread metastases (supraclavicular and abdominal lymph nodes, haemoptysis suggesting lung mets). The hard, heavy testicular lump and age group support the diagnosis of a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour, likely a teratoma. Immediate referral, imaging, and tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG) are necessary.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man complains of a lump in his right scrotum of 1 year’s duration. This is gradually growing larger in size and gives him some discomfort. Examination of his scrotum reveals a cystic lump, about 7 cm in diameter, above and behind the left testis, which is minimally tender. Transillumination is positive and shows septa within the lump. There is a smaller similar lump on the other side of which he is unaware.
items.explanation: An epididymal cyst is a benign cystic swelling arising from the epididymis. It typically lies above and behind the testis, transilluminates well, and may be bilateral. The presence of septa helps distinguish it from a hydrocele. Surgery is reserved for symptomatic cases.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has been brought by his parents to A&E with a red, swollen scrotum. On examination the child is not in any pain and there is redness and oedema around the penis and perineum.
items.explanation: Painless scrotal swelling in a child with oedema and erythema suggests idiopathic oedema of the scrotum, often allergic in origin. It is self-limiting and non-tender, helping distinguish it from testicular torsion. Doppler ultrasound can be used in uncertain cases to avoid unnecessary surgery.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a swelling in his right scrotum, which he says feels like ‘a third testis’. He noticed it in the shower and is worried that he has got cancer. He has no symptoms. On examination he has a lax, cystic swelling on top of his right testis. It is not tender and transillumination is hazy.
items.explanation: A spermatocele is a cystic swelling from the epididymal ducts, often described by patients as a “third testis”. It is soft, non-tender, and transilluminates hazily. Aspiration may reveal barley-coloured fluid containing dead sperm. It’s distinct from an epididymal cyst, which is often larger and multiloculated.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with a swelling in his left hemiscrotum, which he discovered by chance in the bath. On examination the testis feels separate from the swelling, which is about 2 cm in diameter and above the testis. It transilluminates and comes down on traction to the testis.
items.explanation: An encysted hydrocele of the cord is a fluid-filled remnant of the processus vaginalis, typically found above the testis along the spermatic cord. It transilluminates and is distinct from the testis on palpation. Its mobility and benign nature make it easy to distinguish from other swellings.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man complains of a dragging discomfort in the left side of his scrotum. He noticed an irregular lump in his scrotum separate from the testis. He thinks he has had this for many years but only recently he noticed discomfort in the lump. On examination he has a bunch of veins in the scrotum and the testis feels normal. On lying down the veins disappear. Abdominal examination in the left renal area does not show any abnormality.
items.explanation: A varicocele is a dilated pampiniform venous plexus, often described as a “bag of worms” in the scrotum. It is most commonly left-sided due to the anatomical angle of the left testicular vein into the left renal vein. The swelling disappears on lying down and may cause discomfort or infertility. Rarely, it may be secondary to renal pathology.

options: squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman has had a UTI treated but has persistent microscopic haematuria seen on urine dipstick. She’s not worried but her GP refers her to the one-stop haematuria clinic.
items.explanation: J Painless haematuria is the presenting complaint in over 80 percent of patients with transitional cell carcinoma. Other symptoms include frequency, dysuria, urgency, loin pain secondary to ureteric obstruction, recurrent urinary tract infections or microscopic haematuria. Investigation involves urine cytology, intravenous urogram, ultrasound scanning and flexible cystoscopy. Risk factors include smoking, chronic ingestion of analgesics (e.g. phenacetin), cyclophosphamide therapy, and history of radiotherapy to the pelvis. Chemical exposures are also implicated.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with weight loss, loss of appetite and shortness of breath has recently noticed a left-sided varicocele which does not disappear on lying supine.
items.explanation: C The classic triad of haematuria, loin pain and a palpable abdominal mass is seen in fewer than 20 percent of renal cell carcinoma cases. Paraneoplastic syndromes such as anaemia, polycythaemia or hypercalcaemia may occur. Contrast CT is useful in demonstrating tumour extension and metastases.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with new-onset hypertension is admitted to hospital for investigation. His creatinine is 134 µmol/L. After imaging he is advised to tell his brother to undergo family screening and genetic counselling.
items.explanation: F Polycystic kidney disease, an autosomal dominant condition, presents typically in the fourth decade with loin pain or haematuria. Family screening by ultrasound is recommended, and cysts may also be seen in liver, spleen, or pancreas.

items.stem: An 18-year-old is travelling in the Australian outback during his gap year. He returns to London to run the marathon which he does successfully. The next day he attends A&E concerned about his dark red urine. He is otherwise completely asymptomatic but is admitted to hospital.
items.explanation: H Rhabdomyolysis caused by strenuous exercise leads to muscle injury with release of myoglobin into the urine, causing dark discoloration. Management includes aggressive fluid resuscitation and monitoring to prevent acute renal failure.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man from Egypt presents with weight loss and haematuria. Pseudotubercles and nodules seen on cystoscopy are biopsied.
items.explanation: schistosomiasis E Schistosomiasis (bilharzia) involves trematode infestation; ova are deposited in the bladder wall leading to pseudotubercles and potential squamous cell carcinoma development.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with a testicular swelling that has increased in size gradually over a period of years. On examination the swelling transilluminates and the testis cannot be felt separate from the swelling.
items.explanation: D A hydrocele is a fluid collection in the tunica vaginalis causing the testis to be impalpable; treatment is usually surgical when indicated.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man complains of severe pain and swelling over the last 48 hours in his right scrotum. Testis and epididymis are very tender. He reports unprotected intercourse.
items.explanation: I Acute epididymo-orchitis presents with tender swelling; often due to sexually transmitted infections in younger men or bacterial causes in older men, managed primarily with antibiotics.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man with a history of undescended testes presents with weight loss and a hard, painless testicular lump.
items.explanation: E Although seminomas are common, in this context a history of undescended testes raises concern for non-seminomatous malignancy; evaluation includes tumour markers and imaging.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy wakes at night crying from severe testicular pain associated with vomiting.
items.explanation: K Testicular torsion, characterized by severe pain and vomiting, is a surgical emergency requiring prompt intervention.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a left-sided fluctuating scrotal swelling that worsens on standing.
items.explanation: A Varicocele presents as a “bag of worms” and may be associated with infertility, often requiring surgical repair.

items.stem: A 75-year-old man describes difficulty passing urine with a white scar and ballooning foreskin.
items.explanation: A Phimosis involves fibrous contraction of the preputial aperture leading to ballooning and obstructive symptoms; managed by circumcision.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman due for hysterectomy with chronic renal failure.
items.explanation: G In this patient, a pelvic mass compressing the urinary tract is suspected, commonly related to gynaecological pathology leading to renal failure.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with a history of recurrent urine infections and vesico-ureteric reflux presents with voiding difficulty.
items.explanation: B Repeated childhood urinary infections and reflux may cause urethral stricture in adulthood, necessitating surgical repair.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man, 1 week post-TURP, reattends in discomfort unable to pass urine.
items.explanation: F Post-TURP clot retention may block the urethral lumen; management includes catheterization with three-way irrigation.

items.stem: An 84-year-old man complains of difficulty passing urine, nocturia, hesitancy, and terminal dribbling.
items.explanation: E In older men, benign prostatic hypertrophy commonly causes voiding difficulties with associated obstructive symptoms.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with a history of hesitancy, nocturia, frequency and terminal dribbling fails a trial without catheter despite being on an alpha-blocker. Rectal examination reveals a smooth enlarged prostate. He is otherwise fit and healthy and his biopsy results are negative for cancer.
items.explanation: C Patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia may initially be managed with transurethral resection when medical therapy fails.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has recently had a routine blood screen and is reported to have an elevated PSA of 5.5 ng/mL. He is otherwise asymptomatic.
items.explanation: K An elevated PSA in an asymptomatic patient should be repeated to confirm the result before further invasive tests.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man attends your clinic reporting that his twin brother has been diagnosed with prostate cancer.
items.explanation: J A positive family history warrants screening for prostate cancer.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man with prostate cancer attends your clinic complaining of newonset back pain.
items.explanation: F New-onset back pain in prostate cancer patients mandates evaluation with a bone scan, often with dexamethasone to reduce inflammatory oedema.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man is diagnosed with prostate cancer and staging confirms the “absence of secondary spread of disease.
items.explanation: A Radical prostatectomy is indicated in suitable candidates with localized disease and good performance status.

options: ultrasound of kidneys and bladder residual

items.stem: 35-year-old woman presents 2 years after the birth of her child with urinary leakage on coughing, standing and sneezing.
items.explanation: J Pelvic floor exercises address stress incontinence due to pelvic support weakness.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with slowing of his urinary flow and terminal urethral dribbling. He has a past history of a treated sexually transmitted disease.
items.explanation: I An urethrogram is indicated in young men to evaluate for urethral stricture following infection.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman presents with recent onset of severe urinary urgency and bladder pain. Urinary dipstick shows no nitrates, protein 1+ and blood 2+.
items.explanation: B Cystoscopy and additional imaging are used in the workup of haematuria in older women.

items.stem: An 80-year-old man presents to the urology clinic with poor flow, frequency and nocturia. He is noted to have an elevated creatinine.
items.explanation: D Ultrasound assessment of post-void residual helps evaluate incomplete bladder emptying in obstruction.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman who has had two previous colposuspensions for urinary incontinence now complains of mixed urge and stress leakage.
items.explanation: E Video urodynamics provides detailed assessment of bladder function in mixed incontinence cases.

options: simple analgesia and discharge home with outpatient follow-up
lead: 1 A 40-year-old man has had a PCNL to treat a renal 2.5-cm stone. At the end of the procedure there is gross bleeding from the nephrostomy track. Nephrostomy tamponade fails to stop the bleeding.
2 A 35-year-old woman, in the first trimester of pregnancy, presents with severe right loin pain.
3 A 50-year-old woman with diabetes presents with severe left loin pain, pyrexia, tachycardia and a white cell count of 24 000. Intravenous urogram shows no func- tion on the initial 10-minute film.
4 A 37-year-old man presents with left renal colic. CT urogram shows a 5-mm stone in the lower third of the left ureter with moderate hydronephrosis.
5 A 27-year-old man presents with severe loin pain. Plain x-ray shows a staghorn calculus.
unparsed: 1. G. embolization
2. I. ultrasound kidneys
3. H. nephrostomy
4. A. simple analgesia and discharge home with outpatient follow-up
5. F. percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
1. G In post-PCNL bleeding unresponsive to tamponade, selective renal embolization is the next step.
2. I In pregnancy, ultrasound is the preferred modality to assess for obstructing calculus.
3. H In suspected pyonephrosis, urgent nephrostomy is required for decompression.
4. A Small stones (≈5 mm) may pass spontaneously with conservative management and analgesia.
5. F A staghorn calculus, often associated with infection, may require PCNL for definitive management.

items.stem: An incidental lump found during inguinal hernia repair that is benign.
items.explanation: D Lipoma of the cord is a benign fatty mass often encountered incidentally during hernia repair.

items.stem: A 60-year-old smoker with a throbbing lump in the right groin showing an expansile pulsation.
items.explanation: B Femoral aneurysm presents as an expansile, pulsatile mass usually due to atherosclerosis or trauma.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy with a new significant groin lump post-unsuccessful laparoscopy for undescended testis.
items.explanation: A Maldescended testis (cryptorchidism) is a congenital condition that may be associated with infertility and malignancy risk.

items.stem: An 80-year-old man with a right-sided scrotal mass that reduces on lying flat.
items.explanation: E An inguinal hernia typically presents with a reducible groin mass which may worsen on standing.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman with right leg pain and firm, matted groin masses.
items.explanation: K Inguinal lymphadenopathy requires further investigation to determine the underlying cause.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has muscle-invasive transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder extending to multiple sites along the right ureter and involving the renal pelvis. 2 An 83-year-old man with a PSA of 10 ng/mL and positive TRUS biopsy results denies lower urinary tract symptoms. He does not want any surgical intervention. 3 A 45-year-old man has raised PSA of 29 ng/mL and positive TRUS biopsy results. His brother died of prostate cancer aged 60 years. 4 A 30-year-old man with a history of renal stones has been on a business trip and taken diclofenac and codeine throughout his meetings. He returns to attend A&E with further pain. 5 A 15-year-old female complains of severe loin pain when voiding.
items.explanation: J For muscle-invasive bladder cancer with multifocal involvement, radical surgical intervention with urinary diversion is indicated.

unparsed: 2. K. active surveillance
3. I. radical prostatectomy
4. E. ultrasound of urinary tract
5. D. micturating cysto-urethrogram
2. K In asymptomatic patients with low PSA, active surveillance is the management of choice.
3. I A positive family history and elevated PSA support the need for radical prostatectomy.
4. E Ultrasound is the preferred initial investigation for suspected obstructive uropathy in renal stone patients.
5. D A micturating cysto-urethrogram is used to diagnose vesicoureteric reflux in young patients.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with acute cholecystitis undergoes ultrasound, which incidentally detects a renal lesion that is benign.
items.explanation: C Simple cysts are common incidental findings on ultrasound in older patients; they are typically benign.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with a 3-month history of haematuria, weight loss, fevers, lethargy, loin pain, and a palpable mass.
items.explanation: K Renal cell carcinoma may present with the classic triad of haematuria, loin pain, and a palpable mass, though only in a minority of cases.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man after a motorbike accident presents with an expanding left loin mass, bruising, and haematuria.
items.explanation: H A perirenal haematoma is usually secondary to trauma, presenting with bruising and swelling.

items.stem: A 37-year-old HIV-positive man presents with haematuria, swinging pyrexia, raised white cell count and a tender left loin mass.
items.explanation: F In immunocompromised patients, a renal abscess should be considered when there is tenderness, pyrexia, and raised inflammatory markers.

items.stem: An 18-year-old man presents with a swelling in his left testicle. On examination, the swelling is tense, smooth, fluctuant, and transilluminates. The testis cannot be felt separately from the swelling. The patient wants treatment for this swelling.
items.explanation: Excision of cyst is the treatment for a benign transilluminating testicular cyst.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset pain and swelling in his left testicle. On examination, the left testicle lies higher than the right, is erythematous, and is exquisitely tender.
items.explanation: Reduction and fixation is required for acute testicular torsion.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a painless lump in his right scrotum that he first noticed last week. On examination, the swelling is hard and irregular and does not transilluminate. A CT scan rules out lymph node involvement.
items.explanation: Orchidectomy and radiotherapy manage testicular cancer without nodal involvement.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of pain and swelling in his right testicle and pain on passing water. On examination, his left scrotum is swollen, erythematous, and tender. Urine dipstick shows white cells.
items.explanation: Antibiotics treat epididymo-orchitis presenting with infection signs.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man presents with pain and swelling in his scrotum. On examination, a hard, irregular mass is felt in the left scrotum that does not transilluminate. A CT scan demonstrates the presence of enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes.
items.explanation: Orchidectomy and chemotherapy are indicated for testicular cancer with nodal spread.

items.stem: An 87-year-old man has a transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy following admission for acute urinary retention. Histology shows a T1 prostate cancer.
items.explanation: Active surveillance avoids overtreatment in elderly T1 prostate cancer.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer presents with worsening bony pain in his left hip. He is currently on a course of hormonal treatment.
items.explanation: External-beam radiotherapy palliates bone pain in metastatic disease.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man is diagnosed with a T2 prostate cancer. He expresses a wish to have curative therapy but mentions that he would like to reduce the risk of developing impotence as a result of therapy.
items.explanation: Brachytherapy provides curative treatment with lower sexual side effects.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of poor stream and dribbling at the end of micturition, which is bothering him. He is found to have smooth prostatic enlargement on digital rectal examination. His PSA is 7.5 ng/mL.
items.explanation: Finasteride reduces prostate volume and improves BPH symptoms.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man who has benign prostatic hyperplasia has been treated with finasteride for over a year. He presents to the clinic because he has found no benefit in his symptoms since being started on medical management.
items.explanation: TURP is indicated when medical therapy fails for BPH.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with blunt trauma and macroscopic haematuria, stable vitals, normal abdominal and PR exam.
items.explanation: CT scan is the investigation of choice for stable blunt renal trauma with haematuria.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with acute suprapubic pain and inability to pass urine; bladder palpable 6 cm above pubis.
items.explanation: Bladder scan and catheterisation manage acute urinary retention.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man after pelvic trauma with blood at the urethral meatus and inability to void.
items.explanation: Anterograde urethrogram evaluates suspected urethral injury with meatal blood.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with left loin pain radiating to groin and 6 mm stone at VUJ causing hydronephrosis on CT.
items.explanation: Cystoscopy with retrograde stent relieves obstructing ureteric stone.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with PSA 14.0 ng/mL, asymptomatic, DRE shows enlarged, hard, irregular prostate.
items.explanation: Transrectal ultrasound and biopsy confirm prostate cancer.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with left-sided loin pain, fever and rigors. On examination, there is a palpable mass on the left side. Her pulse is 106/min and her blood pressure 104/64 mmHg. A KUB film done in the emergency department shows a 7 mm stone at the vesicoureteric junction.
items.explanation: Nephrostomy decompresses infected obstructing stones.

items.stem: A 56-year-old male who has a 3-day history of frank haematuria presents with sudden-onset suprapubic discomfort and an inability to pass urine.
items.explanation: Free-way catheter and irrigation relieve retention with haematuria.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe right loin pain that radiates to the groin. On examination, there is microscopic haematuria on dipstick but no other abnormality. A KUB X-ray confirms the presence of a 4 mm stone in the ureter.
items.explanation: Analgesia is sufficient for small ureteric stones.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man presents with loin-to-groin pain. An intravenous urogram shows a 1 cm stone in the renal collecting system.
items.explanation: ESWL fragments a 1 cm renal calculus.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of left loin pain. Examination yields no abnormality. A KUB X-ray demonstrates a staghorn calculus in the left renal collecting system. A DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan shows a split function of 10% in the left kidney and 90% in the right.
items.explanation: Nephrectomy is indicated for a poorly functioning staghorn kidney.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with suprapubic pain and a sudden inability to pass urine. On examination, there is a palpable suprapubic mass that is dull to percussion. A bladder scan demonstrates 750 mL in the bladder.
items.explanation: Urethral catheterization decompresses the bladder in acute retention.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with suprapubic pain and a sudden inability to pass urine. On examination, there is a palpable suprapubic mass that is dull to percussion. This was preceded by a 4-week history of passage of frank haematuria, including the occasional clot. Three failed attempts have been made at urethral catheterization.
items.explanation: Cystoscopy evaluates urethral obstruction after failed catheter attempts.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with suprapubic pain and a sudden inability to pass urine. On examination, there is a palpable suprapubic mass that is dull to percussion. There is no significant past medical or surgical history. Three failed attempts have been made at urethral catheterization.
items.explanation: Suprapubic catheterization is indicated when urethral catheterization fails.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with suprapubic pain and a sudden inability to pass urine. On examination, there is a palpable suprapubic mass that is dull to percussion. A urethral catheter is passed successfully and a 500 mL residual volume is recorded. You see the patient the next day on the ward round, and he asks you what will happen next.
items.explanation: Trial without catheter assesses return of normal voiding after decompression.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with a history of overflow incontinence. He does not complain of any pain and is still able to empty his bladder, although this takes some time and there is dribbling at the end of the stream. On examination, the bladder is palpable 5 fingerbreadths above the pubis.
items.explanation: Checking urea and electrolytes evaluates renal function in chronic retention.

options: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder

items.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with sudden-onset back pain that occurred while walking. He has been having difficulty passing urine over the past few months and admits to terminal dribbling. On examination, there is dullness to percussion in the suprapubic region.
items.explanation: Prostate carcinoma causes obstruction and back pain.

items.stem: An 18-year-old woman presents with a 24-hour history of burning sensation on micturition. She has also been passing water more frequently than usual. On examination, she is tender suprapubically, but there is no tenderness in either renal angle.
items.explanation: Acute cystitis presents with dysuria and frequency.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with malaise and a long history of difficulty in voiding urine. Abdominal examination is normal except for a suprapubic mass that is dull to percussion. A per rectum exam reveals a large, smooth prostate gland.
items.explanation: BPH leads to bladder outlet obstruction and retention.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with difficulty voiding and a weak stream. He had similar symptoms 6 years ago, and the underlying cause was found to be benign prostatic hyperplasia, for which he had a transurethral resection of the prostate. Abdominal examination was normal and per rectum examination demonstrated no mass.
items.explanation: Bladder neck stenosis is a complication of TURP.

items.stem: A 12-month-old boy is brought to the general practice by his mother with irritability, fever and occasional blood in the nappy. On examination, a large mass is felt on the left side of the abdomen. The child has dropped two centile lines for weight and height over the last 6 months.
items.explanation: Nephroblastoma presents as abdominal mass and hematuria.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department after being hit by a reversing car. He has an episode of macroscopic haematuria, but abdominal and per rectum examinations show no other abnormality. His blood pressure is 114/74 mmHg and his pulse 86/min.
items.explanation: CT scan is the investigation of choice in a young trauma patient with hematuria because it gives detailed cross‐sectional images of the kidneys and retroperitoneum to detect renal lacerations or vascular injuries.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man presents with acute-onset suprapubic pain and an inability to pass urine. On examination, he is visibly uncomfortable and the bladder is percussable 6 cm above the pubis.
items.explanation: Bladder scan and urethral catheterisation are used when an elderly man presents with a palpable bladder and retention; the scan confirms bladder distension and catheterisation relieves the obstruction.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man was cycling home when his bike skidded on ice and he crashed into a post box. On admission to the emergency department, he has complained of an inability to pass urine and on examination there is blood at the external urethral meatus.
items.explanation: An anterograde urethrogram is performed in a patient with blood at the external urethral meatus after trauma to delineate the site and extent of a suspected urethral injury.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man presents with sudden-onset left loin pain that radiates to his groin. He has been unable to pass urine over the last 24 hours. He has a history of a right nephrectomy for a renal cell carcinoma. A spiral CT scan confirms the presence of a 6 mm stone at the left vesicoureteric junction and a left hydronephrosis.
items.explanation: Cystoscopy with retrograde ureteric stenting is indicated in a patient with a solitary kidney and obstructive uropathy from a stone at the vesicoureteric junction to promptly relieve the obstruction and protect renal function.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man is referred to the clinic by his general practitioner with a prostate-specific antigen level of 14.0 ng/mL. He has no other symptoms. Abdominal examination shows no abnormality, but an enlarged, hard, irregular prostate gland is palpable per rectum.
items.explanation: Transrectal ultrasound and biopsy is the gold standard for evaluating suspected prostate cancer in a patient with an elevated PSA and an abnormal digital rectal exam.

options: Torsion of the hydatid of Morgagni

items.stem: A 23-year-old man has a firm, painless irregular mass in his right testicle which has enlarged over 4 months.
items.explanation: Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours peak in men aged 20–30, whereas seminomas occur in older men.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has a non-tender, fluctuant scrotal mass which causes discomfort when he wears tight pants. The scrotum transilluminates and the testis is not palpable.
items.explanation: Hydrocoeles are fluctuant, transilluminating scrotal masses in which the testis is not separately palpable.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has an intermittent lump in his left scrotum which is associated with groin discomfort. It is not possible to feel the upper limit of the mass within the scrotum.
items.explanation: Inguinal hernias are intermittent, reducible masses; the examiner cannot get above the mass.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man notices a 1cm diameter lump in his scrotum which on examination is adjacent to, but feels separate from, the testicle.
items.explanation: Epididymal cysts are retention cysts adjacent to but separate from the testicle.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has an acutely tender mass in the right side of his scrotum which has been associated with episodic dysuria during the previous 6 months. He is tender to testicular palpation and there is a mass adjacent to and apparently involving the testicle.
items.explanation: Epididymo-orchitis presents with an inflammatory mass, tenderness, and urinary symptoms.

options: Torsion of the hydatid of Morgagni

items.stem: A 28-year-old man has scrotal pain in both testes, associated with a purulent urethral discharge. The pain is made marginally more comfortable by a scrotal support.
A 16-year-old boy with maldescent of the testicle has sudden onset of right testicular pain. On palpation the testicle is in a high-lying position in the scrotum.
A 22-year-old man develops sudden onset of testicular pain. On transillumination of the scrotum there is the appearance of a localized dark region adjacent to the testicle.
A 13-year-old boy has pain and swelling in his scrotum 24 h after being hit by a cricket ball.
A 12-year-old boy with neck swelling develops a unilateral swollen tender testicle.

unparsed: Epididymo-orchitis which may have occurred in association with a sexu- ally transmitted infection or urinary tract infection. Relief of pain on scrotal elevation is Prehn’s sign, distinguishing this condition from testicu- lar torsion, although this is an inferior test compared to Doppler assess- ment of blood flow for the latter condition.
Testicular torsion which is associated with a high transverse
(‘bell-clapper’) lie.
Torted hydatid of Morgagni. The ‘blue dot sign’ is pathognomonic (when
it occurs). The appendage is excised at scrotal exploration.
Scrotal haematoma. An ultrasound scan may be undertaken to deter- mine the extent of any underlying testicular injury but this will be painful.
Mumps orchitis. One-third of male adolescents with mumps develop orchitis, which is unilateral in 80%. In a third of these patients testes atrophy.

items.stem: A 35-year-old motorcyclist with bilateral fractured femurs has haematuria following a road traffic collision. There is blood at the penile meatus and a high-riding prostate on rectal examination.
Painless haematuria, with frequency of micturition, in a 28-year-old man who spent 4 months trekking in Tanzania and Rwanda 1 year ago. FBC reveals an eosinophilia.
Haematuria, weight loss, and mild renal angle tenderness in a 55-year-old woman with recent onset of back pain and white cell count of 5 × 10^9/L.

A 45-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and a history of recurrent urinary tract infections has microscopic haematuria, loin pain, and tenderness of the renal angle. Her temperature is 38.2 °C and white cell count is 21 × 10^9/L.
A 55-year-old man develops sudden onset of severe colicky left loin pain radiating to the groin. Treatment with NSAIDs and drinking several glasses of water appears to relieve the pain overnight.

unparsed: A
This suggests pelvic fracture which may be associated with disruption of
the urethra. Great care should be taken in catheterizing the patient so as
not to risk further urethral damage.
I
In this case the patient may have been infected by *Schistosoma haematobium*,
which can be acquired even after short exposure such as swimming
in freshwater lakes in Africa. Fork-tailed cercariae are liberated from the
intermediate host, a species of freshwater snail. They penetrate the skin
or mucus membranes of humans, the definitive host, forming schistosomulae
which pass to lungs and liver and thence to the portal vein, before
the mature worms migrate to the venules draining the pelvic viscera.
Painless haematuria is the first and most common symptom. Frequency
occurs due to later bladder neck obstruction.
G
Haematogenous metastases to lungs and bone may cause respiratory
symptoms, bone pain, or pathological fractures.
F
The renal pelvis is inflamed and there may be small abscesses in the renal
parenchyma. This is usually caused by organisms moving in a retrograde
direction from the bladder. Differentiation from a perinephric abscess
and to exclude obstruction should be made by early renal ultrasound
as soon as possible. Adequate fluid administration and antibiotics are
indicated.
G
This is probably an episode of renal colic which has resolved following
passage of a small stone.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man presents with a 5-year history of a poor flow, hesitancy, frequency, nocturia and postmicturition dribbling. A flow rate showed a Qmax of 7 mL/s with a voided volume of 270 mL and a residual of 100 mL.

A 40-year-old woman presents with urinary incontinence when coughing, sneezing and during her fitness class. She has had three children delivered vaginally. The first labour was prolonged and she had a repair of a second-degree tear.

A 16-year-old man presents with a long history of hesitancy and worsening urinary stream. He also complains of postmicturition dribbling, which may occur some minutes after he completes his normal void. He had a significant fall astride a bar injury as a child.
A 40-year-old woman presents with urinary frequency, urgency and episodes of urge incontinence. She had a transient episode of unilateral blindness 2 years prior.
A 40-year-old man has a long history of intermittent low back pain but develops acute onset of difficulty passing urine. On examination he has a palpable bladder and an area of saddle anaesthesia.
items.explanation: BPH (B) often presents with slow stream, hesitancy, frequency, incomplete emptying. - Stress incontinence (I) is loss of urine with coughing or exercise. - Urethral stricture (J) may follow trauma (fall astride) or infection. - MS (E) can cause frequency, urgency, urge incontinence. - Prolapsed disc (F) can cause cauda equina syndrome with retention, saddle anaesthesia.

options: Abdominal X-ray of kidneys, ureters and bladder (KUB)

items.stem: A patient presenting with dysuria and frequency. Routine observations reveal a temperature of 38.6°C.
A 25-year-old long-distance runner presenting with severe right-sided loin pain and vomiting.
items.explanation: Abdominal X-ray KUB.

items.stem: A middle-aged man presenting with urinary hesitancy, a poor stream and terminal dribbling postmicturition with evidence of renal dysfunction.
A 75-year-old man presenting with urinary frequency, nocturia and weight loss. An irregular mass is evident on the prostate on digital examination.
A middle-aged female who has had five vaginal deliveries presenting with urinary leakage when coughing or laughing.
items.explanation: Urine dipstick (A) is first-line for suspected UTI. - KUB X-ray (H) can detect radio-opaque renal stones in flank pain. - Renal ultrasound (D) looks for hydronephrosis and residual volume in obstruction. - PSA (C) is used to investigate possible prostate cancer. - Urodynamic studies (G) diagnose stress/urge incontinence.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man presents with a firm, nontender lump in his right testicle.

A 23-year-old woman presents with right-sided loin pain which radiates to the groin. The pain comes and goes in waves. She also complains of frequency of micturition. Dipstick urine test reveals 4+ blood. The only abnormality on examination is tenderness in the right loin.

An 88-year-old man presents via his GP with suprapubic pain and a history of frequency and passing only very small amounts of urine for 1 week. He has had long-standing problems with nocturia and poor stream. He has a tender palpable mass arising from the pelvis. His PSA is 5 ng/mL (NR 0-4 ng/mL).
A 52-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and frequency and a gradual onset of left testicular pain and swelling. Dipstick urine reveals 3+ blood, 2+ leukocytes and nitrites.
items.explanation: Testicular teratoma (I) is a painless, firm testicular lump in a young man. - Ureteric colic (K) presents with colicky flank-to-groin pain, haematuria. - BPH (A) can cause acute on chronic retention with palpable bladder. - Epididymitis (C) is gradual onset scrotal pain, often with UTI findings.

stem: Regarding trauma, which of the following statements is true? (Non-accidental injuries (NAI))
options: It is the fifth most common cause of death overall.
It is the second most common cause of death and disability below 40 years of age.
One-year mortality following a proximal femoral fracture in patients over 65 years is 30%.
Trauma is predominantly secondary to high-energy injuries.
Less than 25% of children who die of abuse have had previous contact with health or social services.
explanation: %. A proximal femoral fracture in the elderly carries a high one-year mortality rate.
_raw_ans: 1. C. One-year mortality following a proximal femoral fracture in patients over 65 years is 30%. A proximal femoral fracture in the elderly carries a high one-year mortality rate.

stem: Regarding trauma assessment, which of the following statements is false?
options: The patient, mechanism of injury, and injury are the keystones of management.
It is as essential to identify obvious injuries as it is to identify the occult (hidden) injuries.
High-velocity bullet injuries are associated with cavity formation.
Blunt injuries can be direct (impact) or indirect (force transmission).
Knife injury over a limb is easy to evaluate.
explanation: Knife injuries may be deceptively complex despite an unassuming appearance.
_raw_ans: 2. E. Knife injury over a limb is easy to evaluate. Knife injuries may be deceptively complex despite an unassuming appearance.

stem: In relation to blunt injuries, which of the following statements is false?
options: The mechanisms are direct or indirect.
In indirect injury, associated injuries may be present and should be sought.
In chest injuries, damage to abdominal organs is rare.
Overt injury should lead the clinician to
explanation: Blunt chest trauma can injure abdominal organs due to force transmission across the diaphragm.
_raw_ans: 3. C. In chest injuries, damage to abdominal organs is rare. Blunt chest trauma can injure abdominal organs due to force transmission across the diaphragm.

stem: In relation to covert injuries, which of the following statements is true?
options: A deductive approach is not necessary.
A look-everywhere approach is not helpful.
A focused approach that limits the scope of your assessment is not useful.
Head to pelvis CT is part of a look-everywhere approach.
Screen patients where clinical signs are obvious.
explanation: A comprehensive CT from head to pelvis aids in detecting hidden injuries.
_raw_ans: 4. D. Head to pelvis CT is part of a look-everywhere approach. A comprehensive CT from head to pelvis aids in detecting hidden injuries.

stem: In relation to covert injuries, which of the following statements is false?
options: Electrocution = burn (obvious) and posterior dislocation of the shoulder (covert).
Dashboard = patella fracture (obvious) and posterior dislocation of the hip (covert).
Inhalational injury = facial burns (obvious) and laryngeal oedema (covert).
Left-side impact RTA = left pneumothorax with chest wall contusions (obvious) and liver laceration (covert).
Flexion-distraction = head injury (obvious) and cervical spine fracture (covert).
explanation: Left-side impact typically causes splenic rather than liver injury.
_raw_ans: 5. D. Left-side impact RTA = left pneumothorax with chest wall contusions (obvious) and liver laceration (covert). Left-side impact typically causes splenic rather than liver injury.

stem: In relation to NAI in children, which of the following statements is false?
options: History is inconsistent with the injury sustained.
There are likely to be injuries of differing ages or duration.
There may be aggressive behaviour from the carers.
A femoral shaft fracture in a 6-month-old is not suspicious of NAI.
explanation: Femoral shaft fractures in non‐ambulatory infants are highly suspicious for non-accidental injury.
_raw_ans: 6. E. A femoral shaft fracture in a 6-month-old is not suspicious of NAI. Femoral shaft fractures in non‐ambulatory infants are highly suspicious for non-accidental injury.

stem: Which of the following statements is false with regard to a polytrauma patient?
options: A drop in body temperature occurs.
There is a generalised immune response.
The patient has compensatory mechanisms to blood loss.
Diversion from protocol should be avoided.
explanation: Sometimes clinical judgment requires deviation from rigid protocols in polytrauma care.
_raw_ans: 7. E. Diversion from protocol should be avoided. Sometimes clinical judgment requires deviation from rigid protocols in polytrauma care.

stem: Regarding mechanisms of trauma, which of the following statements is false?
options: The most common cause of blunt trauma is a motor vehicle accident (MVA).
A 10% increase in impact speed equates to a ~40% increase in pedestrian fatality.
Seat belts reduce the risk of death or serious injury for front-seat occupants by ~20%.
For head-on collisions, airbags reduce the risk of fatality by ~30%.
Motorcyclists have a higher rate of mortality than car occupants involved in a MVA.
explanation: %. The protective effect of seat belts is greater than the stated 20%, making option C false.
_raw_ans: 8. C. Seat belts reduce the risk of death or serious injury for front-seat occupants by ~20%. The protective effect of seat belts is greater than the stated 20%, making option C false.

stem: Regarding airway assessment, which of the following statements is false?
options: If the patient is talking, he or she does not have an imminently compromised airway.
Suction of the airway may be required.
Nasopharyngeal and Guedal airways are useful adjuncts.
GCS of 7 is not an indication for a definitive airway.
Cervical spine control is required throughout airway assessment.
explanation: A GCS of 7 is not an indication for a definitive airway. A GCS of 7 indicates the need for definitive airway management.
_raw_ans: 9. D. A GCS of 7 is not an indication for a definitive airway. A GCS of 7 indicates the need for definitive airway management.

stem: Regarding assessing disability, which of the following can be responsible for a reduced consciousness level?
explanation: Head injury, hypovolaemia, hypoglycaemia, and alcohol can all lower consciousness.
_raw_ans: 10. E. All of the above. Head injury, hypovolaemia, hypoglycaemia, and alcohol can all lower consciousness.

stem: Which of the following are not routine adjuncts to the primary survey?
options: Bloods including FBC, U&Es, clotting screen and glucose
Radiographs of the C-spine, chest and pelvis
explanation: CT imaging is not part of the immediate primary survey.
_raw_ans: 11. E. CT with or without angiography. CT imaging is not part of the immediate primary survey.

stem: Regarding the secondary survey, which of the following is not part of the AMPLE assessment?
explanation: Pain assessment is important clinically but not part of the AMPLE mnemonic.
_raw_ans: 12. C. Pain assessment. Pain assessment is important clinically but not part of the AMPLE mnemonic.

stem: Regarding paediatric trauma, which of the following combination of observations is optimal for a preschool child (<5 years)?

Pulse 160 bpm, SBP 90, RR 40, UO 1 mL/kg/hour
Pulse 140 bpm, SBP 80, RR 30, UO 1 mL/kg/hour
Pulse 140 bpm, SBP 90, RR 40, UO 1.5 mL/kg/hour
Pulse 140 bpm, SBP 90, RR 30, UO 1.5 mL/kg/hour
explanation: These vital signs fall within the normal range for preschool children.

stem: Regarding to Hazards of imaging and radiation Which of the following statements are true?
options: Low-osmolality contrast media (LOCM) are safer than their higher-osmolality counterparts.
Routine steroid prophylaxis is recommended before use of contrast in the high-risk patient.
In the diabetic, metformin should be stopped before using contrast.
The majority of ionising radiation comes from medical exposure from investigations.
Radionuclide imaging allows function to be studied.
explanation: LOCM have a better safety profile and radionuclide imaging assesses function; the other statements are incorrect.

stem: Regarding to Diagnostic imaging Which of the following statements is false?
options: Conventional x-rays will delineate different soft tissue reliably.
Dedicated transducers can help in endocavitary ultrasound (US).
Change in the frequency of an US wave can be caused by red blood cells.
The higher the frequency of the US wave, the greater the resolution of the image.
explanation: Plain radiographs do not reliably differentiate soft tissues.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?

stem: Regarding to Orthopaedic imaging Which of the following statements is false?
options: Synovitis can be detected by plain x-ray.

stem: Regarding to Imaging in trauma Which of the following statements are false?

stem: About Wound closure The following statements are true except:
options: Mass closure technique is the usual method used for abdominal wall.
Sutures lose 50% of their tensile strength at the knot.

explanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) is the leading cause of toxin-related death in the United States. Tobacco smoke—particularly smoke released from the tip of the cigarette, which has 2.5 times more CO than inhaled smoke—produces a significant amount of the gas; nonsmokers working in closed quarters with smokers may have carboxyhemoglobin levels as high as 15%, easily enough to cause headache and some impairment of judgment. Firefighters are at particularly high risk for CO intoxication. The pathophysiology of CO poisoning is unclear. It is known to cause an adverse shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, to cause direct cardiovascular depression, and to inhibit cytochrome a3 within the electric transport chain (thereby hindering ATP production). Tissue hypoxia is the result. Treatment is directed toward increasing the partial pressures of O2 to which the transalveolar hemoglobin is exposed. In most cases, administering 100% oxygen through a tightly fitted face mask will result in a serum elimination half-life of COHb of 80 minutes (compared with 520 minutes when breathing room air). In severe cases, where coma, seizures, or respiratory failure are present, the partial pressure of O2 is increased by administering it in a hyperbaric chamber with an atmospheric pressure of 2.8. In this situation, the serum elimination half-life is reduced to 23 minutes. In any case, the oxygen therapy should continue until the COHb levels reach 10%. Methylene blue is the treatment for methemoglobinemia, not carboxyhemoglobinemia.

Treatment of cardiac dysfunction includes maintenance of adequate oxygenation and judicious fluid administration to avoid fluid overload and development of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. The elevated central venous pressure (suggesting volume overload) argues against hemorrhagic or septic shock but is consistent with cardiogenic shock. The echocardiogram findings are not consistent with cardiac tamponade; the classic finding with tamponade is right atrial collapse at end-diastole (during atrial relaxation) due to the increased pericardial pressure. The echocardiogram findings are also not consistent with a pulmonary embolism of the main pulmonary artery trunk; this would present with right ventricular strain. The echocardiogram findings of a hypokinetic left ventricle are most consistent with cardiogenic shock, possibly from an acute myocardial infarction.

items.stem: 39-year-old male has a moderate-grade fever after one day from incisional hernia repair. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry over the right lower lobe. CXR shows right lower lobe collapse.

46-year-old female with a BMI of 51 underwent complicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy. 7 days post-op she developed SOB, tachycardia, and undetectable BP. ECG shows changes consistent with right ventricular strain.

A 37-year-old male underwent exploratory laparotomy for a bullet injury in the abdomen. The wound was initially healing well, but upon examination, it is observed that the surgical incision has separated and the underlying tissues are exposed.

A lady underwent sleeve gastrectomy 2 days earlier. She presents with tachycardia and tachypnea. Chest examination is normal. Abdominal examination shows mild epigastric tenderness but a normal-looking laparoscopic incision. Gastrografin meal shows contrast leak from the gastrojejunostomy.

A patient presents following a fall from a third-story window and on primary survey is not maintaining adequate oxygen saturation on high-flow oxygen, is hypotensive, has a raised JVP with left tracheal deviation and the right hemi-thorax is hyper-resonant with no air entry.
items.explanation: This is a classic presentation of a right-sided tension pneumothorax. The hallmark signs include hypoxia, hypotension, raised JVP, tracheal deviation away from the affected side (to the left), hyper-resonance, and absence of breath sounds. These findings occur due to trapped air creating a one-way valve effect, compressing intrathoracic structures and impairing venous return. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate needle decompression in the second intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, followed by chest drain insertion.

items.stem: A patient with a background of known alcohol excess presents with minor abrasions to the arms but no evidence of head injury. Chest is clear and heart sounds are normal. There is a reduced GCS 9/15 (E3, V2, M4) but no evidence of haemodynamic instability. Pupils are equal and reactive.
items.explanation: A reduced GCS without any obvious traumatic cause or haemodynamic instability in a patient with alcohol excess points toward hypoglycaemia. Chronic alcohol use can impair gluconeogenesis, especially in the context of poor nutrition. Hypoglycaemia is a critical and reversible cause of altered consciousness and must always be considered early in the primary survey (the “D” of ABCDE: Disability). Rapid glucose administration is essential in management.

items.stem: A patient presents with evidence of significant deep penetrating trauma at the level of the fifth/sixth intercostal space in left hemi-thorax. The patient has a raised JVP and muffled heart sounds, and is haemodynamically unstable with a tachycardia and hypotension.
items.explanation: This presentation aligns with Beck’s triad: hypotension, raised JVP, and muffled heart sounds—indicating cardiac tamponade. The trauma location (left 5th–6th intercostal space) is in close proximity to the heart. Accumulation of blood or fluid in the pericardial sac impairs ventricular filling, leading to reduced cardiac output and haemodynamic instability. Immediate pericardiocentesis is required to relieve pressure and restore circulation.

theme: Types of Shock and Blood Transfusion

options: Anaphylactic shock  B.Autologous blood transfusion  C. Cardiogenic shock  D. Hypovolaemic shock  E. Mismatched blood transfusion  F. Neurogenic shock  G. Septic shock

items.stem: A 50-year-old man is undergoing partial hepatectomy for secondary metastasis. The operation proceeded smoothly for the first couple of hours, after which the surgical team noticed unusual bleeding in the form of oozing from all the wound sites. The patient has two intravenous cannula sites through one of which he is on his first unit of blood.
items.explanation: E. Mismatched blood transfusion – Diffuse oozing during first unit of transfusion indicates an acute hemolytic reaction with DIC.

items.stem: A fit 30-year-old woman while gardening suddenly became very short of breath, had intense itching with rash and complained of a painful red spot on her arm. She has been brought to the A&E department and is hypotensive, hypoxic with warm peripheries.
items.explanation: Anaphylactic shock – Sudden dyspnea, rash, and hypotension after an insect sting is classic anaphylaxis.

items.stem: A fit 25-year-old man fell from a height of 40 feet at a building site. He has been brought in unconscious with a GCS of 13 and flaccid limbs. He has been immobilised in a spinal frame and has an intravenous line.
items.explanation: F. Neurogenic shock – High spinal injury with flaccid limbs and hypotension results from loss of sympathetic tone.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man of ASA anaesthetic category 3, underwent an emergency closure of a perforated duodenal ulcer. The anaesthetic and operation were uneventful. On the first postoperative day, he complained of feeling very unwell with a systolic blood pressure of 80 mm Hg with no unusual signs in his abdomen; there was impaired conscious level and peripheral vasoconstriction.
items.explanation: C. Cardiogenic shock – Post-operative hypotension with poor perfusion in a high-risk patient suggests acute pump failure.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man of ASA 1 anaesthetic risk underwent a total gastrectomy for stomach cancer. While in the ITU, 12 hours postoperatively, his BP has fallen to 80 mm Hg systolic, he has not put out any urine over the past 3 hours and he is hypoxic with oxygen saturation of 92%.
items.explanation: D. Hypovolaemic shock – Falling blood pressure, anuria, and hypoxia after major surgery point to volume loss.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has been admitted as an emergency with a 4-day history of severe right upper quadrant pain, vomiting, jaundice and intense pruritus and is very toxic - high temperature with rigors and hyperdynamic circulation.
items.explanation: G. Septic shock – Ascending cholangitis with fever, rigors, and hyperdynamic circulation leads to sepsis-induced shock.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman is due for a bilateral mastectomy. She has requested a bilateral breast reconstruction at the same time. However, she is a strict Jehovah’s Witness and would under no circumstances have a heterologous blood transfusion.
items.explanation: B. Autologous blood transfusion – A Jehovah’s Witness refusing donor blood can receive only her own pre-donated blood.
